ui.faqIntro: Straight answers about travelling with AussieCamps.
ui.faq1a: AussieCamps is an iPhone app for finding places to camp and stay around Australia. It bundles a directory of 74,000+ places so the details stay readable without reception, and it turns the ones you save into a road trip with an ordered route, dates, notes and to-dos.
ui.faq2a: More than 74,000 places: campgrounds, caravan parks, roofed accommodation, farm and station stays, backpacker hostels, roadside rest areas, day-use areas, dump points, potable water, laundromats, information centres, long-vehicle parking, experiences and other useful stops.
ui.faq3a: The place directory is bundled with the app, so names, categories, descriptions, fees, amenities, opening hours and conditions stay readable well beyond signal. Live services such as weather, routing, Street View, photos and provider pages still need a connection.
ui.faq4q: Can I plan a multi-stop road trip?
ui.faq4a: Yes, and it is the app's main feature. Add places as stops, drag them into order, attach a date and arrival notes to each one, see the driving distance leg by leg and across the whole trip, open directions to the next stop, check the weather at each one, tick stops off as visited and keep the packing list beside the itinerary. Itinerary details can sync to Calendar.
ui.faq5a: Two kinds. Smart collections (Liked, Starred, Want to visit, Visited, Pins and All saved) fill themselves as you mark places. On top of those you can create your own named collections with an icon and notes for a region, a season, a vehicle or a shortlist.
ui.faq6q: Can I filter for free camps or caravan access?
ui.faq6a: Yes, and combinations of them. Filters cover category, fee type, minimum rating, online booking, state or territory, and detailed feature groups for access, amenities, activities, services and affiliations, so “free camping areas with toilets and drinking water in Queensland” is a single query.
ui.faq7q: What is on a place screen?
ui.faq7a: Photos, a description, opening hours, fees, terms and conditions, amenities and features grouped by type, current alerts, ratings, contact and booking details, weather, Street View where coverage exists, directions, and nearby alternatives.
ui.faq8a: A standard map and a satellite view built on Apple's flyover imagery, which you can tilt and rotate for real 3D terrain. Street View, built on Apple's Look Around imagery, gives the street-level view from the place screen.
ui.faq9q: Can I see prices in my own currency?
ui.faq9a: Yes. Choose your currency in settings and set the conversion rate, and reported fees are shown in that currency alongside the Australian dollar figure.
ui.faq10q: Can I book a campsite in AussieCamps?
ui.faq10a: Open the booking details for a place to reach its provider and check live availability, prices and terms.
ui.faq11q: Are camping rules the same across Australia?
ui.faq11a: No. Rules vary by state, territory, council, park and individual site. Always follow current signs, land-manager conditions, fire restrictions and official alerts.

fuel-cost-calculator.metaTitle: Road Trip Fuel Cost Calculator Australia
fuel-cost-calculator.metaDescription: Work out petrol or diesel for an Australian road trip from distance, L/100 km and price per litre. Shows litres, total cost and cost per km, with the formula and a worked example.
fuel-cost-calculator.title: Road trip fuel cost calculator for Australia
fuel-cost-calculator.intro: Enter the distance, your vehicle’s loaded fuel use and the price per litre. You get the litres the drive will burn, the fuel bill and the cost per kilometre, so the whole route can be budgeted before the first fill.
formula: Fuel cost = litres × price per litre (A$/L)
Cost per km = fuel cost ÷ distance
fuel-cost-calculator.formulaNote: The calculator rounds litres to one decimal place and money to the cent. Nothing else is added: tolls, oil and tyre wear are separate lines in a budget.
example: A 1,000 km drive in a vehicle using 12 L/100 km at A$2.08 a litre, the petrol average across the five largest cities in Fuel Plan data for 5 August 2026.
The same drive in a diesel vehicle at that day’s diesel average of A$2.47 a litre costs 120 × A$2.47 = A$296.40.
assumptions: Fuel use is the loaded figure. A campervan, a roof load or a caravan on the back burns more than the brochure number, so measure your own if you can.
City averages are a starting point. Remote roadhouses usually charge more, so raise the price for outback legs.
Distance is the whole route, including the detours to campgrounds, lookouts and towns off the highway.
faq: How do I find my vehicle’s real fuel use?

Fill the tank, reset the trip meter and drive as you normally would. At the next fill, divide the litres added by the kilometres driven and multiply by 100. That is your L/100 km for the vehicle as loaded, which is the number this calculator needs.
How do I work out fuel cost per km?
Divide L/100 km by 100 and multiply by the price per litre. At 12 L/100 km and A$2.08 a litre that is 0.12 × 2.08, about A$0.25 a kilometre.
Which fuel price should I use?

Use the fuel your vehicle takes and the most recent price you can find for the region. Fuel Plan’s five-city averages for 5 August 2026 were A$2.08 a litre for petrol and A$2.47 for diesel; expect more in remote areas.
fuel-cost-calculator.ctaText: AussieCamps maps {restAreas} rest areas and {dumpPoints} dump points across Australia and turns saved places into a multi-stop route with distances.

drive-time-calculator.metaTitle: Driving Time Calculator Australia: Real Road Trip Days
drive-time-calculator.metaDescription: Estimate how long an Australian driving day really takes from distance, road type and stops. Shows the average speeds used, the formula and a worked example.
drive-time-calculator.title: Driving time calculator for Australian road trips
drive-time-calculator.intro: Maps apps quote moving time on a clear road. This calculator plans the day you will actually drive: an average speed for the kind of road, plus the time spent stopped for fuel, food and breaks.
formula: Average speeds: 85 km/h motorway or open straight, 70 km/h main highway, 60 km/h winding or coastal, 45 km/h narrow, steep or gravel
drive-time-calculator.formulaNote: The speeds are planning averages that allow for towns, roadworks, slow vehicles and overtaking lanes. They are not speed limits.
example: A 250 km day on a winding coastal road with three stops.
250 ÷ 60 × 60 = 250 minutes of driving. Three stops add 3 × 20 = 60 minutes.
The day takes 310 minutes, or 5 h 10 min. On a main highway at 70 km/h the same distance and stops take 4 h 34 min.
assumptions: Each stop counts as 20 minutes: a fuel stop, a meal, a toilet break or a driver change.
Night driving is not planned for. Wildlife is most active around dawn and dusk, so aim to arrive before dark.
Unsealed roads vary with the weather and the season. Check conditions with the state road authority before a gravel leg.
faq: Why is the result longer than my maps app?
Navigation apps estimate moving time close to the posted limits. This calculator adds the road character and the time you spend stopped, which is where a long day usually runs over.
Which road type should I choose for a campervan?

Use main highway for most sealed national highways, winding or coastal for hilly and coastal routes, and narrow, steep or gravel for unsealed roads and mountain passes. A heavy campervan or a caravan on a climb is slower again.
Does the result include fuel and meal stops?
Only the stops you enter. Add one for each refuel, meal or break you expect; each one adds 20 minutes to the day.
drive-time-calculator.ctaTitle: Know where the day ends before you start it.
drive-time-calculator.ctaText: AussieCamps maps {campgrounds} campgrounds and {restAreas} rest areas, and builds a multi-stop route with the driving distance between stops.

campsite-cost-calculator.metaTitle: Campsite Cost Calculator: Per Person vs Per Site
campsite-cost-calculator.metaDescription: Compare a campsite fee charged per adult with one charged per site for your party and nights. Shows the break-even party size, the formula and a worked example in AUD.
campsite-cost-calculator.title: Campsite cost calculator: per person or per site?
campsite-cost-calculator.intro: Some campgrounds charge per adult per night and others price the whole site. Which one is cheaper depends on how many adults are in your party, so this calculator prices both for the same stay.
formula: Per-adult total = adults × nights × fee per adult
Per-site total = nights × fee per site
Break-even party size = fee per site ÷ fee per adult
campsite-cost-calculator.formulaNote: Above the break-even number of adults the per-site price is cheaper; below it the per-adult price is cheaper.
example: Two adults staying five nights, comparing A$20 per adult per night with A$50 per site per night.
Per adult: 2 × 5 × A$20 = A$200. Per site: 5 × A$50 = A$250. Per adult is A$50 cheaper.
The break-even party size is A$50 ÷ A$20 = 2.5 adults, so with three adults the per-adult total rises to A$300 and the per-site price wins.
assumptions: Children and concession holders are often charged a different rate. Enter adults only, or adjust the fee to an average.
Booking fees and park entry fees are separate. Add them to the per-site figure when comparing like with like.
The figures you enter are the only inputs; check the current fee on the official booking page.
faq: When is a per-site fee cheaper?
When the number of adults is larger than the per-site fee divided by the per-adult fee. At A$50 a site and A$20 an adult that is 2.5, so a party of three or more pays less per site.
Do national park campgrounds charge per person?
Many state park campgrounds charge per adult per night, while holiday parks usually price a site. The fee basis is set by each land manager, so read it on the official page before comparing.
campsite-cost-calculator.ctaText: AussieCamps maps {campgrounds} campgrounds with fees and facilities where the land manager lists them, and links each one to its official page.

currency-converter.metaTitle: AUD Currency Converter for Travellers (RBA Rates)
currency-converter.metaDescription: Convert Australian dollar prices to and from NZD, USD, GBP, EUR, CNY, INR, SGD, JPY and KRW using dated Reserve Bank of Australia reference rates.
currency-converter.title: Australian dollar converter for trip planning
currency-converter.intro: Convert an Australian price into the currency you think in, or the other way round. The rates are Reserve Bank of Australia reference rates with a stated date, so you know exactly what the number is based on.
formula: Converted amount = amount ÷ rate of the currency you convert from × rate of the currency you convert to
Each rate is the number of units of that currency per A$1
currency-converter.formulaNote: Converting through the Australian dollar keeps every pair consistent: NZD to USD uses the same two rates as the AUD conversions.
example: A$100 at a rate of 1.2033 NZD per Australian dollar.
Going the other way, NZ$100 ÷ 1.2033 × 1 = A$83.10.
assumptions: Reference rates are mid-market figures for planning. Banks, card networks and exchange counters add their own margin or fees.
Rates move every business day. Use the result to judge a price, not as a quote.
faq: Which exchange rates does the converter use?
Reserve Bank of Australia reference rates, shown with the date they apply to, expressed as units of each currency per Australian dollar.
Why does my bank charge a different amount?
Banks and card networks use their own rate and often add a margin or a foreign transaction fee, so the amount charged differs from a reference conversion.
currency-converter.ctaTitle: See fees in your own currency.
currency-converter.ctaText: AussieCamps shows reported fees alongside the Australian dollar figure in the currency you choose, at a conversion rate you set once.

water-tank-calculator.metaTitle: Campervan Water Tank Calculator: Days Off Grid
water-tank-calculator.metaDescription: Turn fresh and grey water tank sizes into days off grid for your party. Shows the litres per person used, the formula and a worked example for an Australian campervan trip.
water-tank-calculator.title: Campervan water tank calculator: how many days off grid?
water-tank-calculator.intro: Tank sizes in litres only become useful once they are expressed in days. Enter your fresh and grey water capacity and the number of people, and the calculator shows how long each tank lasts and which one sets your limit.
formula: Fresh water days = fresh tank (L) ÷ (people × 11 L)
Grey water days = grey tank (L) ÷ (people × 9 L)
Days off grid = whichever of the two is lower
water-tank-calculator.formulaNote: 11 litres of fresh water and 9 litres of grey water per person per day cover drinking, cooking and washing up with careful use. Showers on board use far more.
example: A campervan with a 100 L fresh tank and a 90 L grey tank, travelling with two people.
The fresh tank runs out first, after about four and a half days, so plan a refill before day five.
assumptions: The per-person figures are averages. Hot weather, cooking with water and showers raise them.
Toilet cassettes are a separate tank and are not included.
Empty grey water only where it is allowed, such as a dump point or an approved site.
faq: How much water does one person use per day in a campervan?

This calculator assumes about 11 litres of fresh water per person per day for drinking, cooking and washing up, and about 9 litres of grey water. A daily shower on board uses far more, so plan for it separately.
Which runs out first, fresh or grey water?
Whichever tank gives the lower number of days. With the same tank sizes, more people or more washing shortens both; the calculator shows the two side by side so you know which one sets the limit.
water-tank-calculator.ctaTitle: Find the next refill and dump point.
water-tank-calculator.ctaText: AussieCamps maps {water} water filling points and {dumpPoints} dump points across Australia, with the facilities each one lists.

support.title: How can we help?
support.lede: Clear answers for maps, saved places, trip planning and the road ahead.

sections.heading: Finding places
paragraphs: Use Explore to search by place name, address or description. Move the map and choose the current-area option to focus results around the visible region.

Filter by place category, fee, rating, online booking, state and detailed feature groups for access, amenities, activities and services. Combine only the filters that matter so useful alternatives remain visible.
Facilities, fees, access and management can change. Follow current signs and the land manager, then send a correction so the directory can improve.

sections.heading: Saved places
paragraphs: Liked, Visited, Want to Visit and Starred update automatically when you mark places. Pins and All Saved provide other quick views.
Create named collections with an icon and notes, then add any place. Use them for a region, season, vehicle or shortlist.
The app supports private iCloud sync for saved states, collections and trip data when iCloud is available and enabled.

sections.heading: Trip planner
paragraphs: Create a trip, add places and drag them into order. Each stop can carry its own arrival date, notes, weather and visited status, and the planner shows the driving distance leg by leg and across the whole trip.
Road routing depends on available MapKit directions. The planner retains the stops if a leg fails, but you must confirm current road access yourself.
Start with a camping essentials preset or make your own tasks. Trip progress keeps the list beside the itinerary, and itinerary details can sync to Calendar.

sections.heading: Maps, weather and live details
paragraphs: Switch between the standard map and a satellite view built on Apple's flyover imagery, which tilts and rotates into 3D terrain. Street View, built on Apple's Look Around imagery, opens from the place screen where coverage exists.
Current and forecast weather requires live data. Save critical forecasts and official warnings before leaving coverage.
The bundled place directory keeps core place details available beyond reliable signal. Live maps, routing, weather, photos and external provider pages may require reception.

sections.heading: Prices and currency
paragraphs: Choose your currency in settings and set the conversion rate. Reported fees are then shown in that currency alongside the Australian dollar figure, which helps when you are visiting and not fluent in AUD.
Open a place's booking or contact details to check availability, price and terms with the provider. Prices in the app are reported figures, not live quotes.

sections.heading: Premium and account
paragraphs: Map and place details are free, together with two saved lists.
Premium adds unlimited saved lists, trip planning, advanced filters, place weather and road trip routes.
Open the Premium screen and use Restore Purchases while signed into the Apple account used for the original transaction.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.lede: AussieCamps helps you plan a trip without turning your journey into an advertising profile.

sections.heading: Information stored on your device
paragraphs: Saved places, collection membership, trips, notes, checklist items and preferences are stored for the app to work. Location can be used to show your position and nearby places after you grant permission.

sections.heading: iCloud
paragraphs: When iCloud is available and enabled, the app can use your private iCloud database to sync saved states, collections and app records across your devices. Apple provides the underlying service and applies its own terms.

sections.heading: Live Apple services
paragraphs: Map display, directions, Look Around, weather, calendar integration and widgets may use Apple frameworks. Requests and data handling for those services are governed by Apple. Calendar access occurs only after permission and is used to add trip itinerary information you request.

sections.heading: External links and website logs
paragraphs: Place details can open booking providers, websites, social profiles, phone numbers, email addresses and map apps. Those services receive information according to their own policies when you choose to open them.
Hosting providers may process routine technical logs such as IP address, browser type and requested URL for delivery, reliability and security.

sections.heading: Website analytics
paragraphs: This website uses Google Analytics 4 to understand which pages are read and how visitors find the app. Google processes this data on our behalf as our processor. For visitors in the European Economic Area, the United Kingdom and Switzerland, the service is provided by Google Ireland Limited.

Analytics records the pages you view, your device and browser type, an approximate location derived from your IP address and the App Store links you click. Google Analytics 4 does not log or store IP addresses, and it never receives your name, your email address or anything you save in the app.

Analytics uses two first-party cookies, _ga and one whose name starts with _ga_ followed by our measurement ID, and both last up to 13 months. In the European Economic Area, the United Kingdom and Switzerland they are set only after you accept them. Until then no analytics cookie is stored and Google receives only cookieless measurements that carry no identifier. You can change your choice at any time with the Privacy choices link at the bottom of every page.
Google signals and ad personalisation are switched off, and analytics data is deleted after 14 months. This website does not use advertising trackers.

sections.heading: Retention and control
paragraphs: You can delete app records through the app and manage iCloud data through your Apple account. Removing the app can remove local data, while synced copies may remain in iCloud until separately deleted.

sections.heading: Children and contact
paragraphs: AussieCamps is a general travel utility and is not directed to children. Do not submit personal information about a child through support.
For privacy questions, contact AussieCamps support.

terms.title: Terms of use
terms.lede: AussieCamps is a planning aid. It does not replace official signs, land-manager directions, emergency warnings, road advice or your responsibility to travel within your capability.

sections.heading: Travel information changes
paragraphs: Places, prices, access, facilities, phone coverage, weather, fire conditions, roads and booking arrangements can change without notice. Verify critical details with the responsible authority or provider before travel and again close to departure.

sections.heading: No booking or access guarantee
paragraphs: A listing does not guarantee that a place is open, legal for your setup, reachable by your vehicle or available. External booking and contact links are provided for convenience. Contracts are between you and the third-party provider.

sections.heading: Safety and lawful use
paragraphs: You must obey signs, permits, closures, fire restrictions, road rules and directions from rangers, Traditional Owners, emergency services and land managers. Do not use the app while driving.

sections.heading: User data
paragraphs: You are responsible for notes, trip plans and other information you save. Keep separate copies of permits, bookings and safety-critical plans when loss of access could put a trip at risk.

sections.heading: Purchases
paragraphs: Any in-app purchase is processed by Apple and subject to the terms shown at purchase. Features, packaging and prices may change where allowed. Use Apple’s purchase tools for billing, cancellation and refund matters.

sections.heading: Intellectual property and contact
paragraphs: AussieCamps branding, interface and original editorial content belong to their respective owner. Place names and public facts remain the property or responsibility of their original sources.
Questions can be sent to AussieCamps support.

great-ocean-road-camping-guide.title: Great Ocean Road camping guide: a 3-day route
great-ocean-road-camping-guide.description: Surf beaches, rainforest bends and a final sunset over the Twelve Apostles.
great-ocean-road-camping-guide.imageAlt: Great Ocean Road coast in Victoria
great-ocean-road-camping-guide.intro: Three days gives the Great Ocean Road enough breathing room for lighthouse walks, forest detours and an evening beside the Southern Ocean. Drive west from Torquay and keep the final night near Port Campbell or Warrnambool.

sections.heading: Day 1: Torquay to Apollo Bay
body: Leave Melbourne early and make Torquay the first proper stop. Bells Beach, Point Addis and the clifftop road around Aireys Inlet are better enjoyed before the afternoon traffic builds.
Apollo Bay works well for the first night. A holiday park gives you showers, power and an easy resupply, while nearby national park camps offer a quieter base. Book summer weekends well ahead.

sections.heading: Day 2: Cape Otway and the forest
body: Turn into Great Otway National Park for tall forest, waterfalls and the Cape Otway coast. Aire River East and Aire River West are useful bases when access conditions suit your vehicle. Johanna Beach is exposed but memorable in settled weather.

Expect weak reception away from towns. Carry water, check fire restrictions and do not rely on arriving late at a small campground. Coastal wind can make a mild forecast feel much colder after sunset.

sections.heading: Day 3: Port Campbell and the western cliffs
body: Reach the Twelve Apostles early, then continue to Loch Ard Gorge and the quieter lookouts beyond Port Campbell. The scenery improves when you leave time to walk instead of collecting viewpoints through a windscreen.
Finish in Port Campbell or continue to Warrnambool for a wider choice of caravan parks, groceries and fuel. If you are returning to Melbourne, the inland highway is faster than retracing the coast.

sections.heading: Drive it westbound
body: Travelling Melbourne to Warrnambool puts you on the ocean side of the road, which matters on a route where the lookouts are almost all on the coast. Eastbound you spend the trip crossing traffic to reach every stop.

The road is narrow, winding and busy with tour coaches, and it carries a poor crash record involving visiting drivers. Overtaking opportunities are rare and the pull-offs are small, so plan on a slow average and let faster traffic past.
Allow three days minimum. Done in one it becomes four hours of concentration past things you did not stop for, which is the single most common regret on this route.
tips: Coach traffic and few passing spots

sections.heading: Where the camping actually is
body: Aire River and Johanna Beach are the standout low-cost options inside Great Otway National Park, both requiring booking through Parks Victoria and both filling over summer and school holidays. Neither has powered sites.

Apollo Bay and Port Campbell carry the commercial parks with showers, laundry and power, and they are the practical reset points on a three-day run. Book these well ahead between December and January.
Free camping along the road itself is essentially non-existent and heavily policed. Treat the corridor as a booked-accommodation route rather than one you can improvise through.
tips: No realistic free camping on the road
Apollo Bay and Port Campbell for services

sections.heading: Timing the Twelve Apostles
body: Sunset is the classic time and also when the car park is fullest, with coaches arriving in a block. Sunrise gives you comparable light with a fraction of the people, and the walk down to Gibson Steps is far more pleasant early.

The helicopter flights operate from beside the visitor area and give the only view that shows the full stack formation. They are weather dependent and worth booking for the morning so a cancellation can be moved.

Loch Ard Gorge, a few minutes further west, is quieter than the Apostles and arguably the better stop. The shipwreck story and the beach access make it worth more than the ten minutes most people give it.

sections.heading: The Otways and the wildlife
body: Turning inland into the Otways gives you tall wet forest, Hopetoun Falls, Triplet Falls and the Otway Fly treetop walk, all within a short drive of the coast road. It is a completely different landscape and a good wet-weather option.

Cape Otway is the reliable place to see wild koalas along the road through the manna gums, though numbers have fluctuated with the health of the trees. Watch for them from the vehicle rather than approaching, and never feed them.
Glow worms appear in the Melba Gully area after dark, and the walk is short and easy. Take a red light and let your eyes adjust rather than sweeping a torch around.
tips: Koalas along the Cape Otway road
Red light for the glow worms

sections.heading: Beyond the Twelve Apostles
body: Most traffic turns around at the Apostles, which means the coast west to Warrnambool through the Bay of Islands and the Bay of Martyrs is quieter and arguably as good. It is worth the extra hour.
Warrnambool itself has the Logans Beach whale nursery between May and October and works as a final night before turning inland or continuing to South Australia.
Port Fairy at the western end is a preserved fishing town with good camping and far fewer visitors than the eastern half of the route, which makes it a calm final night.
Check the Parks Victoria site for current campground status before you leave Melbourne, since storm damage and fire recovery work close individual sites at short notice along this coast.
tips: Traffic thins west of the Apostles
Whales at Warrnambool May to October

east-coast-road-trip-sydney-cairns.title: Sydney to Cairns: a 14-day camping road trip
east-coast-road-trip-sydney-cairns.description: Two weeks of beach camps, green hinterland and warm northern mornings.
east-coast-road-trip-sydney-cairns.imageAlt: Tropical east coast road in Queensland
east-coast-road-trip-sydney-cairns.intro: Sydney to Cairns is about 2,500 kilometres before detours. Fourteen days is quick, so choose a few long stops instead of sleeping in a different town every night.

sections.heading: Sydney to the Mid North Coast
body: Break the first drive around Myall Lakes or Port Macquarie. Myall Lakes brings quiet water and national park camping, while Port Macquarie makes food, laundry and a powered site easy.
Turn inland for Dorrigo if rainforest walks matter more than another beach night. The plateau is cooler, the road climbs sharply and cloud can settle quickly around the ranges.

sections.heading: Northern NSW and south-east Queensland
body: Byron Bay is popular for a reason, but nearby caravan parks fill early and traffic is slow in holidays. Brunswick Heads, Lennox Head and the Tweed can provide a calmer base.

Crossing into Queensland, choose between the Gold Coast hinterland and the coast. Springbrook National Park adds waterfalls and cooler nights. K'gari needs separate planning for tides, vehicle permits and sand driving.
tips: Do not drive tired after a beach day

sections.heading: The long run to Cairns
body: The distance between the Sunshine Coast and Airlie Beach is larger than it looks. Split it around Agnes Water, Rockhampton or Cape Hillsborough, then give Airlie Beach a rest day.

Mission Beach is a gentler final stop before Cairns. By this point the climate is tropical, cassowary warnings matter and swimming advice changes by season. Check local signs before entering any water.

sections.heading: Fourteen days is tight for this distance
body: Sydney to Cairns is roughly 2,400 kilometres by the direct inland route and considerably more if you follow the coast properly. Two weeks means averaging around 200 kilometres a day with stops, which is comfortable only if you resist adding detours.

The common mistake is trying to include the Whitsundays, Fraser Island, the Daintree and a Great Barrier Reef trip in the same fortnight. Each of those wants two days minimum, and together they consume the entire trip.
Pick three highlights and treat the rest as driving days with a swim. Trying to do everything produces a trip where you were constantly in the vehicle.
tips: 200 km a day is the realistic pace

sections.heading: The stops that justify a second night
body: Byron Bay, Noosa, Airlie Beach and Port Douglas are the places where a single night leaves you packing up before you have done anything. Each has walks, beaches and boat trips that need a full day.
Between them, Coffs Harbour, Hervey Bay, Rockhampton and Townsville work as single-night transit stops with services, fuel and a caravan park. There is no need to make these interesting.

If you are heading for the reef, Cairns and Port Douglas are the two departure points and both need a spare day for weather. Reef trips are cancelled often enough that a same-day-arrival booking is a gamble.
tips: Two nights: Byron, Noosa, Airlie, Port Douglas

sections.heading: Stingers, crocodiles and swimming
body: North of about Gladstone, marine stingers make unprotected ocean swimming unsafe roughly from November to May. Stinger nets and full-body suits are the standard precaution and the signage is reliable, so follow it rather than judging by how calm the water looks.

Estuarine crocodiles are present in waterways from about Rockhampton north, and that includes rivers, creeks and beaches that look completely benign. Never swim, clean fish or camp at the water's edge in croc country, and obey every warning sign.

The safe swimming options up north are patrolled beaches inside stinger nets, freshwater pools where signage confirms it, and the many town lagoons. Cairns and Airlie Beach both have excellent free public lagoons for exactly this reason.
tips: Stinger season roughly November to May
Town lagoons are the safe swim

sections.heading: Fuel, distances and the inland alternative
body: The Bruce Highway is the coastal spine and carries heavy truck traffic, roadworks and flood closures in the wet season. It is not a scenic road for much of its length, which surprises people expecting ocean views.
Fuel is available regularly along this route, unlike most of Australia, so the planning issue is time rather than range. Roadhouse prices north of Townsville rise noticeably.

In the wet season, from roughly November to April, sections of the Bruce close with flooding and the tropical north gets serious rain. The dry season from May to October is the straightforward time to do this drive.
tips: Dry season is May to October
Bruce Highway floods in the wet
Fuel is not the constraint here

sections.heading: Island detours worth the time
body: K'gari, the Whitsundays and Magnetic Island are the three island detours on this route, and each needs at least two days including transfers. Adding all three to a fortnight is what breaks the itinerary.
K'gari requires four-wheel drive and a vehicle permit or a tour, and it has strict dingo safety rules that must be followed. Choose one island and do it properly rather than rushing all three.
Whichever islands you choose, book the boat trip early in your stay in that town so a weather cancellation can be rescheduled rather than lost entirely.
Cyclone season in the tropical north runs from November to April, and a system can close the Bruce Highway and ground reef trips for several days at a time.
tips: Each island needs two days minimum

perth-to-broome-road-trip.title: Perth to Broome camping road trip
perth-to-broome-road-trip.description: White dunes, coral reefs, red gorges and the long bright road north.
perth-to-broome-road-trip.imageAlt: Red cliffs and coast in Western Australia
perth-to-broome-road-trip.intro: The west coast changes colour as you drive north from Perth. Limestone gives way to red river gorges, Ningaloo water and the long Pilbara stretches before Broome.

sections.heading: Perth to Shark Bay
body: Use Cervantes or Jurien Bay for the first night and visit the Pinnacles outside the hottest part of the day. Continue through Geraldton to Kalbarri, leaving time for both the coastal cliffs and inland gorge lookouts.
Shark Bay is a detour, not a quick roadside stop. Base around Denham or a nearby caravan park for at least two nights if you want Monkey Mia, Shell Beach and Francois Peron country.

sections.heading: Ningaloo and Karijini
body: Cape Range National Park and Exmouth deserve several nights. Book national park camps early in the dry season and confirm water, shade and generator conditions. Coral Bay is smaller and often busy.
The inland turn to Karijini adds serious distance. Roads, heat and gorge access change with conditions. Stay at an authorised campground and carry more water than a coastal day would suggest.

sections.heading: Pilbara to Broome
body: Break the final run around Port Hedland or Eighty Mile Beach rather than forcing a very long day. Roadhouses can have limited hours, so fuel before you need it.
Broome is an easy place to stop moving for a while. Caravan parks book out in the dry season, particularly around school holidays and major events. Reserve before leaving the Pilbara.

sections.heading: Distances change how you plan
body: Perth to Broome is roughly 2,200 kilometres and the towns are far apart, with long stretches where the next fuel is several hundred kilometres away. This is the trip where range planning stops being theoretical.
Ten days is the minimum that allows stops at Kalbarri, Shark Bay, Coral Bay and Exmouth. Two weeks lets you add Karijini, which is the single best detour on the route and adds around 600 kilometres.
Book accommodation at Exmouth, Coral Bay and Broome in the dry season, because they fill with southern travellers escaping winter and there is no overflow capacity.
tips: Ten days minimum, two weeks better
Dry season books out up north

sections.heading: Ningaloo is the reason to go
body: Ningaloo Reef comes within a few metres of the beach at Coral Bay and Turquoise Bay, which makes it the most accessible major reef in the country. You can snorkel straight off the sand without a boat.

Whale shark tours run from roughly March to July and humpback swims later in the season. Both book out and both are weather dependent, so allow a spare day and book early in your stay rather than at the end.

Turquoise Bay has a drift snorkel where the current carries you along the reef. Get out before the sandbar at the southern end, because the current continues past it and swimming back against it is genuinely hard.
tips: Whale sharks roughly March to July
Exit the Turquoise Bay drift early

sections.heading: Karijini and the gorges
body: Karijini National Park sits inland from the coast and holds the best gorge country in Western Australia, with Dales Gorge, Hancock Gorge and Weano all offering swimming in deep pools. The park is remote and the roads in include unsealed sections.

The gorge walks are graded and some are genuinely serious, involving scrambling, cold water and confined spaces. People have died in these gorges, and flash flooding after rain is the specific hazard. Do not enter a gorge if rain is forecast anywhere upstream.
There is no fuel inside the park and the nearest services are at Tom Price or Auski. Arrive with a full tank, plenty of water and enough food, because the campgrounds are basic and there is no shop.

sections.heading: Season, heat and the wet
body: This route works in the dry season, roughly May to October, when the north is warm and dry and the roads are open. The wet season brings extreme heat, humidity, cyclones and road closures across the Pilbara and Kimberley.

Even in the dry, daytime temperatures north of Carnarvon are high and the sun is severe. Carry far more water than feels necessary, start walks early, and treat the middle of the day as time to be somewhere shaded.

Cyclone season runs roughly November to April in the north west. If you are travelling in that window, monitor warnings daily and understand that a cyclone will close roads and towns with little notice.
tips: Dry season is May to October

sections.heading: Shark Bay and the stops between
body: Shark Bay is a World Heritage area with the Monkey Mia dolphins, the stromatolites at Hamelin Pool and Shell Beach, made entirely of shells metres deep. It is a substantial detour off the highway and worth a full day.
Kalbarri sits between Perth and Shark Bay with coastal cliffs and the inland gorges including Nature's Window. The park closes tracks in extreme heat, so summer visits need an early start.
Broome itself deserves two nights for Cable Beach, the Staircase to the Moon on the right dates and the pearling history at the museum.
Karijini and Ningaloo both sit a long way off the highway, so decide which you are including before leaving Perth rather than trying to fit both into a tight schedule.
tips: Shark Bay is a full-day detour

brisbane-to-cape-tribulation.title: Brisbane to Cape Tribulation camping route
brisbane-to-cape-tribulation.description: Beach towns give way to reef islands and rainforest as the coast turns tropical.
brisbane-to-cape-tribulation.intro: North of Brisbane the seasons change faster than the scenery. Give the drive at least two weeks and move your longest days away from the places you most want to swim, walk or sit still.

sections.heading: Brisbane to the Capricorn Coast
body: Start with Noosa or the Cooloola coast, then decide whether K'gari fits your vehicle and schedule. Island travel brings permits, tide windows and soft sand, so it should never be treated as a spontaneous side road.
Agnes Water is a comfortable break before the longer central coast distances. Restock in major towns and avoid turning a late finish into night driving through wildlife country.

sections.heading: Whitsundays to the wet tropics
body: Cape Hillsborough offers forest, beach and a quieter night before Airlie Beach. Airlie is the practical base for Whitsunday trips, with more services and busy holiday parks.

Mission Beach slows the pace again. Read cassowary signs, secure food and follow seasonal swimming advice. Inland, the Atherton Tablelands can be cooler and provides waterfalls, farm stays and caravan parks.

sections.heading: Daintree and Cape Tribulation
body: Cross the Daintree River with enough fuel and daylight. Mobile reception can be patchy, roads may be affected by heavy rain and large vehicles need to check access carefully.
Choose a legal campground or caravan park and keep food secure. Check crocodile warnings and never assume a beach or creek is safe for swimming because other people are near the water.

sections.heading: Where the Daintree changes the rules
body: North of the Daintree River the road becomes narrower, steeper and partly unsealed beyond Cape Tribulation. The Bloomfield Track to Cooktown is four-wheel drive only, prohibited in most rentals, and impassable after rain.

The Daintree River ferry is the only crossing and runs to set hours with a queue in peak season. Check the operating times before planning a late return, because being on the wrong side after the last ferry means a very long detour.
Accommodation north of the river is limited and books out. There is no supermarket and fuel is expensive, so restock in Mossman or Port Douglas before crossing.
tips: Ferry has set hours and queues

sections.heading: Crocodiles are the constraint up here
body: Estuarine crocodiles inhabit every waterway in the tropical north, including creeks, mangroves, estuaries and the beaches themselves. The Daintree and Cape Tribulation coast is prime habitat and the risk is real rather than theoretical.

Do not swim in or beside any waterway unless it is a designated safe swimming area. Do not camp within a few metres of the water, do not clean fish at the edge, and do not stand in the shallows for a photograph.
The safe swimming here is in the designated freshwater holes such as Mossman Gorge and Emmagen Creek, and even those carry signage worth reading each visit because conditions change.
tips: Read the signage on every visit

sections.heading: Rainforest, reef and the wet season
body: The Daintree is the oldest continuously surviving rainforest on the planet and the boardwalks at Marrdja and Dubuji are the easiest way to see it properly. Early morning gives the best chance of cassowaries and the fewest people.
Cape Tribulation is where the rainforest meets the reef, and reef trips run from Cape Trib and Port Douglas. The northern reef sites are generally in better condition than those closer to Cairns.
The wet season, roughly November to April, brings heavy rain, road closures and stinger season. The dry season is the straightforward time to visit and also when the roads and tours reliably operate.

sections.heading: Breaking the drive from Brisbane
body: Brisbane to Cape Tribulation is around 1,900 kilometres and needs a minimum of five driving days to be enjoyable. The Sunshine Coast, Hervey Bay, Airlie Beach and Townsville are the natural overnight breaks.
The Bruce Highway carries heavy freight and is not a scenic drive for much of its length. Treat the southern half as transit and save the time for the tropical north, which is what you came for.
Consider flying to Cairns and hiring there if your time is limited. It removes four days of driving and puts you straight into the part of the route that is genuinely distinctive.
tips: Flying to Cairns saves four days

sections.heading: Cassowaries and driving in the wet tropics
body: Southern cassowaries live in the rainforest between Mission Beach and the Daintree and are struck by vehicles regularly. Signed cassowary zones require reduced speed and they mean it.
They are large, powerful birds and can be dangerous if approached or fed. Never feed one, keep well back, and if one approaches put a tree or your vehicle between you rather than running.
Mission Beach and Etty Bay south of Cairns are the other reliable cassowary areas, and Etty Bay in particular sees them come onto the beach.
The Daintree ferry queue can exceed an hour in peak season, so aim to cross mid-morning or late afternoon rather than around the middle of the day.
tips: Put an object between you, do not run

melbourne-to-adelaide-coastal-route.title: Melbourne to Adelaide coastal camping route
melbourne-to-adelaide-coastal-route.description: Sea cliffs, fishing towns and empty Coorong beaches on the slower road west.
melbourne-to-adelaide-coastal-route.imageAlt: Limestone coast between Victoria and South Australia
melbourne-to-adelaide-coastal-route.intro: The coastal road from Melbourne to Adelaide works best over five to seven days. It combines the Great Ocean Road with volcanic country, fishing towns and the long lagoons of the Coorong.

sections.heading: Melbourne to Port Fairy
body: Follow the Great Ocean Road through Torquay and Apollo Bay, then stay west of the busiest viewpoints for the night. Port Campbell, Warrnambool and Port Fairy all have caravan parks and groceries.
Do not underestimate fatigue on the winding section. Short distances take time and wildlife becomes harder to see near dusk.

sections.heading: The Limestone Coast
body: Cross into South Australia through Mount Gambier, where sinkholes, crater lakes and full-service caravan parks make an easy reset. Continue to Beachport or Robe for a coast night.
Check whether beach tracks suit your vehicle and rental agreement. Soft sand, tide and changing access make local advice more valuable than an old track report.

sections.heading: Coorong to Adelaide
body: The Coorong is long, windswept and sparse. Camp only in designated areas, carry water and protect food from wildlife. Fire rules can be strict even when evenings feel cool.
Approach Adelaide through Meningie and the lower Murray, or take more time around the Fleurieu Peninsula. Finish with a powered site if you need laundry and a full vehicle reset.

sections.heading: Two routes, two very different trips
body: The coastal route through the Great Ocean Road and Warrnambool to Mount Gambier is roughly 900 kilometres and takes at least four days done properly. The inland Western Highway is around 730 kilometres and can be driven in a long day.

The coastal option gives you the Twelve Apostles, the Bay of Islands, Cape Bridgewater and the Limestone Coast. The inland option gives you the Grampians, which is a serious destination in its own right.
If you have a week, do the coast one way and the Grampians on the return. That covers both and avoids driving the same road twice.
tips: Four days minimum for the coast

sections.heading: The Limestone Coast and the sinkholes
body: Mount Gambier sits on limestone country and the Blue Lake changes colour dramatically from grey to intense blue around November each year. Umpherston Sinkhole, a collapsed cave turned into a sunken garden, is free and genuinely unusual.

Cave diving in the region is world-renowned and strictly certification-controlled. The Kilsby Sinkhole and Piccaninnie Ponds have snorkelling options for people without cave qualifications, and the water clarity is extraordinary.
Robe and Beachport further north are quieter coastal towns with good camping and far fewer visitors than the Victorian side of the border. They make an easy final night before Adelaide.
tips: Blue Lake turns blue around November

sections.heading: Crossing the border
body: South Australia enforces fruit fly quarantine at the border, and fresh fruit and vegetables cannot be carried in. Disposal bins are provided at the checkpoint and fines apply for carrying prohibited produce, whether or not you knew.
Plan your shopping around this: buy fresh produce after the border rather than before it. This catches out a substantial number of travellers who stock up in Victoria the night before crossing.
There is also a time zone change of half an hour between Victoria and South Australia, which matters for ferry bookings, tour times and campground check-in.
tips: No fresh produce into South Australia

sections.heading: Whales, seals and the southern coast
body: Southern right whales calve along this coast between roughly May and October, and Logans Beach at Warrnambool has a purpose-built viewing platform where they come close to shore. Nearby Portland and Cape Bridgewater add seal colonies.

Cape Bridgewater has one of the largest Australian fur seal colonies on the mainland, reachable by a clifftop walk. The blowholes and the petrified forest walk nearby make it a half day rather than a quick stop.
Tower Hill, an extinct volcano near Warrnambool, is a wildlife reserve with emus, koalas and kangaroos in an unusually accessible setting. It is free and quiet in the early morning.
tips: Tower Hill is free and quiet

sections.heading: The Coorong and the Murray mouth
body: East of Adelaide the Coorong stretches for over a hundred kilometres of lagoon behind a dune barrier, with camping, birdlife and almost nobody. It is a very different landscape from the limestone coast.
The Murray mouth at Goolwa marks the end of Australia's largest river system, and the barrages and ferry crossings around it are worth the detour before the run into Adelaide.
Allow time for the Fleurieu Peninsula on the approach to Adelaide, where McLaren Vale and the coast at Victor Harbor make an easy final day.
Grampians access roads and walking tracks have been affected by fire and flood in recent years, so confirm the specific track is open before building a day around it.
tips: Murray mouth is worth the detour

tasmania-camping-loop.title: Tasmania camping loop: 10 days from Hobart
tasmania-camping-loop.description: Granite bays, tall forests and cold mountain mornings on a lap from Hobart.
tasmania-camping-loop.imageAlt: Granite coast and blue water in Tasmania
tasmania-camping-loop.intro: Ten days is enough for a rewarding Tasmanian loop if you accept that one coast will always tempt you to stay longer. Carry warm layers in every season and leave room for weather to change the order.

sections.heading: Hobart to the east coast
body: Leave Hobart for the Tasman Peninsula or head directly to Freycinet. National park entry needs a valid pass and popular camps around Freycinet use booking arrangements that can change by season.
Continue north through Bicheno to the Bay of Fires. Use established campgrounds, protect fragile dunes and expect simple facilities away from town.

sections.heading: North to Cradle Mountain
body: Launceston is the best place to restock before turning west. Cradle Mountain weather can move from sun to sleet in a single afternoon, and the visitor transport system affects how you reach walks.
Stay at a campground or holiday park that suits your heating, power and shower needs. A cold wet night is easier when your gear has somewhere to dry.

sections.heading: West coast and the return south
body: Strahan and the west coast bring long bends, wet forest and slower driving. Fuel early and avoid building a tight schedule around a road that rewards patience.
Return through the central highlands or Mount Field National Park. If conditions turn poor, choose the lower and safer route rather than forcing an alpine plan.

sections.heading: Getting the vehicle there
body: The Spirit of Tasmania sails Geelong to Devonport and takes vehicles, with day and night crossings across Bass Strait. Fares are set by vehicle length and height, book out over summer, and the strait can be genuinely rough.

Flying and hiring locally is the alternative and frequently cheaper for a shorter trip, since the ferry plus fuel to Geelong adds up. Hire vehicles in Tasmania are limited in peak season and should be booked early.
Whichever way you arrive, Tasmania has strict quarantine on fresh produce, plants and honey. Eat or dispose of fruit and vegetables before boarding rather than having them confiscated.
tips: Flying and hiring is often cheaper
No fresh produce across the strait

sections.heading: Ten days and the shape of the loop
body: A clean circuit from Hobart runs east coast to Bay of Fires, across to Launceston, west to Cradle Mountain, down the west coast through Strahan, and back via Lake St Clair and the Derwent Valley. That is roughly 1,400 kilometres.
Tasmanian distances look small and drive long. The roads are winding, often narrow, and the west coast in particular is slow. Budget well above what the map suggests, especially in a campervan.
Two nights at Cradle Mountain and two on the east coast are the ones worth protecting. Everything else can flex around weather, which in Tasmania it will need to.
tips: Roads drive far longer than they look

sections.heading: Cradle Mountain and the park pass
body: A Tasmania Parks Pass is required for vehicle entry to national parks and a holiday pass covering all parks for eight weeks is far better value than individual day entries if you visit more than two.

Cradle Mountain runs a mandatory shuttle bus from the visitor centre during the day, with private vehicle access restricted. Plan around the shuttle timetable and book the pass in advance in peak season.

Dove Lake circuit is the accessible highlight at around two hours. The summit climb is a serious six to eight hour day with exposed scrambling and weather that changes fast, and it is not a casual walk.
tips: Shuttle bus is mandatory at Cradle
Summit climb is a serious day

sections.heading: Weather and the west coast
body: Tasmania's weather is the most changeable in the country and the west coast is one of the wettest places in Australia. Four seasons in a day is a genuine description rather than a saying, and alpine areas can get snow in any month.

Carry warm and waterproof layers even in January, and treat any walk above the treeline as an alpine outing regardless of the forecast at the car park. People get into trouble on Tasmanian day walks every season.
The west coast towns of Strahan, Queenstown and Zeehan are worth the detour for the Gordon River cruise and the mining history, and they are considerably quieter than the east.
tips: Treat walks above treeline as alpine
West coast is wet and quiet

sections.heading: Wineglass Bay and the east coast
body: Freycinet's Wineglass Bay lookout is around an hour and a half return and the beach itself adds another hour each way. The car park fills early in summer and a shuttle operates in peak season.
The Bay of Fires further north has free and low-cost camping behind orange lichen-covered granite and white sand, and it is one of the best stretches of coastal camping in the country.
Bruny Island south of Hobart adds a day and delivers cheese, oysters, a lighthouse and some of the best coastal scenery in the state.
Book the Spirit of Tasmania as early as your dates allow, because vehicle spaces on the popular sailings sell out months ahead over summer.
tips: Bay of Fires has free camping

darwin-kakadu-litchfield-loop.title: Darwin, Kakadu and Litchfield camping loop
darwin-kakadu-litchfield-loop.description: Waterfalls, stone country and wide floodplains beneath the Top End dry-season sky.
darwin-kakadu-litchfield-loop.intro: A week from Darwin can connect Litchfield, Kakadu and Mary River, but water access, campgrounds and roads change sharply between wet and dry seasons.

sections.heading: Litchfield first
body: Drive south from Darwin and settle into a designated Litchfield campground before chasing waterfalls. Wangi Falls, Florence Falls and other swimming areas open or close according to conditions.
Never treat clear water as permission to swim. Read crocodile and closure signs at every location, every time.

sections.heading: Across to Kakadu
body: Allow more than one night in Kakadu. The park is vast and distances between art sites, wetlands and campgrounds add up quickly. A park pass and separate campground arrangements may apply.
Cooinda is a useful serviced base, while simpler camps trade facilities for location. Carry water, fuel conservatively and check roads after any rain.

sections.heading: Mary River and the return
body: Mary River wetlands make a slower final leg before Darwin. Stay back from water edges and follow local crocodile advice, including at boat ramps and fishing spots.
The Top End heat remains serious in the dry. Walk early, rest through the hottest hours and keep drinking water accessible inside the vehicle.

sections.heading: The wet and the dry decide everything
body: The dry season, roughly May to October, is when this loop works: roads open, waterfalls accessible, humidity manageable and campgrounds operating. The wet season closes large parts of Kakadu and makes travel genuinely difficult.
The shoulder months at either end are the sweet spot. Waterfalls still run strongly in May and June after the wet, while the roads have reopened and the crowds have not fully arrived.

In the wet, from November to April, expect extreme humidity, monsoonal storms, road closures and many walks and campgrounds shut. Some people prefer it for the scale of the waterfalls, but it is not a straightforward trip.
tips: Dry season is May to October
May and June for full waterfalls
Wet season closes much of Kakadu

sections.heading: Crocodiles govern every water decision
body: Kakadu and Litchfield are both serious crocodile country and estuarine crocodiles are present in waterways that look completely safe. Every year animals are removed from swimming holes, and the survey status of a hole can change between seasons.

Swim only where current signage explicitly permits it, and check on the day rather than relying on a guidebook or a previous visit. Wangi Falls and Florence Falls in Litchfield are the commonly open ones, and even they close after surveys.

Do not camp at the water's edge, clean fish beside a river or launch a kayak in unsurveyed water. Freshwater crocodiles are also present and are generally harmless if left alone, but distinguishing them from a distance is not a skill to rely on.
tips: Only swim where signed open today
Never camp at the water's edge

sections.heading: Kakadu permits, passes and culture
body: Kakadu requires a park pass, purchasable online, and it is a living cultural landscape jointly managed with its Traditional Owners. Some areas are restricted and photography is prohibited at certain rock art and ceremonial sites.

The rock art at Ubirr and Nourlangie is among the oldest continuous artistic tradition anywhere, some of it tens of thousands of years old. Take a guided walk if one is running, because the interpretation transforms what you are looking at.
Respect closures and restricted areas without exception. These are not administrative boundaries but conditions of access to somebody's country.
tips: Guided walks transform the rock art

sections.heading: Vehicle requirements and Litchfield
body: Much of Kakadu's best country, including Jim Jim Falls and Twin Falls, requires a high-clearance four-wheel drive and involves creek crossings. A two-wheel drive still reaches Ubirr and Burrungkuy (Nourlangie) in the dry season. The Kakadu access report currently lists Gunlom Road as high-clearance 4WD only, and some hire companies do not allow 2WDs on unsealed roads, so check the access report and your rental terms.

Litchfield is considerably more accessible, with Florence, Wangi and Tolmer falls all reachable in a two-wheel drive on sealed roads. For travellers without a four-wheel drive, Litchfield delivers more per day than Kakadu.
Check your rental agreement before attempting any unsealed road here. Most standard hire agreements prohibit them entirely, and recovery in this country is expensive.
tips: Jim Jim and Twin Falls need 4WD
Check hire terms before unsealed roads

sections.heading: Darwin as a base
body: Darwin has the services, supermarkets and hire depots that nothing else up here does, plus Mindil Beach markets in the dry season and the Museum and Art Gallery explaining Cyclone Tracy and the 1942 bombing.

Do the big shop in Darwin before heading into either park. Inside Kakadu, Jabiru has a supermarket and service station and the Cooinda store sells fuel and groceries. Fuel is also considerably cheaper in town.
Katherine and Nitmiluk Gorge sit south of the loop and are worth adding if you have the days, with boat trips and canoeing through the gorge system.
Waterfall access in Kakadu opens progressively as the wet recedes, so a May visit may find some sites still closed that will be open by June.
tips: Mindil markets run in the dry

adelaide-to-uluru-road-trip.title: Adelaide to Uluṟu: an outback camping route
adelaide-to-uluru-road-trip.description: Flinders ridges, underground Coober Pedy and red desert horizons all the way north.
adelaide-to-uluru-road-trip.imageAlt: Red outback road in central Australia
adelaide-to-uluru-road-trip.intro: Adelaide to Uluṟu is a long desert journey, not a single transfer. Seven to ten days allows time for Ikara, Coober Pedy and the Red Centre without stacking exhausting drives.

sections.heading: Adelaide to the Flinders
body: Break north around the Clare Valley or reach Hawker for the first major base. Ikara-Flinders Ranges rewards at least two nights, with walks starting early before the heat rises.
Check park entry, campground booking and road conditions. Unsealed gorge roads may be unsuitable after rain or under a rental agreement.

sections.heading: Coober Pedy to the border
body: The Stuart Highway opens into long distances after Port Augusta. Coober Pedy provides fuel, groceries, repairs and a memorable roofed night underground if you want a break from the tent.
Continue through Marla with a firm fuel plan. Roadhouses can change hours and mobile coverage is not a safety system.

sections.heading: Uluṟu and beyond
body: Turn west at Erldunda for Uluṟu-Kata Tjuṯa National Park. Stay in authorised accommodation around Yulara and respect closures, cultural guidance and photography restrictions.
Alice Springs is another substantial drive. If it follows your Uluṟu stay, add Kings Canyon only when time, fuel and road access genuinely fit.

sections.heading: The Stuart Highway and its distances
body: Adelaide to Uluru is roughly 1,600 kilometres, most of it on the Stuart Highway through country with very few towns. Coober Pedy, Marla and Kulgera are the main service points and the gaps between them are substantial.

Carry more water than you think you need, a minimum of four litres per person per day plus a reserve for the vehicle. Fuel range should assume the next station may be closed, because in this country it sometimes is.
Allow four days each way at a sensible pace. Done faster it becomes an endurance exercise, and fatigue on straight outback roads is a well-documented killer.
tips: Four litres of water per person per day
Four days each way is sensible

sections.heading: Coober Pedy is worth a night
body: Coober Pedy is the opal mining town where much of the population lives underground to escape the heat, and the dugout homes, underground churches and hotels are genuinely unusual rather than a novelty.

Summer temperatures regularly exceed forty degrees and the underground accommodation is the practical choice as well as the interesting one. The Breakaways, a short drive out, are best at sunrise or sunset.

Do not walk near mine shafts. The area around the town is riddled with unmarked and unfenced shafts, and people have died falling into them. Stay on marked areas and never walk backwards while taking photographs.

sections.heading: Uluru and respecting the site
body: Climbing Uluru has been prohibited since 2019 at the request of the Anangu Traditional Owners. The base walk, around ten kilometres, is the proper way to experience it and shows you far more than the climb ever did.
Some areas of the rock are sacred and photography is prohibited there, marked by signage. Respecting those signs is a basic condition of visiting, not an optional courtesy.
Start the base walk early. Summer temperatures make it dangerous after mid-morning and rangers close sections when the forecast exceeds a threshold. Carry more water than the distance suggests.
tips: No photography at signed sacred areas
Start the base walk at first light

sections.heading: Kata Tjuta and Kings Canyon
body: Kata Tjuta, around fifty kilometres from Uluru, is arguably the more impressive formation and the Valley of the Winds walk is the best in the park. It is exposed and closes in heat, so start it at dawn.

Kings Canyon sits between Uluru and Alice Springs on the Red Centre Way, and the rim walk is a three to four hour circuit with a steep initial climb and genuine drop-offs. It is the highlight of many trips out here.

Uluru-Kata Tjuta needs its own park pass: as of October 2026 it costs $38 per adult for 3 days or $50 for a year, and under-18s go free. Buying online is quickest, but you can also buy one at the park entry station. Watarrka, containing Kings Canyon, is separate, so check what your route needs before arriving at a gate.
tips: Valley of the Winds at dawn
Kings Canyon rim walk is 3 to 4 hours

sections.heading: Sunrise, sunset and the viewing areas
body: There are designated sunrise and sunset viewing areas for both Uluru and Kata Tjuta, and they fill with coaches. Arriving early enough to park and walk to a spot away from the main platform is worth the effort.
Photography restrictions apply at signed sacred areas and commercial photography needs a permit. The Field of Light installation and the various dining experiences book out well ahead in peak season.
Consider flying one leg if time is short, since Ayers Rock Airport has direct services and the drive is the same in both directions.
Summer temperatures at Uluru regularly exceed forty degrees and walks close on extreme days, which makes winter the far more comfortable season for this route.

sydney-south-coast-camping.title: Sydney to the Sapphire Coast camping guide
sydney-south-coast-camping.description: Quiet coves, spotted gums and small coastal towns between Sydney and Eden.
sydney-south-coast-camping.imageAlt: NSW South Coast beach and forest
sydney-south-coast-camping.intro: The NSW South Coast can fill a long weekend or two relaxed weeks. Outside peak holidays, the rhythm is simple: a short drive, a swim or walk, then camp before dark.

sections.heading: Sydney to Jervis Bay
body: Leave Sydney through Royal National Park or take the faster highway south. Kiama and the Shoalhaven make good food stops before the beaches around Jervis Bay.
National park, council and commercial campgrounds all use different booking systems. Summer and Easter sites disappear early.

sections.heading: Murramarang to Bermagui
body: Murramarang National Park mixes spotted gum forest with small beaches and wildlife around camp. Store food properly and keep a respectful distance from kangaroos.
Batemans Bay, Moruya and Narooma cover fuel and groceries. Bermagui gives the trip a slower small-town night before the more remote coast south.

sections.heading: Mimosa Rocks to Eden
body: Mimosa Rocks has beautiful simple campgrounds, but access, water and facilities vary. Read the exact campground page before turning in.
Finish around Eden for caravan parks, roofed stays and a full resupply. In fire or storm conditions, stay flexible and use the main highway rather than forcing a park road.

sections.heading: The stretch that makes this trip
body: South of Wollongong the coast opens into Jervis Bay, Ulladulla, Batemans Bay and the Sapphire Coast, with white sand beaches and national parks running most of the way to the Victorian border. It is around 500 kilometres to Eden.

Jervis Bay has some of the whitest sand in the world at Hyams Beach and Booderee National Park, which is jointly managed with the Wreck Bay Aboriginal Community and charges its own entry fee separate from NSW parks.

The Grand Pacific Drive and Sea Cliff Bridge just south of Sydney are worth the slower coastal start rather than taking the highway. It adds under an hour and is one of the better short drives in the state.
tips: Take the Sea Cliff Bridge route

sections.heading: Booking national park campgrounds
body: NSW National Parks campgrounds along this coast are booked online and the popular ones, particularly in Murramarang and Booderee, sell out months ahead for summer and school holidays. Walk-up availability is rare.
Vehicle entry fees apply to many parks separately from camping fees, and an annual All Parks Pass is worth it if you are visiting several. Check whether your campground booking includes entry.
Outside peak periods the same sites are quiet and frequently available a few days ahead, which makes autumn and spring the easy time to do this route.
tips: Book NSW parks months ahead in summer

sections.heading: Kangaroos on the beach and other wildlife
body: Pebbly Beach and Depot Beach in Murramarang are known for eastern grey kangaroos on the sand, and they are entirely wild despite being habituated to people. Do not feed them, and keep a distance, because large males can be dangerous.
Whale migration passes this coast twice a year, northbound roughly May to July and southbound September to November. Eden has a whale festival and land-based viewing from headlands is genuinely good.
Seals, dolphins and little penguins are all present along the coast, and Montague Island off Narooma runs tours to a seal colony and penguin rookery. Trips are weather dependent.
tips: Whales May to July, then Sept to Nov

sections.heading: Bushfire awareness on this coast
body: The South Coast was severely burnt in the 2019 to 2020 fires and remains high risk in summer. Fire danger ratings are posted at park entrances and on roadside signs, and total fire bans are common in summer.

Have a plan for a catastrophic day, which usually means leaving early rather than sheltering. Campgrounds in forested areas are among the worst places to be, and roads close quickly once a fire is running.
Download the Fires Near Me app or equivalent and check it daily in summer. Reception is patchy along parts of this coast, so check while you have signal rather than assuming you can look it up later.
tips: Reception is patchy, check in advance

sections.heading: Oysters, dairy and the food stops
body: The Clyde River at Batemans Bay and the Pambula and Wapengo estuaries produce some of the best oysters in the country, sold directly from the growers at a fraction of restaurant prices.
Bermagui, Central Tilba and Milton are the food stops worth planning around, with Tilba a preserved dairy village and Milton a good base between Ulladulla and Jervis Bay.
Eden at the southern end has the Killer Whale Museum and works as either a turning point or a stop on the way into Victoria.
NSW National Parks releases campground bookings on a rolling window, and the best coastal sites for summer are taken within minutes of becoming available.
tips: Central Tilba is a preserved village

nullarbor-crossing-camping-guide.title: Crossing the Nullarbor: camps, fuel and preparation
nullarbor-crossing-camping-guide.description: A huge sky, a straight road and more life along the plain than first meets the eye.
nullarbor-crossing-camping-guide.imageAlt: Eyre Highway across the Nullarbor Plain
nullarbor-crossing-camping-guide.intro: Ceduna to Norseman is roughly 1,200 kilometres. The Eyre Highway is sealed, but wind, heat, wildlife, fuel spacing and fatigue still demand a conservative plan.

sections.heading: Before Ceduna
body: Service the vehicle, check the spare tyre and learn how to use the jack before leaving a major centre. Fill water containers and keep food that can survive a delayed day.
Ceduna is the last broad resupply before the crossing. Check South Australian and Western Australian biosecurity rules before carrying fruit, vegetables, honey or plant material west.

sections.heading: Across the plain
body: Use Penong, Nullarbor Roadhouse, Border Village, Eucla and Madura to divide the drive. Fuel prices are part of remote travel, and passing an open pump to save a little can erase your margin.
Do not drive at dawn, dusk or night if you can avoid it. Wildlife and stock are harder to see, and fatigue builds quietly on long straight sections.

sections.heading: Camping and the Bight
body: Use legal roadside, roadhouse or caravan park options and keep clear of truck rest areas. Some coastal tracks are exposed, unsealed or unsuitable after weather.
Cliff lookouts along the Great Australian Bight are unforgettable, but barriers and warnings matter. Wind is powerful and cliff edges are unstable. Keep well back.

sections.heading: The scale of it
body: The Eyre Highway between Norseman and Ceduna is around 1,200 kilometres, including the 90 Mile Straight, the longest straight stretch of sealed road in Australia at 146.6 kilometres. Roadhouses are the only services and they are spaced 100 to 200 kilometres apart.
Three days is a comfortable crossing. Two is possible and tiring, and one is dangerous. Fatigue is the single biggest risk out here, more than mechanical failure or wildlife.
Fuel is available at every roadhouse but at a substantial premium over city prices. Budget for it rather than trying to stretch between the cheaper ones, which is how people run dry.
tips: Fuel is expensive, budget for it

sections.heading: Preparation that actually matters
body: Carry at least twenty litres of drinking water regardless of season, a working spare with the tools to fit it, and enough food for a day longer than you plan. Mobile coverage exists only near roadhouses and towns.
Tell someone your route and expected arrival. If you break down, stay with the vehicle: it is shelter, it is visible from the air and the road, and walking in this country has killed people.
Consider a satellite messenger or a personal locator beacon. They are cheap to hire and are the only reliable way to call for help across most of the crossing.
tips: Stay with the vehicle if you break down

sections.heading: Wildlife, road trains and driving hours
body: Kangaroos, wombats, emus and camels are all active around dawn and dusk, and a strike at highway speed will disable a vehicle. Drive only in full daylight and accept a shorter day rather than pushing into the last light.

Road trains up to 53.5 metres run this highway constantly. Overtaking one requires a very long clear stretch, and the turbulence as they pass is significant in a high-sided vehicle. Give them room and do not sit in the blind spot.
Stop every two hours. The road is straight, the scenery repeats and hypnosis is a genuine documented phenomenon here. The roadhouse stops exist for exactly this reason.

sections.heading: What is actually worth stopping for
body: The Bunda Cliffs, where the Nullarbor Plain drops straight into the Southern Ocean, are the visual highlight and there are several signed lookouts along the highway. They are unfenced, so keep well back from the edge.
The Head of Bight is a southern right whale nursery between roughly June and October, with a boardwalk and viewing platforms. It is one of the best land-based whale viewing sites in the country.

Eucla has the ruins of the old telegraph station being swallowed by sand dunes, and the golf course spanning the crossing has holes at roadhouses along the route. Also note the time zone changes, including an unofficial one used locally.
tips: Head of Bight whales June to October

sections.heading: Where to actually sleep
body: Roadhouses along the Eyre Highway offer powered and unpowered sites, and there are free rest areas and gravel pits between them where overnight stops are permitted. The roadhouse option buys a shower and security.
Several free camps sit along the Bunda Cliffs with no facilities and extraordinary positions. They are exposed, unfenced and have no water, so they suit self-sufficient vehicles only.
Norseman and Ceduna bookend the crossing and both are worth a proper rest stop, with services, fuel and somewhere to sleep before or after the long stretch.
Quarantine applies in both directions, with fruit fly checks entering South Australia and a separate checkpoint entering Western Australia, so plan the fridge for both.

queensland-outback-way.title: Queensland outback camping route
queensland-outback-way.description: Sandstone gorge walks, stock-route towns and ancient country across western Queensland.
queensland-outback-way.intro: Carnarvon Gorge to Boodjamulla crosses very large distances. Ten days is a minimum for meaningful stops, and the cooler dry months are far kinder for walking and camping.

sections.heading: Carnarvon Gorge
body: Book a base near Carnarvon Gorge and start walks early. Takarakka and national park arrangements differ, so confirm the exact site, access and facilities.
Carry water on every walk and do not plan a long gorge day immediately after a full driving day.

sections.heading: Longreach and Winton
body: Longreach provides repairs, groceries and a strong dose of pastoral history. Winton adds dinosaur country and makes a sensible second base before turning farther west.
Fuel distances grow and reception thins. Ask locally about road conditions, especially after rain, and avoid unsealed shortcuts that do not suit your vehicle.

sections.heading: Boodjamulla
body: Boodjamulla National Park is remote and seasonal access matters. Confirm the road, campground booking, fuel range and whether your vehicle setup is suitable before leaving Mount Isa or Camooweal.
Stay longer than one night if conditions allow. The journey is too substantial to treat the park as a quick photograph before turning around.

sections.heading: Distances and the roadhouse rhythm
body: Outback Queensland runs on roadhouses rather than towns, and the gaps between fuel can exceed 200 kilometres. Winton, Longreach, Barcaldine and Charleville are the main service centres and everything between them is sparse.
Fuel range is the planning constraint. Fill at every opportunity rather than at every need, and carry twenty litres of drinking water minimum plus food for an extra day.
Mobile coverage exists in towns and disappears between them. Tell someone your route and expected arrival, and consider hiring a satellite messenger for the remoter legs.

sections.heading: Dinosaurs and the inland sea
body: Winton and Richmond sit on some of the richest dinosaur fossil country in the world, and the Australian Age of Dinosaurs facility near Winton holds the largest collection of Australian dinosaur fossils. Tours run to a working laboratory.
Lark Quarry preserves a set of dinosaur trackways, and the drive out is unsealed and can close after rain. Check conditions before committing, because the road becomes impassable quickly.
Richmond and Hughenden complete the fossil trail to the north, and together they explain the inland sea that covered this country. It is a genuinely unusual thing to build a road trip around.
tips: Lark Quarry road closes after rain
Fossil trail runs Winton to Richmond

sections.heading: Unsealed roads and the wet
body: Many outback Queensland roads are unsealed and close entirely after rain, sometimes for days, because driving them wet destroys the surface and attracts substantial fines. Closure is enforced and not advisory.
Check road conditions with the relevant council or the state road authority before setting out each day. A dry forecast where you are means nothing if it rained upstream two days ago.
The wet season, roughly November to March, brings extreme heat as well as closures. The dry season from April to October is when this country is comfortable and accessible.

sections.heading: Artesian baths and stargazing
