body: The Great Artesian Basin feeds hot bore baths in many outback towns, and soaking in mineral water at forty degrees under a desert sky is one of the genuine pleasures of this trip. Mitchell, Cunnamulla and Eulo all have facilities.

The night skies out here are among the darkest accessible anywhere, with essentially no light pollution. Charleville has the Cosmos Centre with telescope viewing, and any roadhouse car park will show you the Milky Way properly.
Bring a red torch and give your eyes twenty minutes to adjust. A phone screen at full brightness ruins night vision for everyone nearby, and out here that is a real loss.
tips: Artesian bore baths in many towns
Some of the darkest skies anywhere

sections.heading: Longreach and the Stockman's Hall of Fame
body: Longreach holds the Australian Stockman's Hall of Fame and the Qantas Founders Museum, including a decommissioned 747 you can walk through. Together they explain the inland far better than the landscape alone does.
Winton has the Waltzing Matilda Centre and the Musical Fence, and the town's pubs are worth an evening. These inland towns depend on visitor spending, so stopping matters more here than on the coast.
Charleville and Cunnamulla in the south link back towards New South Wales, and both have artesian bore baths and dark sky facilities.
Unsealed outback roads close after rain and stay closed until they dry, which can be several days, so build flexibility into any route using them.

south-west-wa-camping-loop.title: South West WA camping loop from Perth
south-west-wa-camping-loop.description: Vineyards, giant karri forest and granite bays on the green edge of Western Australia.
south-west-wa-camping-loop.imageAlt: Turquoise bay in south-west Western Australia
south-west-wa-camping-loop.intro: A Perth to Esperance loop can take ten days, but two weeks lets Margaret River, the karri forests and the south coast feel like places rather than fuel stops.

sections.heading: Perth to the capes
body: Head south through Bunbury toward Busselton and Margaret River. Caravan parks are plentiful, while national park camps need closer attention to booking, water and fire conditions.
Hamelin Bay and the capes are exposed to changing wind. Choose the side of the coast that fits the forecast rather than locking every night months ahead.

sections.heading: Karri country to Albany
body: Pemberton and Walpole trade surf for tall forest, cooler nights and winding roads. Give wet gear time to dry and watch for wildlife through shaded sections.
Albany makes an excellent two-night reset with history, coastal walks, food and repairs. Summer remains fire season even when the forest feels green.

sections.heading: Esperance and Cape Le Grand
body: The drive from Albany to Esperance is long enough to deserve a break. Reach Cape Le Grand with food, water and a confirmed campground if staying inside the park.
Beach access is not a promise that every vehicle belongs on the sand. Check local conditions, tyre advice and rental exclusions before leaving sealed roads.

sections.heading: Wildflowers and the season
body: Western Australia's wildflower season runs roughly August to November, moving south as the year progresses, and the south west is at its best in September and October. It is one of the largest wildflower displays on the planet.
Spring is also when the whales pass and the weather is mild, which makes it the single best window for this loop. Summer is hot and dry inland, though the coast stays pleasant.
Winter brings rain and cold to the south west, and while the forests are beautiful in it, camping is considerably less comfortable and some unsealed tracks become difficult.

sections.heading: Karri forests and the climbing trees
body: The karri forests around Pemberton and Walpole hold some of the tallest hardwood trees in the world. The Valley of the Giants Tree Top Walk near Walpole is a suspended walkway forty metres up through the canopy.

The Gloucester Tree and Dave Evans Bicentennial Tree are climbable fire lookouts with metal spikes driven into the trunk and no safety harness. They are genuinely exposed and not for anyone uncertain about heights.
Beedelup Falls and the Karri Forest Explorer drive link the best of the forest country, and there are several campgrounds within it. Book through the WA parks system in peak season.
tips: Book WA parks sites in spring

sections.heading: Margaret River and the coast
body: Margaret River is the wine region but the coastline is the reason to camp here, with a string of surf breaks, limestone caves and the Cape to Cape track running 123 kilometres between the two lighthouses.
The caves at Jewel, Lake and Mammoth are separately ticketed and worth choosing between rather than doing all of them. Ngilgi Cave near Yallingup is the most accessible.

Cellar door tastings frequently charge a fee credited against purchase, and cycling between them is not practical here because the distances are larger than they look. Use a tour if you want to taste properly.
tips: Cape to Cape track is 123 km
Wineries are too spread out to cycle

sections.heading: Sharks, rips and swimming safely
body: The south west coast has genuine surf and strong rips, and many beaches are unpatrolled. Swim between the flags where they exist and, where they do not, be conservative about entering the water at all.

White sharks are present along this coast and there have been incidents. The practical response is to avoid dawn, dusk and murky water, avoid swimming alone, and follow any beach closure without argument.
Rip currents cause far more trouble than sharks. If caught in one, do not swim against it: swim parallel to the beach until you are out of the pull, or float and signal for help.
tips: Avoid dawn, dusk and murky water
Swim parallel out of a rip

sections.heading: Albany and the south coast
body: Albany has the National Anzac Centre, one of the better museums in the country, and the Gap and Natural Bridge on the granite coast nearby. The Torndirrup peninsula is exposed and spectacular.

Denmark and Walpole between Albany and Pemberton have the Valley of the Giants and Greens Pool, where granite boulders shelter a calm swimming area. This coast is cooler and wetter than the Margaret River side.
Fremantle and Rottnest Island bookend the loop at the Perth end, and Rottnest is a car-free day trip reached by ferry.
Wildflower timing shifts each year with rainfall, so check current reports rather than assuming a fixed date range when planning a spring trip.
tips: South coast is cooler and wetter

victoria-high-country-camping.title: Victoria High Country camping road trip
victoria-high-country-camping.description: River camps, clear mountain air and winding roads beyond Bright and Omeo.
victoria-high-country-camping.imageAlt: Mountain road in Victoria High Country
victoria-high-country-camping.intro: Victoria's High Country offers sealed touring, rough four-wheel-drive tracks and everything between. Build the route around the least capable vehicle in your group.

sections.heading: Bright and Mount Buffalo
body: Bright is the easiest place to fuel, shop and check the forecast. Mount Buffalo National Park adds granite views and booked camping at Lake Catani when open.
Alpine nights can be cold in summer. Carry insulation and rain gear even when the valley forecast looks settled.

sections.heading: Harrietville to Omeo
body: The Great Alpine Road climbs through Harrietville and Dinner Plain before descending to Omeo. It is sealed, but weather, cyclists and sharp bends keep speeds low.
Use a holiday park or established campground around Omeo before taking on more remote roads. Ask locally about closures and recent storm damage.

sections.heading: River camps and seasonal roads
body: Howqua Hills and other river valleys can be popular, basic and vulnerable to flood or fire closures. Camp on durable ground and keep clear of riverbanks in rising weather.
Many mountain tracks close seasonally. A closed gate is not an invitation to find a way around it.

sections.heading: Four-wheel drive tracks and seasonal closures
body: The High Country's famous tracks, including Billy Goat Bluff and the Blue Rag Range, are four-wheel drive only, steep and often closed seasonally. Seasonal road closures typically run from the Queen's Birthday weekend in June to the Melbourne Cup weekend in November.
The sealed roads through Bright, Mount Beauty, Omeo and Dargo remain open year round and reach excellent camping without needing a four-wheel drive. Do not assume you need one to enjoy this region.

Check the Parks Victoria closure list before planning any track. Driving a closed seasonal road carries fines and does real damage to a surface that is closed precisely because it is fragile when wet.

sections.heading: Rivers, huts and the cattlemen's history
body: The high plains are dotted with historic cattlemen's huts, many maintained by volunteer associations. They are emergency shelter rather than accommodation, and the convention is to leave them stocked, swept and available.
The Mitta Mitta, Ovens and Howqua rivers all have excellent riverside camping, much of it free and first come. These fill fast over long weekends and summer, and the access tracks vary in difficulty.
Craig's Hut on the Mount Stirling road is the best known, rebuilt after fires and reached by a moderate drive. It is worth the detour for the view across the ranges alone.
tips: River sites fill on long weekends

sections.heading: Alpine weather and fire risk
body: Snow falls on the high plains from roughly June to September and can occur outside those months. Even in summer, alpine nights are cold and weather changes fast, so carry warm layers regardless of the forecast in Bright.

Summer brings serious bushfire risk to this country, and the High Country has burnt repeatedly. Check fire danger ratings daily, understand that campgrounds in forest are poor places to shelter, and leave early on bad days.
Total fire bans are common through summer and prohibit all open flame including solid fuel barbecues. Carry a gas cooker, which is generally still permitted, and check the specific ban conditions.
tips: Check fire ratings daily in summer
Gas cooker for total fire ban days

sections.heading: Bright, Beechworth and the rail trails
body: Bright is the natural base with services, breweries and the Murray to Mountains Rail Trail, a sealed cycle path running to Beechworth and Wangaratta. Bike hire is straightforward and the trail suits all abilities.
Autumn is Bright's season, with European deciduous trees turning through April and May and the Autumn Festival drawing crowds. Book accommodation well ahead for that window.
Beechworth is a well preserved gold rush town with the Ned Kelly history, and Milawa nearby has the food and wine. Together they make an easy two-day loop off the alpine roads.
tips: Autumn colour through April and May

sections.heading: Fly fishing and the rivers
body: The Mitta Mitta, Howqua, Delatite and King rivers hold trout and the region is one of Australia's best fly fishing areas. A Victorian recreational fishing licence is required and easily bought online.
Closed seasons apply to some waters to protect spawning, generally over winter. Check the current rules for the specific river before fishing, because they differ between waters.
Mount Buffalo is the accessible alpine option with sealed road access to the plateau, granite tors and walks suitable for most people.
Seasonal road closures are published annually by Parks Victoria, and the dates shift slightly each year with conditions, so confirm before planning an alpine track.

flinders-ranges-camping-guide.title: Flinders Ranges camping guide
flinders-ranges-camping-guide.description: Ancient folded ranges, dry creek beds and campfire-coloured evenings around Ikara.
flinders-ranges-camping-guide.intro: The Flinders Ranges are easiest from April to October. Use Hawker or Wilpena as a base, then decide whether the rougher northern roads fit your vehicle and experience.

sections.heading: Hawker and Ikara
body: Hawker is the practical gateway for fuel, food and local road advice. Inside Ikara-Flinders Ranges National Park, choose a booked campground that matches your setup and walking plans.
Start ridge and pound walks early. Carry water and respect cultural guidance around Ikara and other significant places.

sections.heading: Brachina and Bunyeroo
body: The gorge roads reveal geology and wildlife at a slower pace. Conditions change after rain and creek crossings can close, so check with the park before entering.
Yellow-footed rock-wallabies are best watched quietly from a distance. Do not feed wildlife or crowd a sighting with vehicles.

sections.heading: North to Parachilna and Arkaroola
body: Parachilna provides a memorable pub stop before the road pushes farther north. Arkaroola is remote, with private accommodation and activities that benefit from advance booking.
Fuel range, tyres and heat matter more beyond the central park. Turn back early if the road or vehicle is not right.

sections.heading: Wilpena Pound and the walks
body: Wilpena Pound is a natural amphitheatre roughly seventeen kilometres long, and the walks range from the easy Wangara Lookout to the demanding St Mary Peak, which is the highest point in the ranges at 1,171 metres.

St Mary Peak is a serious six to eight hour day with scrambling near the summit. Adnyamathanha Traditional Owners ask visitors not to climb to the summit itself for cultural reasons, and the outside route to Tanderra Saddle is the respectful alternative.
Start early in any season. Summer temperatures here exceed forty degrees and walks become genuinely dangerous, with rangers closing tracks on extreme days.
tips: Traditional Owners ask you not to summit St Mary Peak
Tracks close on extreme heat days

sections.heading: When to visit
body: Autumn and spring are the seasons here. April to May and August to October give comfortable temperatures for walking and, after winter rain, the wildflower displays through the ranges can be exceptional.
Summer is severe, with sustained heat above forty degrees and real risk on any walk. Winter is cold at night with occasional frost but pleasant for walking during the day, and the country is green.
The ranges are also excellent for stargazing, with almost no light pollution. Clear winter nights are the best of the year for it.
tips: Winter nights are best for stars

sections.heading: Roads, fuel and the northern ranges
body: The sealed road reaches Wilpena via Hawker, and beyond that the Flinders becomes unsealed. Brachina Gorge, Bunyeroo and the Moralana Scenic Drive are usually accessible in a two-wheel drive when dry but close after rain.
Fuel is available at Hawker, Wilpena, Blinman and Parachilna, and the gaps are meaningful. Fill up whenever you pass one rather than planning to reach the next.
Further north into Arkaroola and the Gammon Ranges the country becomes genuinely remote and four-wheel drive territory. That is a different trip requiring more preparation than the southern ranges.

sections.heading: Geology and Adnyamathanha country
body: The Flinders exposes some of the oldest visible geology on Earth, including Ediacaran fossils that record early complex life. The Brachina Gorge Geological Trail is a self-guided drive through 130 million years of rock.

This is Adnyamathanha country and the ranges carry creation stories that explain the landscape, including the Pound itself. Guided walks with Adnyamathanha guides are available and transform the visit.
Yellow-footed rock wallabies were nearly lost here and have recovered through predator control. They are most visible around Brachina Gorge in the early morning and late afternoon.

sections.heading: Where to stay in the ranges
body: Wilpena Pound Resort has powered sites and a shop, and the Ikara-Flinders Ranges National Park has campgrounds along Brachina and Bunyeroo with no facilities. Rawnsley Park and Willow Springs are private station options.
Book Wilpena in school holidays and long weekends. The bush campgrounds are first come and rarely full outside those windows, but they have no water, so carry everything you need.
Quorn and Hawker at the southern end have the Pichi Richi railway and good bakeries, and both work as the last restock before the ranges.
Summer here is severe enough that walks close on high temperature days, and the ranges are far better visited in autumn, winter or spring.
tips: Station stays are a good alternative

red-centre-way-camping.title: Red Centre Way camping route
red-centre-way-camping.description: Desert waterholes, red walls and long sunsets between Alice Springs and Uluṟu.
red-centre-way-camping.imageAlt: Red Centre gorge and desert road
red-centre-way-camping.intro: The Red Centre Way links Alice Springs, Tjoritja, Kings Canyon and Uluṟu. Sealed and unsealed options differ, so the route must match the vehicle rather than the line on a map.

sections.heading: Alice Springs to Tjoritja
body: Stock water, food and fuel in Alice Springs, then drive west through Tjoritja. Ormiston Gorge and other designated campgrounds make strong bases for early walks.
A visitor pass or campground booking may be required. Keep footwear on around camp and check waterhole safety advice locally.

sections.heading: Kings Canyon
body: Choose the sealed route unless your vehicle, rental terms and current road advice support an unsealed alternative. Kings Canyon Resort provides the main nearby facilities.
Start the Rim Walk early and obey heat closures. Carry enough water for the full route rather than relying on how cool sunrise feels.

sections.heading: Uluṟu and the return
body: Curtin Springs can break the journey before Yulara. Around Uluṟu, follow Anangu requests, park rules and photography guidance.
Do not squeeze sunrise, a long walk and a major onward drive into one day. Desert fatigue is still fatigue.

sections.heading: The loop and its unsealed section
body: The Red Centre Way links Alice Springs, the West MacDonnell Ranges, Kings Canyon and Uluru. The Mereenie Loop Road between Glen Helen and Kings Canyon is unsealed, requires a permit, and is prohibited in most standard hire agreements.
The sealed alternative runs back through Alice and down the Stuart Highway, adding distance but keeping you on bitumen. Decide which you are doing before hiring the vehicle, not after.
The Mereenie permit is inexpensive and available from visitor centres. It exists because the road crosses Aboriginal land, and camping along it is not permitted.

sections.heading: The West MacDonnells are underrated
body: Ormiston Gorge, Ellery Creek Big Hole, Standley Chasm and Simpsons Gap are all within easy reach of Alice on sealed roads, and several have swimming. Ormiston in particular is one of the best gorges in the country.
The water in these gorges is snowmelt-cold year round because it sits in permanent shade. Swimming is a shock even in forty degree heat, and people have got into trouble misjudging it.
The Larapinta Trail runs 223 kilometres through this country and individual sections make excellent day walks from the road. Section three from Standley Chasm is a good sample.
tips: Gorge water is cold year round

sections.heading: Heat, water and walking safely
body: Central Australian summer regularly exceeds forty degrees and walks are dangerous in it. Rangers close tracks when forecasts pass thresholds, and the Larapinta is effectively a winter trail.

Carry at least four litres of water per person for any walk and more in heat. Start at first light and be finished by mid-morning in summer. Dehydration here develops faster than most visitors expect.
Winter, from May to August, is the season: warm days, cold nights that can drop below freezing, and clear skies. Pack for both ends of that range because the diurnal swing is large.
tips: Four litres per person per walk

sections.heading: Alice Springs as a base
body: Alice has the services, supermarkets, mechanics and hospital that nothing else out here does. Restock properly before heading out on any leg, and deal with vehicle issues here rather than hoping.

The Alice Springs Desert Park and the Royal Flying Doctor Service base both explain the country and how people live in it, and both are worth half a day. The Telegraph Station explains why the town exists at all.
Fuel prices rise sharply once you leave. Fill in Alice, and again at Erldunda or Curtin Springs, and treat every roadhouse as a top-up rather than a decision.

sections.heading: Alice Springs and the desert parks
body: The East MacDonnell Ranges east of Alice are quieter than the west and include Trephina Gorge and the historic Arltunga goldfields. They are frequently overlooked entirely.
Both ranges have basic national park campgrounds requiring a Parks and Wildlife pass. Fees are low, facilities are minimal and most sites are first come outside peak season.
Consider the Larapinta Trail as a reason to return, since individual sections make excellent multi-day walks with vehicle support available.
Winter nights in central Australia drop below freezing while days stay warm, so pack for a genuinely large temperature swing rather than a single climate.

kangaroo-island-camping-guide.title: Kangaroo Island camping guide
kangaroo-island-camping-guide.description: Wild beaches, slow roads and wildlife-filled evenings beyond the ferry at Penneshaw.
kangaroo-island-camping-guide.intro: Kangaroo Island is larger and slower than many first visits allow. Four or five nights gives the west end, south coast and quieter northern beaches enough room.

sections.heading: Ferry and first night
body: Reserve the vehicle ferry and arrive with enough time for check-in. Penneshaw is an easy first night, while American River or Kingscote provides more groceries and services.
Check what food and plant material can be taken to the island. Biosecurity protects local agriculture and wildlife.

sections.heading: Flinders Chase and the south coast
body: Drive to Flinders Chase in daylight. Wildlife is active near the road and distances take longer than expected. Park entry and campground bookings are separate checks.
Vivonne Bay works as a central south-coast base. Wind and surf change quickly, so read local swimming advice before entering the water.

sections.heading: North coast and the return
body: Stokes Bay and the north coast reward a slow day. Carry food and water away from the main towns, then refuel before the ferry rather than arriving on fumes.
Leave a generous buffer for the drive back to Penneshaw. A missed ferry is an expensive way to learn how slow island roads can be.

sections.heading: Getting there and the ferry
body: The SeaLink ferry runs from Cape Jervis to Penneshaw, takes about 45 minutes and carries vehicles. Fares are set by vehicle length and the crossing books out over summer and school holidays, so reserve well ahead.
Taking your own vehicle is usually better value than hiring on the island, where the fleet is small and prices reflect that. Fuel on the island is also more expensive, so arrive with a full tank.
The island is larger than most visitors expect at around 155 kilometres end to end, with many unsealed roads. Three days is a realistic minimum and four is better.
tips: 155 km end to end, allow 3 to 4 days

sections.heading: Recovering from the 2020 fires
body: The 2019 to 2020 bushfires burnt roughly half the island, including much of Flinders Chase National Park. Regeneration is well advanced and the landscape is genuinely interesting to see recovering, but some facilities and tracks remain altered.
Check current park status and track openings before planning specific walks. Flinders Chase facilities have been progressively rebuilt and the situation has changed several times since the fires.

The eastern end of the island was largely unburnt and holds much of the wildlife viewing, including Seal Bay and the penguin colonies. Plan around what is open rather than what a pre-2020 guidebook describes.

sections.heading: Wildlife and how to see it responsibly
body: Seal Bay allows a guided beach walk among wild Australian sea lions, one of the few places anywhere this is possible. Bookings are required and the boardwalk option is available without a guide.

Kangaroo Island has a distinct kangaroo subspecies, plus koalas, echidnas and a population of Ligurian honeybees that is the last pure strain in the world. Because of that, importing honey or used beekeeping equipment is prohibited.
Wildlife on roads is the main hazard here. Do not drive after dark: the roadkill rate is high, many roads are unsealed and unlit, and animal strikes are the most common way visitors damage vehicles.
tips: No honey imports to the island

sections.heading: Camping and the food
body: National park campgrounds in Flinders Chase and along the coast are booked through the South Australian parks system and fill in peak season. There are also commercial parks at Penneshaw, Kingscote and American River.

The island produces excellent food: sheep dairy, honey, gin, marron and seafood, with several producers open for tastings. It is one of the better places in the country to eat well from a camp kitchen.
Fresh produce cannot be brought onto the island under South Australian quarantine rules in some circumstances, so check before loading the vehicle in Adelaide.

sections.heading: Remarkable Rocks and the west end
body: Remarkable Rocks and Admirals Arch sit at the western end in Flinders Chase and are the island's signature landscapes. Both are exposed, and the rocks are slippery and unfenced above a considerable drop.
The west end is roughly two hours from the ferry, which makes it a full day out and a strong argument for camping at that end rather than driving back and forth from Penneshaw.
Kingscote and American River on the eastern side have the services and the calmest water, and both are considerably closer to the ferry than Flinders Chase.
Ferry sailings book out over summer and school holidays, and a missed crossing on an island itinerary costs a full day rather than an hour.
tips: Remarkable Rocks are slippery and unfenced

blue-mountains-camping-weekend.title: Blue Mountains camping weekend from Sydney
blue-mountains-camping-weekend.description: Two nights of sandstone lookouts, eucalypt valleys and cold air close to Sydney.
blue-mountains-camping-weekend.intro: A Blue Mountains camping weekend works when the first night is simple and the driving stops before Friday fatigue takes over.

sections.heading: Friday evening
body: For a late departure, use a booked caravan park or campground with clear after-hours arrival instructions. Do not navigate an unfamiliar forest road in darkness just to save an hour in the morning.
Katoomba, Blackheath and Lithgow provide food and fuel. Temperatures can be much lower than Sydney, especially in exposed or high camps.

sections.heading: Saturday in the park
body: Choose one walking area rather than crossing the mountains between lookouts. Blackheath suits Grose Valley views, while Katoomba and Wentworth Falls offer classic cliff walks.
Euroka and Murphys Glen can suit different vehicles and conditions. Check booking, access, fire and water information before leaving sealed roads.

sections.heading: Sunday without the rush
body: Pack camp before the main walk if rain is due. A dry tent in the vehicle makes the trip home much easier.
Return before the late-afternoon motorway queue or stop for an early meal. Wildlife and tired walkers share the roads near dusk.

sections.heading: It is a valley system, not a mountain range
body: The Blue Mountains are a dissected plateau, which means the walks mostly go down first and climb back at the end when you are tired. The Grand Canyon and National Pass tracks both work this way and catch people out.

The Three Sisters at Echo Point is the famous view and the busiest spot. Sublime Point, Govetts Leap and Evans Lookout give comparable views with a fraction of the people, and are worth the short drives.
Katoomba is under two hours from Sydney, which makes this the standard Sydney weekend and means campgrounds and accommodation fill from Friday evening.
tips: Govetts Leap beats Echo Point for crowds

sections.heading: Where to camp
body: Blue Mountains National Park has campgrounds at Euroka, Ingar, Murphys Glen and Perrys Lookdown, most requiring booking through NSW National Parks. Euroka is the most accessible and known for kangaroos.
Vehicle entry fees apply to parts of the park separately from camping fees. The Glenbrook entrance in particular has gate hours, so check closing time before planning a late arrival.
Several campgrounds are two-wheel drive accessible but a few require high clearance, particularly after rain. Check the specific site rather than assuming.

sections.heading: Canyoning, climbing and safety
body: The Blue Mountains are a major canyoning destination and the slot canyons here are world class. They are also cold, technical and require abseiling skills, wetsuits and proper equipment. Guided trips are the sensible entry point.

Flash flooding is the specific hazard. Never enter a canyon if rain is forecast anywhere in the catchment, and understand that rain kilometres away can fill a slot canyon with no warning at the entrance.
On the walking tracks, the cliff edges are largely unfenced and the sandstone crumbles. Stay back from edges, particularly when wet, and do not step past barriers for a photograph.

sections.heading: Weather and bushfire
body: The mountains are consistently around eight degrees cooler than Sydney and can be genuinely cold, with snow occasionally falling in winter. Visitors regularly arrive underdressed after a warm morning on the coast.
Bushfire risk is severe in summer and the area has burnt repeatedly, including catastrophically in 2019 to 2020. Check fire danger ratings daily and have a plan to leave early rather than shelter.
Winter is arguably the best season here: clear air, long views, comfortable walking temperatures and Yulefest, where the mountain towns run midwinter Christmas dinners.

sections.heading: Jenolan Caves and the western side
body: Jenolan Caves sit beyond Katoomba and hold some of the oldest open cave systems in the world. Access roads have been affected by landslips in recent years, so check the current route before driving out.
Tours book ahead and range from easy walkthroughs to adventure caving. The drive in is steep and winding and unsuitable for large vehicles or caravans.
Wentworth Falls and Leura are quieter bases than Katoomba with the same access to the escarpment walks and better food.
Summer bushfire risk is severe here and the area has burnt repeatedly, so check the fire danger rating before committing to a night in forested camping.

australian-alps-camping-route.title: Australian Alps camping route
australian-alps-camping-route.description: High plains, Snowy River camps and the winding mountain road from Jindabyne to Bright.
australian-alps-camping-route.intro: Jindabyne to Bright crosses national parks, river valleys and high roads. Travel after seasonal roads open and keep an alternative ready for sudden alpine weather.

sections.heading: Jindabyne and Kosciuszko
body: Jindabyne is the resupply point for Kosciuszko National Park. Check park entry, campground bookings and road conditions before heading toward Thredbo, Charlotte Pass or Geehi.
Cold wind and fast storms are normal alpine risks. Carry layers, rain protection and a turnaround time on every walk.

sections.heading: Geehi to Omeo
body: Geehi Flats offers river camping when open and conditions are suitable. Keep a safe distance from the water in wet weather and store food securely.
The road toward Omeo is scenic and demanding. Fuel before the remote section, expect limited reception and stop early if fog or fatigue arrives.

sections.heading: Dinner Plain and Bright
body: Dinner Plain provides a high-country break before the descent to Harrietville and Bright. Even in summer, nights can be cold.
Bright has holiday parks, repairs and an easy finish. Seasonal closures can reshape the entire route, so confirm them before departure, not at the gate.

sections.heading: The Alpine Way and the road network
body: The Alpine Way between Khancoban and Jindabyne is the spine of this route, sealed and open year round. Between the June and October long weekends, 2WD vehicles must carry snow chains on the Alpine Way between Thredbo and Tom Groggin, and NPWS recommends chains for 4WD and AWD vehicles too.
Kosciuszko National Park charges vehicle entry, higher in the ski season. The pass is per vehicle per day and an annual option exists if you are visiting repeatedly.
The Barry Way south to Victoria and several other connecting roads are unsealed, steep and seasonally closed. Check status before planning a crossing between states through the park.

sections.heading: Climbing Kosciuszko
body: Australia's highest point at 2,228 metres is reached either from Thredbo via the chairlift and a 13 kilometre return walk on raised steel mesh, or from Charlotte Pass on a longer 18 kilometre return route.

The Thredbo route is the easy option and genuinely accessible for most people in summer. Neither route is technical, but both are fully exposed alpine terrain with no shelter and weather that changes fast.

In winter both become serious snow routes requiring navigation, avalanche awareness and proper equipment. People die on this mountain in winter, most often after underestimating a walk that is easy in January.
tips: Winter is a serious mountaineering trip

sections.heading: Camping in the alpine country
body: Kosciuszko has campgrounds at Thredbo Diggings, Island Bend, Geehi and Tom Groggin among others, most first come and basic. They fill over summer and long weekends and are cold at night in any season.

Above the treeline, camping is restricted to protect fragile alpine vegetation and water catchments, with minimum distances from lakes and roads. Read the park rules rather than assuming a flat spot is available.
Fires are prohibited across large parts of the park including above the treeline, and total fire bans are common in summer. Carry a gas cooker and check the current restrictions.
tips: Alpine camping is restricted above treeline
Fires prohibited in much of the park

sections.heading: Brumbies, huts and the season
body: The high country huts are historic shelters maintained by volunteers, available as emergency refuge rather than accommodation. Leave them clean, close the doors properly and restock any wood.
Wild horses are present in the park and are a contentious management issue. They are large, unpredictable animals: do not approach or feed them, and take particular care driving at dawn and dusk.
Summer, from December to March, gives wildflowers on the high plains and comfortable walking. Winter is the ski season with a completely different set of requirements, costs and road conditions.

sections.heading: The Snowy scheme and the valleys
body: The Snowy Mountains Scheme shaped this country and the visitor centre at Cooma and the Tumut area explain it. Lake Jindabyne and Lake Eucumbene are both products of it and both have lakeside camping.
Yarrangobilly Caves in the north of Kosciuszko has a thermal pool at twenty seven degrees year round, which is an excellent stop after a cold night on the high plains.
Bright and Mount Beauty on the Victorian side connect this route to the High Country, making a longer alpine loop across both states possible.

Between the June and October long weekends, 2WD vehicles must carry snow chains on Kosciuszko Road from the park boundary at the Thredbo River, on the Alpine Way between Thredbo and Tom Groggin and on the full length of Island Bend/Guthega Road. Chains are not compulsory for 4WD and AWD vehicles, but NPWS recommends carrying them, and any driver must fit chains when park signs or rangers say so.
tips: Lake camping at Jindabyne and Eucumbene

sources.label: Kosciuszko Alpine Way drive visitor info

gibb-river-road-camping.title: Gibb River Road camping guide
gibb-river-road-camping.description: Red dirt, deep gorges and station stays across the wild heart of the Kimberley.
gibb-river-road-camping.imageAlt: Red dirt road through the Kimberley
gibb-river-road-camping.intro: The Gibb River Road is a remote journey through changing conditions, not a guaranteed dry-season highway. Vehicle preparation and current local advice decide whether the trip should proceed.

sections.heading: Prepare in Derby
body: Service the vehicle, inspect tyres and carry the equipment needed to change one safely. Confirm road opening, fuel availability and accommodation before leaving Derby.
Rental agreements often restrict the Gibb or its side tracks. Written permission matters more than a verbal assumption at the counter.
tips: Two sound spare tyres where recommended

sections.heading: Gorges and station stays
body: Windjana Gorge, Mount Barnett and Manning Gorge divide the road into meaningful stops. Station and roadhouse arrangements vary, including fuel hours, camping fees and cash or card availability.
Drive to conditions. Corrugations, creek crossings, dust and sharp stones can change within a day, and speed turns manageable damage into a stranded vehicle.

sections.heading: El Questro to Kununurra
body: The eastern end becomes busier around El Questro. Book popular stays and confirm whether side tracks suit your clearance and experience.
Reach Kununurra with time to inspect the vehicle before the next leg. Heat, fatigue and small mechanical problems accumulate across the Gibb.

sections.heading: This is a serious four-wheel drive route
body: The Gibb River Road runs roughly 660 kilometres between Derby and Kununurra, is largely unsealed, heavily corrugated, and includes river crossings. It requires a high-clearance four-wheel drive and is prohibited under almost every standard hire agreement.

Two spare tyres, tyre repair equipment, a compressor and the knowledge to use them are standard rather than optional. Tyre damage is the single most common problem and recovery costs here are substantial.
Specialist four-wheel drive hire companies in Broome and Darwin permit the Gibb and include the necessary equipment. Using one of those is the practical route for visitors without their own vehicle.

sections.heading: The dry season is the only season
body: The road closes in the wet, roughly November to April, when river crossings become impassable and the surface is destroyed by traffic. It typically reopens around May and closes again around October.
Even within the dry, early season crossings can be deep and late season corrugations are at their worst. June to August is the reliable window with the road graded and the gorges full.
Check the road status with Main Roads WA before setting out and again along the way. Sections close independently and a closure partway is a genuine problem given the distances involved.
tips: June to August is the window

sections.heading: The gorges are the reason
body: Windjana, Bell, Galvans, Adcock, Manning and Emma gorges run along the route, most with swimming and several with waterfalls into deep pools. El Questro at the eastern end holds Zebedee thermal springs and Emma Gorge.

Windjana Gorge has freshwater crocodiles basking on the sand, which are generally harmless if left well alone. Estuarine crocodiles are present in some waterways in this region, so follow the signage at every swimming hole.

Most gorges involve a walk in over rock, sometimes scrambling, and the heat is severe. Start early, carry far more water than the distance suggests and do not attempt the longer gorge walks in the middle of the day.
tips: Follow signage at every swimming hole

sections.heading: Fuel, supplies and communication
body: Fuel is available at Imintji, Mount Barnett, Drysdale River and El Questro, at high prices and sometimes with limited hours. The gaps require genuine range planning and carrying additional fuel is common.

There is no mobile coverage across most of the route. A satellite phone or a personal locator beacon is not optional equipment here, and telling someone your route and expected arrival is basic practice.
Stock food and water for longer than the plan. A breakdown or a closed crossing can add days, and the stations along the route are not shops in any conventional sense.
tips: Fuel at four points, high prices
No mobile coverage, carry a PLB

sections.heading: Station stays along the road
body: Several pastoral stations along the Gibb offer camping, meals and fuel, including Mount Elizabeth, Drysdale River and Home Valley. They are the accommodation network for this route and often the only option.
Most take cash and have limited or no online booking, and phone contact may only be possible by satellite. Plan on arriving rather than reserving, and carry cash for fuel and fees.
Allow at least seven days for the road itself, and more if you intend to include the Mitchell Falls detour, which is rough and adds several days.
Check the road status with Main Roads before departure and again along the way, because sections close independently and a closure partway is a serious problem out here.
tips: Carry cash for fuel and fees

sunshine-coast-hinterland-camping.title: Sunshine Coast and hinterland camping loop
sunshine-coast-hinterland-camping.description: Saltwater mornings and cool rainforest nights in one easy loop north of Brisbane.
sunshine-coast-hinterland-camping.intro: A four-day loop can pair the Sunshine Coast with the Blackall Range and Mary Valley, swapping beach crowds for cool forest whenever the weather turns.

sections.heading: Coast to Mary Valley
body: Start around Caloundra or Noosa, then turn inland before the coast traffic steals the day. Noosa North Shore has special access considerations, including ferry and sand-driving conditions.
Kenilworth offers food, a river-town base and several commercial camping options. Confirm flood risk and ground conditions after heavy rain.

sections.heading: Conondale and the range
body: Conondale National Park and nearby forests bring simple camps, walking and cooler nights. Roads can be narrow or unsealed, so check access for caravans and low-clearance vehicles.
Mapleton, Montville and the Blackall Range provide caravan parks and roofed stays when a wet tent no longer feels romantic.

sections.heading: Glass House Mountains return
body: Finish through the Glass House Mountains and keep walks within signed access. Some steep routes require scrambling experience and dry conditions.
Return to Brisbane before Sunday traffic builds, or add a final powered night around Caloundra and leave early Monday.

sections.heading: Coast and hinterland are two different trips
body: The coastal strip from Caloundra to Noosa is beaches, surf and holiday parks, busy and well serviced. The hinterland behind it, through Maleny, Montville and the Glass House Mountains, is rainforest, waterfalls and small towns twenty minutes inland.
Doing both is what makes the loop worthwhile, and they suit different weather. Keep the hinterland for a day when the beach is blown out, because the rainforest walks are better in cloud anyway.
The whole area is compact enough that you can base in one place and day trip. Noosa or Maleny both work as a single base for four or five days.
tips: One base covers the whole loop

sections.heading: Noosa National Park and the headland
body: The coastal track around Noosa headland is the standout walk, passing Tea Tree Bay and Hells Gates with a genuine chance of wild koalas in the trees along the way. It is flat, accessible and can be done in sections.
Parking at the entrance fills by mid-morning in peak season and the shuttle or a walk from Hastings Street is the practical alternative. Go early for both parking and wildlife.
The park has no camping. Accommodation is in Noosa itself, which is expensive, or the holiday parks at Noosaville and Tewantin which are considerably better value.
tips: No camping in Noosa National Park

sections.heading: The Glass House Mountains
body: These volcanic plugs rise abruptly out of flat country and several can be climbed, with Mount Ngungun the accessible option at around an hour return and Mount Beerwah a genuinely steep scramble.

Mount Tibrogargan and Mount Beerwah both carry cultural significance and specific safety warnings, and there have been fatalities on Tibrogargan. Read the track signage and be honest about your scrambling ability.
The lookout on the Glass House Mountains Road gives the classic view without any climbing, and it is best in the early morning before haze builds.
tips: Lookout gives the view without climbing

sections.heading: Waterfalls, markets and the wet season
body: Kondalilla and Mapleton Falls both have short walks with swimming at Kondalilla, and Gardners Falls near Maleny is a local favourite that stays cool through summer. All run best after rain.
Eumundi Markets on Wednesday and Saturday mornings are among the best known in the country and worth planning a day around. Maleny and Montville have the food and craft side of the hinterland.
Summer here is hot, humid and the wet season brings heavy afternoon storms. Autumn and winter are drier, more comfortable for walking and still warm enough to swim on the coast.
tips: Autumn and winter are most comfortable

sections.heading: Beaches and the surf
body: Coolum, Peregian, Marcoola and Mooloolaba give a run of patrolled beaches with easier parking than Noosa. Swimming between the flags matters here because the surf is real and rips are common.
The Noosa Everglades, reached by boat or kayak from Boreen Point, is one of only two everglade systems in the world and considerably quieter than the coastal strip.
Rainbow Beach and the Cooloola section to the north extend the trip towards K'gari, and the coloured sands are worth the drive on their own.
Summer storms build quickly through the afternoon in this region, so plan walks for the morning and expect the hinterland roads to be slick afterwards.
tips: Coolum parks more easily than Noosa

camping-rules-new-south-wales.title: Camping Rules NSW 2026: Free Camping, State Forests & Fees
camping-rules-new-south-wales.description: Free camp in NSW state forests for up to four weeks. Most national park sites need a booking, $6 even when camping is free. 2026 fire bans and fines.
camping-rules-new-south-wales.imageAlt: National park campground in New South Wales
camping-rules-new-south-wales.intro: Yes, you can free camp in New South Wales: every state forest except Cumberland and Strickland allows free, first-come camping for up to four weeks, and some national park campgrounds charge no camping fee, although most of those still take a $6 booking fee. AussieCamps maps 372 NSW national park campgrounds, 869 roadside rest areas and 347 public dump points.

sections.heading: National park campgrounds
body: NSW national parks have more than 365 campgrounds, and most of those listed on the NSW National Parks website need a booking even when camping is free; those free sites charge a $6 booking fee. A few basic listed sites, such as Tuross River campground in Wadbilliga National Park, need no booking, and remote camping at unlisted sites needs none either, though NPWS recommends a trip intention form.

Camping fees and park entry are separate. Vehicle entry fees apply at 45 of the more than 890 parks and reserves, such as $8 a day at Myall Lakes and Murramarang, and a booking covers only the number of people specified and paid for: NPWS can charge for, or turn away, extra occupants.

sections.heading: Free and roadside camping
body: Official advice on rest areas is mixed. Service NSW says rest areas are not for camping, while the July 2026 planning practice note says camping in one may be permitted unless a council or Transport for NSW has put up a no camping or no overnight stays sign.

Camping outside a caravan park or camping ground usually needs council approval unless an exemption in the Local Government Regulation applies, and councils can ban camping on their land with signs. The fine for ignoring a council sign is set by state law at $110 on the spot, and Crown reserves follow the rules of their Crown land manager.
tips: Use car bays, not truck bays

sections.heading: Fire and park alerts
body: Check the NSW RFS fire danger rating, NPWS park alerts and any park fire ban before you light anything. NPWS can declare a park fire ban or close a park when the fire risk is high, separate from a Total Fire Ban.

In national parks, light fires only in designated fireplaces, never break branches or collect fallen timber, and never run a generator during a fire ban. Not every park allows campfires, so check before you go.

sections.heading: Who manages the land you are on
body: NSW camping rules depend on who manages the land. National Parks and Wildlife Service runs the parks, Forestry Corporation of NSW runs the state forests, councils manage their own land, and Crown land managers look after Crown reserves.

In a state forest you can pitch a tent almost anywhere except on roads, in picnic or permit areas, in pine plantations or in closed forest. Sites cannot be booked, the maximum stay is four weeks unless a sign says less, and many forests have no bins, so take rubbish home.

In a national park you must camp in an area set aside for camping, unless the park allows remote camping, and for no more than 21 days in a row unless a park sign or the plan of management sets a different limit. Camping anywhere else in a park carries a maximum penalty of 30 penalty units.
tips: Forests: free, four weeks at most
Parks: 21 days unless signs say otherwise
Councils decide where camping is banned

sections.heading: Booking NPWS campgrounds
body: Popular coastal campgrounds can book out over summer and school holidays, so book as soon as your dates are fixed. The camping fee is charged in full at the time of booking, plus a non-refundable booking fee.
Cancelling 31 days or more before arrival refunds 75% of the fee, and cancelling later refunds 50%. Neither refund includes the booking fee.

The All Parks Pass costs $190 a year and covers vehicle entry at all 45 fee-collecting parks, including Kosciuszko, with restrictions at Chowder Bay and the Cape Byron lighthouse precinct, but no annual pass covers camping. Kosciuszko entry is $29 per 24 hours from the June long weekend to the October long weekend and $17 for the rest of the year.

sections.heading: Fires and total fire bans
body: The statutory Bush Fire Danger Period runs from 1 October to 31 March, although local conditions can change it. During it, the RFS decides each afternoon whether to declare a Total Fire Ban for the next day, and a ban can also be declared on the day itself.

On a Total Fire Ban day you cannot light a fire in the open or use a solid-fuel barbecue, and lighting a fire brings an on-the-spot fine of $2,200, or up to $5,500 and 12 months in jail if it goes to court. In national parks, visitor-owned gas and electric cookers are generally banned too, except inside a caravan or its three-sided annexe.

State forests also declare solid fuel fire bans, during which only gas appliances may be used, with a maximum penalty of $2,200. When forest fires are allowed, keep them under one square metre and 4.5 metres from the nearest log, stump or tree, with 2 metres of ground cleared around them.
tips: Visitor gas generally banned in parks on ban days

sections.heading: Free camping and rest areas
body: Free camping in NSW mostly means state forests, plus national park campgrounds with no camping fee, most of which still charge a $6 booking fee. Camping is generally not allowed in state forest picnic areas, except at rest areas where highways pass through a forest.

Dogs are welcome in all state forests but must be under your control at all times, and Forestry Corporation asks that they stay on a lead. They are not allowed in most national parks, though some regional parks, such as Murrumbidgee Valley Regional Park, accept them, and many forests border national parks.
Councils decide where camping is banned on their land, and many ban it in beachfront car parks, so check the signs and the council's rules before staying overnight.
tips: State forests are the free option
No dogs in most national parks

sections.heading: Marine parks and coastal access
body: NSW marine parks have sanctuary zones where fishing is banned, and the zones are shown on the official zoning maps and in the FishSmart NSW app, because boundaries are not always obvious from the shore.

Beach driving is allowed only on some NSW beaches, and the rules vary: some need a council beach permit, some national park beaches need a park pass, and Worimi Conservation Lands near Port Stephens needs its own vehicle access permit, which annual park passes do not cover.
Many coastal campgrounds sit inside national parks, so the 21-day limit, the no-dogs rule and NPWS fire bans apply even where the beach feels like public land.
Check NPWS park alerts on the morning you travel, because coastal parks close roads after storms and campgrounds after fire or flood damage.
tips: Park rules apply on park beaches

faq: Can you free camp in New South Wales?

Yes. Every NSW state forest except Cumberland and Strickland allows free camping for up to four weeks, first come first served. Some national park campgrounds have no camping fee but still need a booking with a $6 booking fee.
Do you need to book NSW national park campsites?

For most listed campgrounds, yes, including free ones, which charge a $6 booking fee, and popular coastal campgrounds can book out over summer and school holidays. A few basic listed sites, such as Tuross River campground, and remote camping at unlisted sites need no booking.

camping-rules-queensland.title: Camping Rules Queensland 2026: Permits, Free Camps & Fees
camping-rules-queensland.description: No free camping in Queensland parks or forests: permits cost $7.75 a person a night in 2026. Free options are council sites; rest areas allow 20 hours.
camping-rules-queensland.intro: Not in Queensland's parks or forests, where every camp needs a paid permit: $7.75 per person or $31 per family a night in 2026. Free camping means council campgrounds that allow it, and roadside rest areas let you stop for up to 20 hours unless a sign says otherwise, though the state says they are not camping sites. AussieCamps maps 517 Queensland park and forest campgrounds, 1,688 roadside rest areas and 324 public dump points.

sections.heading: Book and pay before arrival
body: You must book and pay for a camping permit before you arrive, online through the Queensland National Parks Booking Service, at a booking office or on 13 QGOV (13 74 68). Bookings open 12 months ahead, and the most popular spots are worth booking at least six weeks out.

Once camp is up, display the camping tag or your permit details on the tent, camping structure or vehicle dashboard. Without a printer, write the permit number, camping area, dates, number of people, surname and registration on paper in a clear weatherproof bag.

sections.heading: Bush camps and vehicle access
body: Bush camping is allowed only in some parks. Camp well away from streams, lakes, walking tracks and picnic areas, and where there are no toilets bury human waste at least 50 cm deep and 50 metres from water, tracks and camps.

If you drive in the recreation areas on K'gari, Bribie Island, Mulgumpin (Moreton Island), Minjerribah (North Stradbroke Island) or at Cooloola, you need a vehicle access permit as well as your camping permit. K'gari, Bribie and Cooloola permits can be booked together in the Queensland National Parks Booking Service, and number-plate cameras there mean the vehicle permit no longer has to be displayed.
tips: Bush camp well away from water
Driving on sand needs a vehicle permit

sections.heading: Alerts, weather and fires
body: Check Queensland park alerts, Bureau of Meteorology warnings and local fire bans before leaving. Queensland does not use the term Total Fire Ban: the Queensland Fire Department declares local fire bans for all or part of a council area, and they cover parks and forests.

Campfires are allowed only in camping areas that permit them, in existing QPWS fireplaces, fire rings or fire locations, with wood you bring in, and never during a fire ban or a QPWS fire prohibition. Gas and spirit stoves can still be used during a fire ban if they cannot throw embers, are contained and are never left unattended.

sections.heading: National parks and the permit system
body: The camping fee from 1 July 2026 is $7.75 per person per night, or $31 per family, meaning one or two adults with children under 18, up to eight people. Children under five camp free, and fees rise slightly every July or August.

The permit system covers about 525 camping areas across Queensland's parks and forests, and none of them has electricity. You must reach your site within 24 hours of the permit start and must not leave it unattended for more than 24 hours.

Camping without a permit, or with more people than it covers, carries a maximum penalty of 20 penalty units. Rangers do issue on-the-spot fines: a group of four at Main Range National Park was fined $322 in 2025 for holding a one-person permit.

sections.heading: Crocodile country changes the rules
body: Estuarine crocodiles live between Gladstone and Cape York Peninsula and throughout the Gulf of Carpentaria, in any waterway and the sea, including freshwater rivers, lagoons and swamps far inland. Obey every crocodile warning sign.

Set up camp well away from the water's edge, because crocodiles have attacked people in tents pitched too close to it. Do not swim or wade in croc country, stay at least 5 metres back from the water's edge, and do not clean fish there.

Report crocodile sightings to the Queensland environment department. Every report is investigated under the Queensland Crocodile Management Plan, and crocodiles that pose a threat to people are targeted for removal.

sections.heading: The wet season and road closures
body: Queensland's cyclone season officially runs from 1 November to 30 April, and communities within 50 km of the coast from Bundaberg to Thursday Island and around the Gulf are the most exposed. Even a category 1 cyclone can damage caravans.
Wet-season rain closes unsealed roads and creek crossings quickly. Check park alerts, QLDTraffic and Bureau of Meteorology warnings every day, and never drive into floodwater.

The dry season, roughly May to October, is the best time for far northern camping, but many Cape York parks stay closed into June or July after the wet. Popular sites fill quickly in school and public holidays, so book at least six weeks ahead.
tips: Book popular sites six weeks ahead

sections.heading: Free camping and council sites
body: Free camping in Queensland means council-approved sites, not parks. Rest areas allow general and recreational vehicles to stop for up to 20 hours unless signed otherwise, but the state says they are not camping sites, and heavy-vehicle rest areas are for truck drivers only.

Councils set their own rules, and some run low-cost campgrounds or allow short stays at signed sites, so check the council's website first. Cities are stricter: Cairns bans camping on council land including roadsides, the Esplanade, parks, car parks and beaches.

Camping on a state-controlled road is illegal unless you are managing fatigue between 4pm and 8am, on a road that is not a motorway or toll road, where no sign bans it, outside a built-up area and at least 200 metres from any kerb or footpath. Fires, generators and detached trailers are not allowed, and rest areas ban generators between 7pm and 7am.

sections.heading: K'gari and dingo safety
body: Always walk in groups on K'gari, because walking or sitting alone outside a fenced area makes a dingo encounter more likely. Families with children under 14 are strongly advised to camp in a fenced campground.
Never store food in your tent, and do not bring food or picnic on the lake shore or beach. Fines of up to $28,495 apply to anyone who disturbs or harms dingoes on K'gari.

Dogs and other pets are not allowed in Queensland national parks, though some conservation parks, state forests and recreation areas accept them. You may drive through a national park with a dog only on gazetted roads, with the dog inside the vehicle and without stopping at day-use areas, lookouts or other sites.
Drones are banned in every camping area in Queensland's protected areas, recreation areas and forests, so keep the drone stored in a container in your vehicle.

faq: Do you need a permit to camp in Queensland national parks?

Yes. Every camp in a Queensland national park, state forest or recreation area needs a permit booked and paid for before you arrive, $7.75 per person or $31 per family a night in 2026, and the tag or permit details must be displayed at camp.
Where can you free camp in Queensland?

Not in parks or forests, which all charge. Free camping means council campgrounds that allow it. Roadside rest areas let you stop for up to 20 hours unless a sign says otherwise, but the state says they are not camping sites, and many coastal councils, including Cairns, ban camping on council land.

sources.label: Where to camp in Queensland parks
Dogs and pets in Queensland parks

camping-rules-victoria.title: Camping Rules Victoria 2026: Free Camping, Forests & Fees
camping-rules-victoria.description: Free camp in Victorian state forests for up to 28 nights, 20 m from water. Bookable Parks Victoria camps are half price until July 2027. 2026 fire rules.
camping-rules-victoria.intro: Yes, you can free camp in Victoria: state forests let you camp almost anywhere for up to 28 consecutive nights if you stay at least 20 metres from waterways, every state forest campground is free except Murrindindi Scenic Reserve, and some Parks Victoria campgrounds charge nothing and take no bookings. AussieCamps maps 438 Victorian campgrounds, 350 of them state forest and Crown land sites managed by DEECA and 88 run by Parks Victoria, plus 651 roadside rest areas and 181 public dump points.

sections.heading: Bookings and campground conditions
body: Bookable Parks Victoria campgrounds need a booking made in advance with your vehicle registration. You no longer have to print or display the permit, but make sure the car registration on your booking is correct; you can update it at any time through 'manage booking' in the confirmation email.

Some park campgrounds are free with no booking, such as Warby-Ovens National Park and King Hut in the Alpine National Park, while others open only in certain seasons: Lake Catani at Mount Buffalo is closed from 31 August to 30 October 2026. Don't take a booked or closed site just because it looks empty.

sections.heading: State forests and roadside stops
body: State forests run on different rules from national parks. You can camp anywhere in a state forest at least 20 metres from a waterway for no more than 28 consecutive nights, but in forest reserves you must use the campgrounds the land manager provides.

Rest areas are built for rest breaks, not camping. Those on major roads are run by Transport Victoria and councils set overnight rules on local roads, so follow the signs at each stop and don't stay overnight unless a sign allows it.

sections.heading: Fire and alpine access
body: Fire conditions in Victoria change from day to day, and on Total Fire Ban days fires are more likely to spread quickly. Check the VicEmergency app and the park alert page every morning in summer, and never light a fire when restrictions prohibit it.
Alpine and forest roads close for winter and after storms. Respect locked gates, and keep a lower-altitude campground in reserve in case the high country turns you back.

sections.heading: Parks Victoria and the booking system
body: Camping fees at 131 bookable Parks Victoria campgrounds have been half price since 1 July 2025, and the Victorian Government has funded that until July 2027. The earlier free-camping scheme at those campgrounds ended on 30 June 2025, so a booking and a fee still apply.

Peak season at Wilsons Promontory is handled through quarterly booking releases, not a ballot. Tidal River bookings for 1 March to 30 June 2027 opened on 28 September 2026, and over the summer peak, 20 December 2026 to 24 January 2027, campsites need a 7-night minimum stay arriving and leaving on a Sunday. Since 1 July 2026 some Great Ocean Road campsites are booked through the Great Ocean Road Coast and Parks Authority.

One booking can now hold up to three campsites in the same campground. Most sites include one vehicle in the fee and Tidal River allows two cars per site, so check the limit on the booking before you bring a second car or trailer.
tips: Up to three sites per booking

sections.heading: State forests and dispersed camping
body: Victoria's state forests have more than 300 campgrounds, and all of them are free except Murrindindi Scenic Reserve, where a small permit fee applies. There are no facilities at informal sites, so bring water, a shovel and every bag of rubbish back out.

Dig toilet holes at least 30 cm deep and 100 metres from any waterway, and tip washing-up water at least 50 metres from rivers and creeks. Building anything permanent or semi-permanent needs a permit.

Seasonal road closures run from June to November each year to protect tracks that are easily damaged when wet. In 2026 most closures in Parks Victoria parks started on 4 or 11 June and lifted on 29 October; check the FFMVic closures map for state forest roads, and expect a fine for driving a closed road.

sections.heading: Fire restrictions and the danger period
body: The Fire Danger Period starts and ends at different dates in each council area, usually before summer and lasting until April or May. For 2026-27 it began on 5 October in East Gippsland and Wellington.

In a state forest, use a purpose-built fireplace if you can, either a site firepit or a portable one, keep the fire under one metre across with three metres cleared around it, and never leave it unattended. During the Fire Danger Period the fire must be in a stone, metal or concrete fireplace or a trench at least 30 cm deep, and in national and state parks you may only use the fireplaces the park provides.

On a Total Fire Ban day, campfires and barbecues or stoves that burn solid or chemical fuel are banned across every district the ban covers, and some bans cover the whole state. CFA warns that lighting a fire on one of those days can bring a fine of more than $40,000, two years in prison, or both.

sections.heading: Free camping and the coast
body: Some coastal councils are strict. Surf Coast Shire, which covers Torquay, Anglesea and Lorne, makes sleeping in a vehicle anywhere in the shire an offence with a $300 on-the-spot fine, so don't sleep in your vehicle in any car park or street there; book a caravan park or campground instead.
Some inland councils run free or low-cost camping areas, and some showgrounds take campers. Check the council website or ask at the visitor centre for the current arrangement.

Wilsons Promontory bans pets, drones, generators, campfires and solid-fuel barbecues, and dogs are generally not allowed in Victorian national parks. State forests are the dog-friendly alternative, with dogs on a lead or under control around camps and facilities.
tips: Some inland towns offer free sites

sections.heading: Alpine and river camping specifics
body: On the Bogong High Plains, dispersed camping is not allowed within 200 metres of the Bogong High Plains or Pretty Valley roads. Firewood is scarce up high, so Parks Victoria asks campers to use a stove.

On licensed Crown river frontages, often grazed by the neighbouring farm, you may camp only in designated areas, for up to 14 nights, more than 20 metres from the water and 200 metres from a house, and without dogs. On unlicensed Crown frontages you can camp more than 20 metres from the water and 200 metres from a house for up to 28 consecutive nights.
Parks Victoria publishes the seasonal road closure list each year, and reading it before planning a High Country loop saves a wasted drive to a locked gate.

Carry a gas stove. On a Total Fire Ban day you can still cook on one if it is stable, nothing flammable is within three metres, you supervise it the whole time and you have at least 10 litres of water on hand.

faq: Can you camp for free in Victoria?

Yes. You can camp in most of Victoria's state forests at no charge for up to 28 consecutive nights, at least 20 metres from waterways, every state forest campground is free except Murrindindi Scenic Reserve, and some Parks Victoria campgrounds such as King Hut and Warby-Ovens are free with no booking.
Do Victorian national park campsites need booking?

Bookable campgrounds do, and their camping fees have been half price since July 2025 and stay that way until July 2027. Wilsons Promontory uses quarterly booking releases rather than a ballot, and some Great Ocean Road sites are now booked through the Great Ocean Road Coast and Parks Authority.

camping-rules-tasmania.title: Camping Rules Tasmania 2026: Free Camps, Parks Pass & Fires
camping-rules-tasmania.description: Free camp in Tasmania at signed council sites, free park camps and forestry land. 2026 Parks Pass prices, new camp fees from 3 November and fire rules.
camping-rules-tasmania.intro: Yes, you can free camp in Tasmania: at council sites that allow it, at free Parks and Wildlife Service campgrounds such as Huon and Teds Beach in Southwest National Park, and on most Sustainable Timber Tasmania land unless a sign prohibits it. Inside national parks you need a Parks Pass, campground fees come on top, and both bookings and fees change on 3 November 2026. AussieCamps maps 27 Tasmanian park campgrounds and 80 public dump points.

sections.heading: Parks passes and bookings
body: A valid parks pass is required to enter any Tasmanian national park, whether you arrive by car, on foot, by bus or by bike, and campground fees are paid on top. Free campsites inside a park, such as the Freycinet walker camps, still need the pass.

Parks and Wildlife Service moves to a new Parks Online Booking System on 3 November 2026 and has paused new bookings for stays from that date at campgrounds including Fortescue Bay and Richardsons Beach at Freycinet. Check when bookings reopen before fixing ferry dates around one site.

sections.heading: Free camps and local rules
body: Council camping sites set their own conditions. Northern Midlands Council issues a free permit for self-contained vehicles to stay up to 48 hours. Central Coast Council allows up to three nights for self-contained vehicles, but it is moving its sites to a paid permit of $15 a night, so check the signs at each site rather than an old review.

On reserved land you must not camp in a designated camping-prohibited area or within 500 metres of a road outside a designated camping area, with a fine of up to 20 penalty units. Sustainable Timber Tasmania welcomes camping on the land it manages except where signs prohibit it.
tips: Council limits vary: check each sign

sections.heading: Weather and biosecurity
body: Tasmanian weather turns fast, and severe cold, wet and windy conditions can arrive at any time of year, even in summer. Pack for cold rain in January and move off exposed camps when the Bureau of Meteorology issues a severe weather warning for damaging winds.
Clean boots, bikes and camping gear before moving between walks and waterways, so soil, seeds and water pests do not travel with you into the wilderness.

sections.heading: Parks passes are compulsory
body: Prices from 1 July 2026: a daily pass costs $49.15 per vehicle carrying up to eight people, or $24.55 per person on foot, bus or bike, and it does not cover Cradle Mountain. The holiday pass covers every national park for up to two months for $98.35 per vehicle, and the annual pass costs $104.75.
Two daily passes cost about the same as one holiday pass, so it pays from the third day of park visits. Buy it online at passes.parks.tas.gov.au before you travel.

Cradle Mountain runs a shuttle from the visitor centre, and private vehicles cannot drive into the park while it operates. The Cradle Mountain daily pass costs $30.70 per adult and includes the shuttle; holiday pass holders buy a shuttle ticket separately.
tips: Private cars wait for the shuttle

sections.heading: Quarantine at the border
body: Tasmania has strict biosecurity rules, and fresh fruit and vegetables are among the items you cannot bring in. X-ray machines and detector dogs screen arrivals at Hobart and Launceston airports.

On the Spirit of Tasmania you can eat your own food on board, but leftovers go in the bins on board or at the biosecurity inspection point as you leave the terminal. Staff at Geelong ask biosecurity questions before boarding, and Biosecurity Tasmania runs random vehicle checks at Devonport.

Penalties apply to restricted items that are not declared, and the rules protect an island that is free of several pests found on the mainland. Eat or bin fresh food before you sail and restock in Devonport.
tips: Bin food before leaving the terminal

sections.heading: Alpine weather in any season
body: Walks above the treeline are alpine outings whatever the forecast at the car park says. Cold, wet and windy weather can arrive in any month on the high plateaus, including in the middle of summer.
Carry warm and waterproof layers on every walk, including in January. Hypothermia develops quickly in wind and rain, even on a short walk from the car.
Sign the logbook at the track head and leave your plan with someone at home, because both are what searchers check first when a walker is overdue.

sections.heading: Free camping and the west
body: Huon and Teds Beach in Southwest National Park take no bookings and charge no camping fee, and Freycinet's Wineglass Bay, Hazards and Cooks Beach walker camps and Encampment Cove on Maria Island are also free to camp. The parks pass still applies inside each park.

Other park campgrounds are booked or first come depending on the season. Fortescue Bay takes bookings from 1 October to 30 April and is first in, first served from May to September, and from 3 November 2026 it charges $24 a site for up to six people.
The west coast is wet, remote and thinly serviced. Fill up and shop in Queenstown or Strahan, because the gaps between towns on that side of the island are long.
tips: Fortescue Bay: $24 a site from 3 Nov
Fuel up before the west coast

sections.heading: Walking track regulations
body: The Overland Track needs a booking and a fee from 1 October to 31 May: $312 per adult, with lower fees for children and concession holders, walking north to south only. Bookings open on the first Tuesday in July, and the fee includes park entry for the walk and the shuttle.
Outside the booking season, from June to September, there is no Overland Track fee, but you still need a parks pass, must register your walk online with PWS and need full winter gear.

Fuel Stove Only Areas ban campfires all year across much of the wilderness, including Cradle Mountain-Lake St Clair, Freycinet, Mount Field, Southwest and the Walls of Jerusalem, whatever the fire danger rating. A few marked sites in the World Heritage Area and Tasman National Park allow fires in existing fireplaces.

On a Total Fire Ban day all outdoor fires are banned in parks. LPG and electric stoves are the only exceptions, methylated spirits and shellite stoves are not allowed, and Freycinet bans every naked flame in the open, gas included.
tips: Fuel Stove Only Areas ban fires
No liquid-fuel stoves on ban days

faq: Do you need a parks pass to camp in Tasmania?

Yes, inside a national park. The pass covers entry and most park campgrounds charge a fee on top. The holiday pass, $98.35 per vehicle for up to two months, beats daily passes from the third day, and council campgrounds outside parks need no pass.
Can you free camp in Tasmania?

Yes, at council sites that allow it, at free park campgrounds such as Huon and Teds Beach in Southwest National Park, and on most Sustainable Timber Tasmania land unless signs say otherwise. On reserved land you cannot camp within 500 metres of a road outside a designated camping area.
