camping-rules-south-australia.title: Camping Rules South Australia 2026: Free Camps, Parks & Fees
camping-rules-south-australia.description: Free camp on SA Crown land for up to 21 days; book national park campsites before you arrive. 2026 fees, fire season dates, fruit fly rules and fines.
camping-rules-south-australia.intro: Yes, you can free camp in South Australia, but only where the land manager allows it: Crown land allows camping for up to 21 days without approval, councils set the rules for their own reserves, and almost every national park campsite must be booked before you arrive, the Simpson Desert parks being the exception. AussieCamps maps 115 South Australian park campgrounds, 391 roadside rest areas and 199 public dump points.

sections.heading: Book before you go
body: Almost every South Australian national park campsite must be booked before arrival, online or through a booking agent, and bookings open up to 12 months ahead; the Munga-Thirri-Simpson Desert parks use the Desert Parks Pass instead. Check how many vehicles a site takes and its facilities before paying, because sites are priced by both.

A campground booking usually covers vehicle entry to that park, with Flinders Chase on Kangaroo Island the main exception. Keep the confirmation on your phone, and expect parks in the affected district to close on catastrophic fire danger days even when you hold a booking.

sections.heading: Campfires and pets
body: Collecting firewood is banned in South Australian parks, so bring clean, untreated wood where fires are allowed and use the pit provided. Ikara-Flinders Ranges bans wood fires from 15 October 2026 to 24 March 2027, and inside Wilpena Pound itself wood, solid-fuel and gas fires are banned all year, except gas at Wilcolo Camp.

Most national parks do not allow dogs or other pets, and Ikara-Flinders Ranges is one of them. Some parks allow dogs on a lead no longer than two metres; the park page says which, and a lead does not override a no-pets rule.

sections.heading: Remote country
body: Outback tracks and desert park roads close after rain, often for days and, after major floods, for months. Check the park alert and the outback road report from the Department for Infrastructure and Transport before leaving the bitumen, and never drive around a closed sign.
Carry more water and fuel than the distance suggests, plus a way to call for help where there is no mobile coverage, such as a satellite messenger or a personal locator beacon.

sections.heading: Parks passes and booking
body: Park entry and camping are separate products. A Multiple Entry Parks Pass covers vehicle entry only, as a single-park pass for 12 months or a multi-park pass for two or 12 months, and camping is still booked on top; the Desert Parks Pass is the exception and includes camping.

Most South Australian parks are free to enter. Where a day fee applies it is usually charged per vehicle, such as $14.40 at Ikara-Flinders Ranges, while Flinders Chase on Kangaroo Island charges each person instead.

Bookings open 12 months ahead, so book school holidays and long weekends as soon as your dates are fixed. Ikara-Flinders Ranges campsites start at $12.30 a night, while the powered sites and permanent tents at Wilpena are run by Wilpena Pound Resort rather than the parks booking system.
tips: Most parks are free to enter

sections.heading: Fruit fly quarantine
body: Travellers cannot bring fruit fly host fruit and vegetables, or some plants and plant products, into South Australia. The list depends on the state you are coming from, and a receipt does not make produce legal.

PIRSA checks vehicles at quarantine stations such as Yamba on the Sturt Highway and at random roadblocks, and from 1 July 2026 the fine for carrying restricted produce is up to $423. Eat or bin it before the border, because there is no disposal at Yamba itself, and restock from a shop once across.

The Riverland has its own controls inside the state. Buy fruit and vegetables there from accredited retailers rather than roadside stalls or markets, and check the current outbreak restrictions before a Murray River leg.
tips: No restricted fruit over the border

sections.heading: Outback travel and permits
body: The Desert Parks Pass gives 12 months of vehicle entry and camping in the far north: Innamincka Regional Reserve, Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre, Malkumba-Coongie Lakes, Munga-Thirri-Simpson Desert, Tallaringa and Witjira, plus entry only to Wabma Kadarbu Mound Springs, where camping is not allowed.

It is mandatory only for the Munga-Thirri-Simpson Desert National Park and Regional Reserve and for travel east of Dalhousie Springs in Witjira, and the Simpson Desert parks close every year from 1 December to 15 March. Elsewhere in the desert parks you can pay day entry and camping fees instead.

On the Oodnadatta, Strzelecki and Birdsville tracks, carry spare parts and two spare tyres, extra water and fuel for delays, and a satellite phone, beacon or UHF radio. Mobile reception is often unreliable once you leave town.
tips: Simpson Desert closed 1 Dec to 15 Mar

sections.heading: Fire restrictions
body: South Australia's Fire Danger Season is set by district. In 2026-27 it starts on 15 October in the Flinders, Eastern Eyre, West Coast and pastoral districts and on 1 November in the South East, Murraylands and Riverland, and runs into April. During it a campfire must sit in a trench 30 cm deep and no more than one square metre, with 4 m cleared around and above it, and a responsible person present at all times with water or an extinguisher.

On a Total Fire Ban day campfires and solid-fuel barbecues are banned. National parks go further and also ban gas and liquid-fuel stoves on those days and may close, so a gas cooker is no workaround inside a park.
Many parks ban wood fires at any time of year, and ForestrySA bans fires in its forests from 1 November to 30 April. Pack a gas cooker and plan meals that never depend on a fire.
tips: No gas stoves in parks on ban days

sections.heading: Coastal and conservation park rules
body: Coorong beach camping needs a permit for each vehicle, is 4WD only and allows one vehicle with up to five people per site. The ocean beach between Tea Tree Crossing and the Murray Mouth closes to vehicles from 24 October to 24 December for nesting birds.

Many conservation parks do not allow camping at all; where they do, camp only at designated sites booked before you arrive. Coastal parks keep vehicles off the dunes, so stay on hard sand and marked tracks.

Crown land is one free alternative to a booked park. Camping there is allowed without approval for up to 21 days, vehicles must stay on established tracks, firewood collection is banned, and misuse can bring a $315 expiation.

Check the park alert on the morning you travel. Fire danger and track closures change quickly over summer, and some arid parks close for the whole season, such as Munga-Thirri-Simpson Desert from 1 December to 15 March.
tips: Coorong beach camping: one permit per vehicle
Tea Tree Crossing to Murray Mouth closed 24 Oct to 24 Dec
Crown land camping: up to 21 days

faq: Do you need a permit to camp in South Australian parks?

Yes, almost everywhere. National park campsites are booked and paid for before you arrive, online or through a booking agent, and the booking usually covers vehicle entry to that park. The Simpson Desert parks use the 12-month Desert Parks Pass instead, which is also compulsory east of Dalhousie Springs in Witjira.
Can you park a campervan anywhere in South Australia?

No. You can camp on Crown land for up to 21 days without approval, at council sites and rest areas where signs allow an overnight stop, and at booked park campsites. Some councils ban or limit overnight stays, so read the sign at the exact spot.

sources.label: CFS what you can and cannot do
Fruit fly: travelling to South Australia

camping-rules-western-australia.title: Camping Rules Western Australia 2026: Free Camps & Fees
camping-rules-western-australia.description: Free camping in WA means signed rest stops for up to 24 hours or approved sites. Park camps cost $10 to $20 per adult a night. 2026 passes, fires, permits.
camping-rules-western-australia.intro: Only in limited places: Western Australia lets you camp outside a licensed caravan park or camping ground only with approval, and the main free exception is a signed overnight rest stop, where you can stay up to 24 consecutive hours. In national parks you camp only in designated campgrounds, at $10 to $20 per adult a night. AussieCamps maps 260 Western Australian park campgrounds and 238 public dump points across those long distances.

sections.heading: Park Stay WA and fees
body: Many national park campgrounds are booked through Park Stay WA, up to 180 days ahead. Fees are per person per night: $10 an adult at campgrounds without facilities, $15 with basic facilities and $20 with additional facilities, and children aged 5 and under camp free.

Campgrounds that cannot be booked are first come, first served, and sites are usually available outside the busiest periods, but vacancies are not guaranteed. Fees are still payable, usually in cash or by self-registration envelope. Arrive early and keep a legal alternative within your fuel range.

sections.heading: Roadside and remote camping
body: Main Roads WA says its 24-hour rest areas are not intended for camping, a stay must not exceed 24 consecutive hours, and no overnight stop is allowed at a rest area without a sign permitting it. Keep heavy-vehicle bays clear for road trains.

Camping anywhere else outside a licensed caravan park or camping ground without approval risks an offence, whether the land is public or private. On private land, the owner's permission covers a stay of up to 5 nights; longer stays also need local government approval. Some local governments run their own designated sites.
tips: Only where a sign allows it

sections.heading: Fire, water and distance
body: Most park campgrounds have no drinking water. Where rainwater or bore water is available, supply is not guaranteed and you should boil, treat or filter it, so carry all the water you need. In national parks, fires are allowed only in the fire rings provided, with at least three metres cleared around them, and restrictions can start without notice.

Collecting firewood, even dead wood, is banned in national parks, nature reserves and conservation parks. In State forest it is allowed only in designated firewood areas in the Perth Hills (with a permit) and the South West, so bring firewood or buy it near where you will burn it. Many parks stop campfires from about 1 December to 31 March, and some never allow them.

sections.heading: The scale changes the planning
body: Western Australia covers about a third of the continent, and the gaps between parks, towns and fuel shape every camping plan. A full or closed campground can cost a day of driving.

Park entry is charged separately from camping at parks such as Karijini and Cape Range: $17 per standard vehicle, or $10 with a concession. The All Parks Pass costs $130 a year ($80 concession) and holiday passes start at $30, so a pass pays off quickly on a run up the coast.
Northern roads and campgrounds follow the weather rather than the calendar. Check DBCA park alerts and the Main Roads WA Travel Map before each leg, and ask the local shire about shire-managed roads.

sections.heading: Free camping and the 24 hour rule
body: Outside paid campgrounds, the main place the state lets you stay overnight without approval is a signed overnight rest stop, for up to 24 consecutive hours. Main Roads WA treats that limit as one to enforce, and the official rules allow no longer stays at roadside sites.

Some local governments run low-cost or free campgrounds for travellers, each with its own stay limit and conditions. Ask the shire or the visitor centre, because the rules change from one shire to the next.

Station stays, where pastoral properties open camping areas to travellers, are a distinctive WA option, and some make a handy stopover on long remote stretches, such as Cheela Plains between Ningaloo and Karijini. Confirm the price, payment method and road access with the station before you arrive.

sections.heading: Water, fuel and communication
body: Carry drinking water for several extra days per person, and treat fuel range as the constraint that shapes the route. Roadhouses can be closed, out of fuel or card-only when the connection drops.
Mobile coverage exists near towns and disappears between them. A satellite messenger or personal locator beacon is standard equipment for remote WA travel, not an optional extra.
Tell someone your route and expected arrival. If you break down, stay with the vehicle: it is shade and shelter, and far easier for searchers to find than a person walking.

sections.heading: Ningaloo, cyclones and the dry
body: Ningaloo Coast campgrounds release bookings monthly, on the first Tuesday at 10am Perth time, a system adopted in September 2026 after an eight-month trial. Stays are capped at 14 nights if any night falls in WA school holidays and 28 nights otherwise.

Severe Tropical Cyclone Narelle damaged every campground along the Ningaloo Coast in 2026. Most Cape Range campgrounds reopened on 27 April but some stayed closed for longer, so check the alert for your exact site.

The north works best in the dry season, roughly May to October, and the cyclone season runs from November to April. Inland summer temperatures regularly pass 40 degrees, and a breakdown in that heat without water is life-threatening.

sections.heading: Permits, pets and park alerts
body: Entering an Aboriginal reserve in Western Australia needs a permit issued through the Department of Planning, Lands and Heritage, applied for before you travel. Permits are not handed out at the boundary.

Some roads need a transit permit even if you never stop. The Great Central Road between Laverton and the Northern Territory border is the best-known example, and the Central Land Council handles the Northern Territory side.
Dogs and other pets are not allowed in many national parks, including Karijini and Cape Range. Plan pet-friendly stops between them before you set off.
DBCA publishes park alerts and Park Stay WA shows availability online, which matters when a closed campground can cost a full day. Confirm both before committing to a long drive.
tips: Apply for permits before you travel
No dogs at Karijini or Cape Range

faq: Can you camp anywhere in Western Australia?

No. Camping outside a licensed caravan park or camping ground needs approval, national park camping is limited to designated campgrounds, and signed overnight rest stops allow up to 24 consecutive hours without approval.
Do WA national parks charge an entry fee?

Some do. Karijini and Cape Range charge $17 per standard vehicle, or $10 with a concession, on top of camping fees of $10 to $20 per adult a night. The All Parks Pass costs $130 a year and holiday passes start at $30.

Temporary accommodation and camping outside caravan parks

camping-rules-northern-territory.title: Camping Rules Northern Territory 2026: Passes & Free Camps
camping-rules-northern-territory.description: NT park camps are booked online at $10 to $20 per adult a night, and visitors need an NT Parks Visitor Pass. Free camping: signed 24-hour rest stops only.
camping-rules-northern-territory.intro: Mostly no: Northern Territory parks allow camping only in marked areas that you book and pay for online, visitors also need an NT Parks Visitor Pass for most parks, and the free option is a roadside rest stop signed for 24-hour overnight camping. AussieCamps maps 102 NT park campgrounds and 23 public dump points, a thin network that makes every booked night count.

sections.heading: Bookings and visitor passes
body: Designated campsites in NT parks, and the Jatbula, Larapinta and Tabletop tracks, are booked and paid for online, and rangers cannot take payment on site. Display the camping tag on your vehicle or tent, ready to show a ranger.

Visitors from outside the Territory need an NT Parks Visitor Pass for most parks and reserves, bought online before you go: $10 for a day, $30 for two weeks or $60 a year per adult. It does not cover Kakadu or Uluru-Kata Tjuta, which sell their own passes through Parks Australia.

sections.heading: Camping outside designated areas
body: Camping outside a designated campground needs a permit, with a fee of $4 per adult. Garig Gunak Barlu on the Cobourg Peninsula has its own permit, $232.10 per vehicle for up to five adults and seven nights, paid at least six weeks ahead, and the park opens only in the dry season.

Some campgrounds (Category C) are run by commercial operators, who set their own fees and handle bookings and payment themselves, so check with the operator before you go. Pets are generally not allowed in NT parks. Dogs can be walked at a few Darwin-area parks such as Casuarina Coastal Reserve and Holmes Jungle Nature Park, and near Alice Springs they may camp with you at Redbank Waterhole campground in Owen Springs Reserve.

sections.heading: Seasonal access and water safety
body: Parks can close at short notice for flooding or bushfire, and most campgrounds stay open all year unless the season shuts them. Check the park page and the NT Road Report before every leg, even when it is dry where you are standing.
Saltwater crocodiles can be in any Top End waterway, so swim only where a sign says it is safe and camp at least 50 metres from the water.

sections.heading: Permits for Aboriginal land
body: Large areas of the Territory are Aboriginal land, and entering it needs a permit from the relevant land council. In the Top End that is the Northern Land Council, which warns that unauthorised entry can bring a fine of 50 penalty units, currently $18,200, under Commonwealth law.

An entry permit covers entry only: fishing or camping must be written into it. Main access roads into major communities need no permit, and the Mereenie Loop uses the Mereenie Tour Pass, free from the Central Land Council in Alice Springs, with no camping allowed along the loop.
Alcohol is banned in most Aboriginal communities unless a permit allows it. Check the rules for every community on your route before travelling with any in the vehicle.
tips: A permit covers entry, not camping
No camping on the Mereenie Loop

sections.heading: Kakadu, Litchfield and park passes
body: Litchfield, Nitmiluk, Watarrka, Tjoritja / West MacDonnell and Judbarra / Gregory all need the NT Parks Visitor Pass. Kakadu needs a Parks Australia pass instead, valid for seven days: $25 per adult in the tropical summer (1 November to 14 May) and $40 in the dry season (15 May to 31 October), although visits from 1 July to 31 October 2026 are also charged the $25 rate. NT residents enter free.
The Jim Jim and Twin Falls area, including Karnamarr campground, is closed for all of 2026. Check the Kakadu access report, which is updated daily, before planning a day around any site.

NT park camping fees follow campground categories: $10 per adult at Category B sites, $15 at Category A and $20 at Category D, with lower child and family rates. Category C campgrounds are run commercially and set their own prices.

sections.heading: Crocodiles and water
body: Saltwater crocodiles live in rivers, creeks, billabongs, estuaries and along the coast across the Top End, and the Territory says it is never completely safe to enter the water. Assume every waterway holds one.
Swimming areas open and close with surveys and water levels, so check the sign and the park page on the day rather than trusting a previous visit or an old guidebook.
Saltwater crocodiles live in fresh water as well as salt water, so a freshwater river or billabong is no guarantee of safety. Keep children well back from the bank and supervise them near water.
tips: Assume crocs in every Top End waterway

sections.heading: The build-up and the seasons
body: The Territory's own calendar runs the dry season from May to September, the build-up from October to December, the wet from January to mid-March and the run-off through March and April. Park campgrounds are busiest from May to September.

Heavy rain and road and park closures can run from November to April, while the waterfalls are at full flow. Some travellers prefer that season, but it means checking every park and road before you commit.
Central Australia swings between extremes. Temperatures can pass 40 degrees between October and April, and winter nights are cold, so pack for a hot afternoon and a cold night in the same day.

sections.heading: Fires, fishing and collecting
body: A fire ban usually lasts up to 24 hours. During one you must not start a fire in the open air, although a small cooking fire is allowed if it burns only while cooking, has 4 metres cleared around it and is always attended, and gas or coal barbecues can still be used.

Outside a ban, small fires for cooking and boiling water need no permit, but the 4 m clearing is still the law, with a maximum penalty of $15,000. Lighting a fire for any other purpose without a permit carries up to $77,000 or five years in prison.
Recreational fishing has bag and size limits, and some barramundi waters close for part of the year. Check the current NT fishing rules for the river you plan to fish.
Plants and animals in NT parks are protected, so leave rocks, plants and artefacts where they are, and gather firewood outside the park from fallen branches only.

faq: Do you need a permit to camp in the Northern Territory?

In NT parks you book and pay for a campsite online and, as a visitor, also hold an NT Parks Visitor Pass. Camping outside a designated campground needs its own permit, and entering Aboriginal land needs a land council permit arranged before you go.
When is camping in the Northern Territory not possible?

Many Top End campgrounds and unsealed roads close during the wet and run-off, roughly November to April, and parks can close at short notice for flooding or fire. Garig Gunak Barlu opens only in the dry season, and Kakadu's Jim Jim and Twin Falls area is closed for all of 2026.

sources.label: How to use the NT parks booking system
Rules for pets in NT parks
NT camping in parks information sheet

camping-rules-act.title: Camping Rules ACT 2026: Where You Can Camp Near Canberra
camping-rules-act.description: The ACT has no free camping: vehicle camping is only allowed at booked campgrounds such as Cotter and Honeysuckle. 2026 fire rules, dogs, fines, closures.
camping-rules-act.intro: No, the ACT has no free camping: vehicle-based camping is only allowed at established campgrounds, each one needs a booking and charges a fee, and camping on other public land without a permit carries up to 20 penalty units. Bushwalkers can camp in remote parts of Namadgi National Park. AussieCamps maps seven ACT Parks campgrounds and the territory's public dump point.

sections.heading: Choose an approved campground
body: Parks ACT lists every bookable place to stay in one place: Cotter, Honeysuckle, Orroral, Mount Clear, Woods Reserve, Blue Range, Kowen, Nil Desperandum at Tidbinbilla, Ready-Cut Cottage and the walk-in Northern Border Campground. Bookings must be made in advance and fees apply.

Woods Reserve in Namadgi is closed until early 2027 for a full upgrade, so plan a Namadgi night around Honeysuckle, Orroral or Mount Clear instead (Mount Clear is unsuitable for campervans and caravans, and Orroral is not suitable for large groups).

sections.heading: Namadgi and remote walks
body: Namadgi protects 106,095 hectares, almost half of the ACT, and entry is free. Honeysuckle, Orroral and Mount Clear take bookings of up to seven consecutive days and ban motorised generators, and at Honeysuckle you bring your own drinking water.

Bushwalkers can camp in remote parts of Namadgi, and the Namadgi National Park Brief Guide shows the walk-in options. Leave your route with someone, because much of the park sits a long way from help.
tips: Namadgi stays: seven days at most

sections.heading: Fire and water
body: Campfires are allowed in only four ACT protected areas: Namadgi National Park, Tidbinbilla Nature Reserve and the Cotter and Uriarra Crossing recreation areas. Use the constructed fireplaces and bring your own firewood, because collecting timber in a park is prohibited.
Cotter Campground has potable water, hot showers and flushing toilets. Treat or boil river and tank water elsewhere before drinking it.

sections.heading: A small territory with clear rules
body: Using public unleased land without a permit, which includes camping on it, is an offence with a maximum penalty of 20 penalty units, or $3,200 for an individual. The conservator can also prohibit camping in a nature reserve outright.
That rule covers roadsides, car parks and nature reserves alike, and Commonwealth-managed National Land in Canberra has its own offence for unauthorised camping.
The rules change at the border. Cross into New South Wales and you are under NSW National Parks or Forestry Corporation rules instead, including free camping in NSW state forests.
tips: NSW rules start at the border

sections.heading: Namadgi and the alpine conditions
body: Namadgi's campgrounds sit in the ranges south-west of Canberra, and nights there run colder than in the city. Pack warm layers even in summer.
In early 2020 the Orroral Valley bushfire burnt over 80% of Namadgi, or 86,562 hectares. Tracks, signs and facilities have been rebuilt in stages, so check the park page for the walk you plan.
Dogs are not allowed in Namadgi or the adjoining Gibraltar Forest Regeneration Area, although they may ride in vehicles travelling between the ACT and NSW on the Boboyan or Brindabella roads.
tips: The 2020 fire burnt 80% of the park

sections.heading: Fire restrictions and the danger period
body: The ACT bushfire season runs from 1 October to 31 March unless the ESA Commissioner varies it. Burning off in the open during the season needs a permit, and so do open-air cooking fires on unleased Territory land in rural areas at any time of year.

On a Total Fire Ban day there are no fires in the open. You may use your own gas barbecue or portable gas or liquid-fuel stove in an ACT park on other days, but not on a Total Fire Ban day, and public gas barbecues are switched off.
Kowen Forest's campground sits behind locked gates and may close during fire danger periods or heavy rain, so check the booking conditions before you drive out.
tips: No stoves in parks on ban days
Kowen can close in fire danger

sections.heading: Using Canberra as a base
body: Commercial caravan parks and holiday parks around Canberra are the practical base for a city visit, with powered sites that the territory's park campgrounds do not offer.
Tidbinbilla Nature Reserve is within an easy drive of the city, and Nil Desperandum there is one of the bookable places to stay in the ACT's parks.
Canberra's national institutions, including the Australian War Memorial and the National Gallery of Australia, have free general admission, which makes a wet day in the city easy to fill.

sections.heading: Cotter and the reserves
body: Cotter Campground, on the Cotter River close to Canberra, has hot showers, potable water, flushing toilets, dishwashing facilities and wood fires permitted. Bookings are essential and dogs are not allowed.
Cotter, Woods Reserve and Blue Range take bookings of up to two weeks within any six-week period.
Blue Range and Kowen accept dogs on a lead, and Woods Reserve will too when it reopens in early 2027, which makes them the ACT's dog-friendly camping options.
The Northern Border Campground on the Canberra Centenary Trail is reached only on foot or by bike, 6.5 km in, with no vehicle access.
tips: Dogs on a lead at Blue Range

faq: Can you free camp in the ACT?

No. Vehicle-based camping is allowed only at established campgrounds, all of which need a booking and charge a fee, and camping on other public land without a permit can bring up to 20 penalty units. Bushwalkers may camp in remote parts of Namadgi.
Do you need to book camping in Namadgi National Park?

Yes. Honeysuckle, Orroral and Mount Clear need bookings made in advance, fees apply and stays are capped at seven consecutive days, although entry to the park itself is free. Woods Reserve is closed until early 2027.

ACT notifiable instrument NI2016-314 (camping in reserves)

is-free-camping-legal-australia.title: Is Free Camping Legal in Australia? Rules by State 2026
is-free-camping-legal-australia.description: Free camping is legal only where the land manager allows it: state forests, some council sites and signed rest areas. The rules in every state for 2026.
is-free-camping-legal-australia.intro: Yes, but only where the land manager allows it: there is no national right to camp wherever a vehicle can park. Free camping is legal in most state forests in New South Wales and Victoria, on South Australian Crown land for up to 21 days, at council sites that say so and at rest areas whose rules allow an overnight stop. Most national park campgrounds charge a fee or need a booking, and some coastal councils, such as Surf Coast Shire in Victoria, fine people for sleeping in a vehicle.

sections.heading: Where free camping is legal: the eastern states
body: In New South Wales every state forest except Cumberland and Strickland allows free, first-come camping for up to four weeks. Some national park campgrounds charge no camping fee but still need a booking, which costs $6.

Victoria lets you camp almost anywhere in a state forest for up to 28 consecutive nights, at least 20 metres from waterways, and a few Parks Victoria campgrounds such as King Hut are free with no booking.

Queensland has no free camping in its parks or state forests, where every campsite needs a paid permit. The free options there are council campgrounds that allow it. Roadside rest areas let you stop for up to 20 hours unless a sign says otherwise, but the state says they are not camping sites.

Tasmania offers free council camps with their own permits and stay limits, free park campgrounds in Southwest National Park (a parks pass is still needed to enter), and camping on most Sustainable Timber Tasmania land unless a sign prohibits it.

sections.heading: Where free camping is legal: the south, west and centre
body: South Australia allows camping on Crown land without approval for up to 21 days, with vehicles kept to established tracks and no firewood collection. National park campsites there must be booked and paid for in advance, except in the Munga-Thirri Simpson Desert parks, which need a Desert Parks Pass instead.
Western Australia requires approval for camping anywhere other than a licensed camping ground, so the free option there is a rest stop signed for up to 24 consecutive hours.
The Northern Territory lists its road rest stops individually, and only those marked for 24-hour overnight camping allow it. Park campgrounds are booked online, and visitors also need a parks pass.

The ACT has no free camping at all: vehicle camping is allowed only at established campgrounds, each booked in advance, and camping elsewhere on public land without a permit can bring a penalty of up to 20 penalty units.

sections.heading: Parking is not permission to camp
body: A legal parking space can still ban sleeping, setting up camp or staying overnight. Look for explicit overnight permission, time limits and vehicle restrictions, not just the absence of a no-camping sign.
Some councils ban sleeping in a parked vehicle outright. Surf Coast Shire on the Victorian coast fines people $300 on the spot for sleeping in a vehicle anywhere in the shire.
tips: Sleeping in a van can be banned

sections.heading: Can you camp on the side of the road?
body: Usually not, unless the spot is a rest area that allows it. Queensland bans camping on a state-controlled road unless you are managing fatigue between 4pm and 8am, outside a built-up area, at least 200 metres from any kerb and 9 metres from the traffic lane, where no sign prohibits it and not on a motorway or toll road, with no fire or generator.

Western Australia's Main Roads allows no overnight stop at a rest area without a sign permitting it, and Service NSW says rest areas are not for camping, although a July 2026 planning note says camping in one may be allowed unless a sign says otherwise.
Where an overnight stop is allowed, keep it to the vehicle, leave the truck bays free for heavy vehicles and move on in the morning.

sections.heading: Fines and how they are set
body: Penalties are set by whoever owns the land, so they vary widely. Camping outside a camping area in a NSW national park carries a maximum of 30 penalty units, the ACT sets a maximum of 20 penalty units ($3,200 for an individual) for using public land, including camping on it, without a permit, and misuse of South Australian Crown land can bring a $315 expiation.
Council fines are set locally, so the amount differs from one council to the next. Check the council's website or the sign at the site.

sections.heading: Self-contained vehicles
body: Some councils allow free camping only for self-contained vehicles with an onboard toilet and waste tanks. Each council defines what counts, so check its conditions before relying on a portable toilet.
Self-containment can open up more sites, but it does not lift the stay limit. The stay limit on the sign still applies, and waste still goes only into a dump point.
tips: Empty tanks only at dump points

sections.heading: Behaviour keeps free sites open
body: Free sites can close or start charging because of rubbish, waste, noise and overcrowding.

Arrive late, leave early, keep the footprint small, take every bag of rubbish with you and use toilets where they are provided. If a site is full, do not invent a new bay on vegetation or a nearby street.

sections.heading: Check before you stop
body: The sign at the site and the land manager's website are the authorities. Camping apps and community listings are good for finding candidates, but they are not a defence if a site turns out to be closed or banned.
Where a listing and a sign disagree, follow the sign. When in real doubt, a low-cost council campground or showground is often within reach and removes the question for a small fee.
Photograph the sign when you arrive. It costs nothing and is the best evidence you have if a notice is later disputed.
tips: A cheap campground ends the doubt

faq: Is free camping legal in Australia?

Yes, but only where the land manager allows it, through signs or a standing rule: there is no national right to camp wherever a vehicle can park. Most state forests in New South Wales and Victoria, South Australian Crown land for up to 21 days, council sites that say so and rest areas whose rules allow an overnight stop are the main legal options; most national park campgrounds charge a fee or need a booking.
Can you camp on the side of the road in Australia?

Usually not. Roadside stops are limited to rest areas whose rules or signs allow an overnight stop, such as Western Australia's signed 24-hour stops. Queensland lets you stop at a rest area for up to 20 hours unless a sign says otherwise, but says rest areas are not camping sites, and it bans camping on state roads outside a narrow 4pm to 8am fatigue exception.

campfires-camping-australia.title: Campfire Rules Australia 2026: Fire Bans and Fines by State
campfires-camping-australia.description: When a campfire is legal in each state: fire seasons, Total Fire Bans, gas stoves on ban days and the fines. Official rules, checked October 2026.
campfires-camping-australia.imageAlt: Legal campfire in a designated fire ring
campfires-camping-australia.intro: A campfire is legal only when there is no fire ban for the district, the land manager allows fires at that site and you keep to the size and clearance rules. Each state runs its own system: NSW, Victoria, South Australia, Western Australia, Tasmania and the ACT declare Total Fire Bans, Queensland declares local fire bans instead, and the Northern Territory's fire bans usually last up to 24 hours.

sections.heading: The rules by state
body: Solid fuel is the constant: on any ban day, wood, charcoal and heat-bead fires are illegal in the affected district, fire rings included. What changes from state to state is the fire season, the size and clearance rules for a legal fire, and whether a gas cooker is still allowed in a park on a ban day.

Read the row for the state you are in, then check the fire authority on the day. Park agencies can add their own bans and closures on top, and those apply even when the fire authority has declared nothing.

sections.heading: Three checks before lighting
body: Check the fire authority for the district, the park alert page and the campground's own rules. In Queensland, call 1800 020 440 or check with the local Rural Fire Service office if you are unsure whether a fire ban applies.

Bans are usually declared the afternoon before, although the RFS can still declare one on the day, so check in the evening and again in the morning to change the dinner plan rather than react at camp.

sections.heading: Firewood and setup
body: Collecting firewood is banned in national parks in most states because fallen timber is habitat, and in Western Australia the ban covers national parks and other conservation reserves. Bring clean, untreated wood from outside the park where fires are allowed.
Use the fireplace provided, clear the area as the rules require and keep water beside you, not in the vehicle. Never light a fire under branches or in strong wind.

sections.heading: Put it out cold
body: Douse the fire with water, stir the ashes and douse again until the remains are cold to the touch. Sand can hide hot embers rather than put them out.
Never leave a fire unattended, including while it burns down or while you sleep. If the wind rises, put it out.

sections.heading: Fire danger ratings and fire bans
body: The Australian Fire Danger Rating System has four levels, Moderate, High, Extreme and Catastrophic, published by district. A Total Fire Ban is declared separately, so check both rather than reading the rating as permission.

On a ban day, campfires and solid-fuel barbecues are illegal in the district. Gas is where the states differ: NSW national parks generally ban visitor-owned gas cookers, ACT parks switch off gas barbecues, South Australian park rules are set park by park, Tasmania allows LPG and electric stoves but not liquid-fuel ones, and Queensland allows contained gas and spirit stoves during a fire ban.
Parks also close on the worst days. South Australian parks and ForestrySA forests may close on ban days, and NPWS can declare its own park fire ban or close a park in NSW when the risk is high.
tips: Solid fuel is banned everywhere on ban days

sections.heading: Where fires are allowed at all
body: Many parks ban fires for part or all of the year. Ikara-Flinders Ranges bans wood fires during its fire ban period, from mid-October 2026 to late March 2027, ForestrySA bans fires in its forests from 1 November to 30 April, and many Western Australian parks stop campfires from about 1 December to 31 March.

Tasmania's Fuel Stove Only Areas ban campfires all year across much of the wilderness, including Cradle Mountain-Lake St Clair, Freycinet and Mount Field. In the ACT, campfires are allowed only in constructed fireplaces in four areas: Namadgi, Tidbinbilla and the Cotter and Uriarra Crossing recreation areas.
The campground page decides in the end, because a land manager's rule is often stricter than the fire danger system and applies all year.

sections.heading: Building and controlling a legal fire
body: Size and clearance rules differ: NSW state forests require a fire under one square metre and 4.5 metres from the nearest tree, Victorian state forests one under a metre across with three metres cleared, and South Australia a trench 30 cm deep during the fire season.
CFA asks for a campfire to be supervised by an awake, alert adult within 50 metres at all times, and only when the wind is under 10 km/h. Those conditions are a good standard anywhere in Australia.
Escaped campfires often start after the people who lit them decided it was nearly out. Treat the fire as live until it is cold to the touch.

sections.heading: Fines and liability
body: Lighting a fire on a Total Fire Ban day in NSW brings an on-the-spot fine of $2,200, or up to $5,500 and 12 months in jail in court. Western Australia issues a $1,000 infringement, with up to $25,000 and 12 months in jail on conviction.

CFA warns that a fire on a Total Fire Ban day in Victoria can bring a fine of more than $40,000, two years in prison or both. In the Northern Territory, lighting a fire for anything other than cooking without a permit carries up to about $77,000 or five years, and failing to clear 4 metres around a fire up to about $15,000; the amounts are indexed, so check the NT page.
If a fire escapes, do not fight it beyond the first seconds. Move away and call triple zero with the clearest location you can give.

sections.heading: Cooking when fires are banned
body: Keep a gas cooker in the vehicle permanently, and check the rule for cookers as well as fires, because some parks ban those too on the worst days.

Never cook inside a tent, an awning or a closed vehicle. Western Australia's gas safety regulator warns that portable outdoor gas appliances must never be used inside a tent, semi-enclosed area, caravan or RV.
Plan meals that need no flame for the days a ban is forecast: cold lunches, wraps and food cooked the night before keep the trip moving.
tips: Never cook in a closed space
Plan cold meals for ban days

faq: Can you have a campfire while camping in Australia?

Yes, when there is no fire ban for the district and the campground allows fires, using the fireplace provided and wood you bring in. During a Total Fire Ban, or a local fire ban in Queensland, solid-fuel fires are illegal everywhere in that area, fire rings included.
Can you use a gas stove on a total fire ban day?

It depends on the state and the land. NSW national parks generally ban visitor-owned gas cookers on those days, ACT parks switch off gas barbecues, Tasmania allows LPG and electric stoves but not liquid-fuel ones, and Queensland allows contained gas and spirit stoves during a fire ban. In South Australia, check the park fire restrictions for the park you are in.

sleeping-in-car-australia.title: Can You Sleep in Your Car in Australia? State Rules 2026
sleeping-in-car-australia.description: Legal in some places, fined in others. Rest-area limits, council bans and national park rules for sleeping in a car in every state, checked October 2026.
sleeping-in-car-australia.imageAlt: Campervan parked at an authorised overnight site
sleeping-in-car-australia.intro: Yes, in the right place: what gets people fined is camping where it is banned, and many councils count sleeping in a parked car as camping. The legal options are booked campgrounds, state forests that allow camping, and rest areas whose rules or signs permit an overnight stop, such as Queensland's 20-hour limit and Western Australia's signed 24-hour stops.

sections.heading: The rules in each state
body: No state publishes one simple yes or no. Road authorities set rest-area limits, councils set the rules for streets, beaches and car parks, and park agencies decide what happens inside national parks, so the answer depends on which of the three owns the ground under your car.

Only Queensland and Western Australia publish a statewide rest-area time limit, and the Northern Territory lists which of its highway rest stops allow overnight camping. Everywhere else the sign at the rest area decides, and advice in New South Wales is mixed: Service NSW says rest areas are not for camping, while a July 2026 planning practice note says camping in one may be permitted unless a sign says otherwise.

sections.heading: Can you sleep in your car in a national park?
body: Only where the park allows camping, which almost always means a designated campground booked or permitted in advance. A car left overnight at a day-use area, lookout or trailhead is camping without permission, whether or not anyone pitched a tent.

Queensland charges $7.75 per person a night for every park and forest campsite in 2026, and the permit applies whether you sleep in a tent or in the car. Northern Territory parks take bookings online only, South Australian parks online or through agents, and NSW limits a stay in any park to 21 days.

A few parks allow dispersed camping. Victoria's Alpine National Park permits it across much of the park, but Parks Victoria asks campers to carry a tent and each park sets its own boundaries, so read the park page first.
tips: Book or hold a permit first
Alpine National Park allows dispersed camping

sections.heading: Rest areas and what their limits mean
body: Queensland lets general and recreational vehicles stay at a rest area for up to 20 hours unless a sign says otherwise, but calls them stopping places rather than campsites. Heavy-vehicle rest areas are for truck drivers only, and generators must stay off between 7pm and 7am.

In Western Australia you can stop for up to 24 consecutive hours at rest areas marked for overnight stays, which Main Roads WA says are not intended for camping, and you need approval to stay overnight anywhere else outside a caravan park or campground. The Northern Territory lists its road rest stops one by one, and only those marked for 24-hour overnight camping allow it.

Wherever you stop, park inside the marked bays, keep truck parking clear and leave the awning, chairs and table packed. A car with people asleep in it reads as a rest stop; a set-up camp reads as camping.

sections.heading: Councils, cities and the coast
body: Local laws are where most fines come from. On the Victorian coast, Surf Coast Shire treats sleeping in a vehicle anywhere in the shire as an offence with a $300 on-the-spot fine, and Cairns Regional Council bans camping on roadsides, the Esplanade, parks, car parks and beaches.

Some inland councils run free or low-cost areas for travellers. Tasmania's Northern Midlands Council, for example, issues free permits for stays of up to 48 hours, but only for fully self-contained vehicles with their own toilet and shower, which rules out most cars.
Read the sign for the exact bay, not just the street. Time limits, permit zones and no-overnight signs often sit side by side, and all of them apply at once.
tips: Read the sign for the exact bay

sections.heading: Doing it safely
body: Choose somewhere with other vehicles, some light and an easy way out. Park facing the exit where you can, keep valuables out of sight and lock the doors while keeping one clear way out.

Ventilation matters more than people expect. A closed car with people asleep in it turns damp and stuffy within hours, and in heat it becomes dangerous, so open windows a little behind insect screens.

sections.heading: Carbon monoxide, heat and cold
body: Never run the engine for heating or air conditioning while you sleep, and never bring a gas heater, cooker or barbecue inside. Western Australia's gas safety regulator warns that portable outdoor gas appliances must never be used inside a tent, semi-enclosed area, caravan, RV or indoors, because of the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning.
Summer heat is the main practical limit on sleeping in a car. Cabins heat quickly after sunrise and stay warm overnight in the north, so start the day early or choose a powered site with shade.
Inland and alpine nights fall below freezing in winter and a car holds little warmth. A sleeping bag rated for the conditions matters more in a vehicle than in a tent.
tips: Never idle the engine while asleep
Rate the sleeping bag for frost

sections.heading: Making a car workable for a night
body: Window shades, insect screens and a proper mattress turn one uncomfortable night into something you can repeat for a week. Without them it works once and wears thin fast.
Level ground matters more than it sounds, because a slope you never notice while parked becomes obvious lying down. Turning the car around is often enough to fix it.
For a longer trip, a small van or a wagon with the seats folded gives far more room than a sedan.

sections.heading: Where a legal night is easiest
body: State forests are the simplest free option in New South Wales and Victoria, where camping is generally allowed for up to four weeks and 28 consecutive nights respectively. NSW forests do not allow camping in picnic areas, and in Victoria you must camp at least 20 metres from waterways.

South Australia allows camping on Crown land for up to 21 days without approval, while Western Australia expects you to use a licensed caravan park, a campground or a signed rest stop unless you have approval.
When in doubt, a basic campground or showground costs little and removes the question. Arrive before dark so you can read the signs and check the access for your vehicle.
tips: Forests: free in NSW and Victoria

faq: Is it legal to sleep in your car in Australia?

Yes, where camping is allowed: booked campgrounds, state forests that permit camping, and rest areas whose rules or signs allow an overnight stop. Many councils count sleeping in a parked car as camping and fine it on streets, beaches and car parks, such as Surf Coast Shire's $300 on-the-spot fine.
Can you sleep in your car in a national park?
Only where the park allows camping, which usually means a designated campground booked in advance. A car left overnight at a day-use area or trailhead counts as camping without permission.

driving-in-australia-overseas-licence.title: Driving in Australia with an overseas licence
driving-in-australia-overseas-licence.description: Licence rules differ between states and territories, especially for longer stays.
driving-in-australia-overseas-licence.imageAlt: Campervan driving on an Australian road
driving-in-australia-overseas-licence.intro: International visitors can often drive on a current overseas licence for a limited period, but each state and territory sets its own conditions.

sections.heading: Check every jurisdiction
body: Confirm the rule with the transport authority for each state or territory on the route. Residency, visa status and length of stay can change what is required.
Carry the original licence. If it is not in English, bring an accepted English translation or International Driving Permit as required.

sections.heading: Vehicle class and rental terms
body: Your licence must cover the vehicle class and weight. A motorhome can be larger than the passenger vehicle you normally drive.
Rental agreements can prohibit unsealed roads, beaches, floodwater and driving after dark. Insurance may not cover a breach.

sections.heading: Australian road habits
body: Drive on the left, learn local roundabout rules and leave more braking distance in a heavy vehicle. Long rural distances make fatigue a major risk.
Stop before tiredness becomes obvious. Avoid dawn and dusk on wildlife-heavy roads.

sections.heading: Rental company conditions sit on top of the law
body: Even where the law permits you to drive, rental companies apply their own rules: a minimum age, a licence held for a minimum period, young driver surcharges and sometimes refusal of licences from particular countries.
Confirm these at booking rather than at the counter. Being refused a vehicle at an airport depot after a long flight is a genuinely difficult problem to solve.
Many agreements also prohibit specific roads, unsealed surfaces and beach driving entirely, with damage on them uninsured. Read those clauses before planning a route.

sections.heading: Translations and international permits
body: A licence not in English needs an accurate English translation or an International Driving Permit, carried alongside the original. The permit supports the licence rather than replacing it, so both must be present.
Get the permit in your home country before travelling, because it generally cannot be issued once you have arrived. It is inexpensive and quick to obtain from the relevant motoring authority.
Carry both documents in the vehicle at all times. Police can require them at a roadside stop and being unable to produce them is an offence in its own right.
tips: IDP supports, never replaces, the licence
Obtain the IDP before you travel

sections.heading: Vehicle class and campervans
body: A standard car licence in most Australian states covers vehicles up to 4.5 tonnes gross vehicle mass and twelve occupants including the driver. Larger motorhomes require a light rigid or medium rigid class.
Your home licence class determines the Australian equivalence, and a car licence in one country does not automatically cover a 4.5 tonne vehicle. Check before booking a large motorhome.
Towing adds further constraints. The combination weight, not just the vehicle, determines what class you need, and exceeding it affects insurance as well as legality.
tips: Large motorhomes may need a higher class
Towing is assessed on combination weight

sections.heading: Insurance and what excess reduction covers
body: Rental excess amounts in Australia are typically high, frequently several thousand dollars. Excess reduction products lower it but commonly exclude windscreens, tyres, undercarriage, water damage and single-vehicle accidents.

Those exclusions cover most of what actually happens on Australian roads, particularly on gravel. Read what is excluded rather than what is covered, and price a separate policy if the exclusions matter.

Third party injury cover works differently from many countries and varies by state. Compulsory third party insurance is included with registration, but property damage to others is not automatically covered.
tips: Excess is often several thousand dollars
Glass and tyres are usually excluded

sections.heading: Roadside assistance and breakdowns
body: Check whether roadside assistance is included with your rental and what it covers in remote areas, because many policies limit towing distance and remote recovery is extremely expensive.

Carry the assistance number written down as well as in a phone, and be able to describe your location using the nearest roadside marker or landmark. In remote areas, staying with the vehicle is always the right decision.
Take photographs of your licence, permit and rental agreement and store them separately, so a lost wallet does not also end the driving part of the trip.
Rental agreements commonly exclude unsealed roads entirely, so confirm what your vehicle is permitted to drive on before planning a route through gravel country.

faq: Can you drive in Australia on an overseas licence?

Yes, as a visitor, provided the licence is current and covers the class of vehicle. The rules are set per state, and each has its own time limit and its own point at which a visitor becomes a resident who must convert.
Do you need an International Driving Permit in Australia?
Only if your licence is not in English. Where it is not, you must carry an official English translation or an International Driving Permit together with the original licence.

interstate-biosecurity-road-trip.title: Interstate biosecurity for Australian road trips
interstate-biosecurity-road-trip.description: Fruit, vegetables, honey, plants, soil and camping gear can be restricted at state borders.
interstate-biosecurity-road-trip.intro: Australia has quarantine zones within the country. Carrying the wrong produce or dirty equipment can spread pests and lead to an on-the-spot fine.

sections.heading: Check before shopping
body: Rules vary by product, origin and destination. Check the official traveller information before crossing a state or quarantine-zone border.
Fresh fruit, vegetables, honey, plants and soil are common concerns. Restrictions can apply even when the item was bought in an Australian supermarket.

sections.heading: Use quarantine bins
body: Eat allowed produce before the border or place restricted items in a quarantine bin. Do not hide food in the vehicle or leave it beside the road.
Keep receipts and packaging when official advice says a commercially treated product is permitted.

sections.heading: Clean camping equipment
body: Remove soil, seeds and plant material from boots, tents, bikes and recovery gear. Dry water equipment before moving between catchments where required.
Clean gear also lasts longer and avoids carrying ants, weeds and pathogens into the next campground.

sections.heading: Fruit fly zones are the main issue
body: South Australia, Tasmania and parts of Victoria and New South Wales maintain fruit fly exclusion zones. Carrying fresh fruit and some vegetables into them is prohibited, with disposal bins provided at borders and checkpoints operating.
Fines apply whether or not you knew, and inspections at the South Australian border and the Tasmanian ferry terminal are routine. Detector dogs work some crossings.
The practical approach is to plan shopping around the borders: run the fridge down before a crossing and restock immediately after. This costs nothing and removes the problem entirely.
tips: Run the fridge down before a border

sections.heading: Tasmania and Western Australia
body: Tasmania restricts fresh produce, plants, soil, honey and used beekeeping equipment on arrival by ferry or air. The rules protect an island free of several mainland pests and are enforced at the terminal.

Western Australia operates quarantine checkpoints on eastern approaches including the Eyre Highway, restricting fruit, vegetables, honey, plants and soil. This catches travellers who stocked up before crossing the Nullarbor.
Both jurisdictions publish current restricted item lists that change with outbreaks. Check before travelling rather than relying on what applied on a previous trip.
tips: Tasmania checks at the ferry terminal
WA checkpoints on the Eyre Highway

sections.heading: Soil, gear and weeds
body: Soil on boots, tent pegs, bicycles and vehicles moves plant pathogens and weed seeds between regions. Phytophthora dieback in Western Australia is spread this way and has devastated large areas of native vegetation.
Clean footwear and gear between regions, use the cleaning stations provided at park entrances in dieback areas, and stay on formed tracks and roads where signage asks you to.
Firewood also moves pests. Several regions restrict moving firewood, and buying local rather than carrying a load across state lines is the safer practice.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: Australia's agricultural industries are free of many pests present elsewhere, and that status depends on internal barriers as much as international ones. A single fruit fly outbreak can cost a region's growers their export markets.
For native ecosystems the stakes are similar. Dieback, myrtle rust and weed incursions have permanently altered large areas, and most of that movement was human-assisted and avoidable.
Complying costs a few minutes and some planning around shopping. Treat the bins at a border as a normal part of a road trip rather than an inconvenience.
tips: One outbreak can close export markets

sections.heading: Planning the fridge around borders
body: Run fresh produce down in the days before a quarantine crossing and restock immediately after. This costs nothing, avoids buying food twice and removes the risk of a fine entirely.

Cooked and processed food is generally fine, so a meal plan built around tinned, dried and cooked items across a border day works well. Check the current restricted list rather than guessing which items count.
Quarantine bins at borders are provided precisely so you can comply without penalty, and using one is treated very differently from being found with undeclared produce.
Restricted item lists change with outbreaks, so check the current position rather than relying on what applied on a previous trip.
tips: Run the fridge down before crossing
Cooked and processed food is usually fine

faq: Can you take fruit and vegetables across Australian state borders?
Often not. Fruit fly exclusion zones and interstate quarantine rules restrict fresh fruit, vegetables, honey and plants, and the restricted list changes by direction of travel and by zone.
What happens at an Australian quarantine checkpoint?

You either bin the restricted items in the disposal bins provided before the line, or you declare them. Disposing costs nothing; being caught with them carries an on-the-spot fine, and inspections on the WA and SA borders are routine.

camping-with-dogs-australia.title: Camping with dogs in Australia
camping-with-dogs-australia.description: Find dog-friendly stays without assuming pets are welcome in parks or shared campgrounds.
camping-with-dogs-australia.imageAlt: Dog resting beside a tent at a pet-friendly campground
camping-with-dogs-australia.intro: A dog-friendly road trip needs a route built around permitted camps, safe exercise, heat and wildlife. National parks commonly prohibit pets.

sections.heading: Choose the right land
body: Check the exact campground rule and any lead requirement. A listing marked dog-friendly may still exclude pets from cabins, beaches, trails or peak periods.
Never take a dog into a prohibited national park, even if it remains inside the vehicle.

sections.heading: Heat and travel
body: A parked vehicle becomes dangerous quickly. Plan walks for cool hours, carry more water than usual and choose shade before arrival.
Secure the dog safely while driving and build rest breaks around places where exercise is allowed.

sections.heading: Wildlife and other campers
body: Keep the dog controlled around kangaroos, livestock, snakes and ground-nesting birds. Do not allow barking or roaming to disturb neighbouring sites.
Collect waste every time, including in remote areas. Ask before approaching another camper or dog.

sections.heading: National parks generally exclude dogs
body: Dogs are prohibited in almost all Australian national parks, in every state, because of the risk to native wildlife and because many parks use 1080 baiting. This is the single biggest constraint on camping with a dog here.
State forests, regional parks, council reserves and private campgrounds are the workable alternatives, and many permit dogs on lead. Some state forests allow dogs off lead outside baiting periods.
Plan the route around dog-friendly places first rather than hoping to improvise. A standard national park itinerary with a dog produces a trip where somebody waits in the vehicle constantly.
tips: Dogs banned in almost all national parks
State forests are the usual alternative
Plan the route around dog-friendly stops

sections.heading: 1080 baiting is the serious risk
body: Sodium fluoroacetate, known as 1080, is used widely for fox, wild dog and rabbit control and is lethal to dogs in tiny quantities. Poisoning can occur from eating bait or from scavenging a poisoned carcass months later.
Baited areas are signed at access points and operations are published in advance by state agencies. Check before entering any state forest, reserve or pastoral area with a dog.
There is no reliable field antidote and death is distressing and rapid. Keep dogs leashed and muzzled in baited areas, or better, avoid those areas entirely.
tips: Risk persists in carcasses for months

sections.heading: Heat and vehicles
body: Heat in a parked vehicle kills dogs quickly, and shade moves through the day. An Australian summer makes leaving a dog in a vehicle unsafe even briefly, which rules out most attractions that exclude dogs.
Hot ground burns paws. Bitumen and sand reach temperatures that cause serious burns, and the test is whether you can hold the back of your hand on the surface for several seconds.
Carry more water for the dog than you think you need and offer it frequently. Dogs dehydrate faster than people in this climate and show it later.
tips: Never leave a dog in a parked vehicle
Test ground temperature with your hand
Carry extra water for the dog

sections.heading: Wildlife, ticks and snakes
body: Paralysis ticks along the east coast are potentially fatal to dogs and preventatives are essential rather than optional in that region. Check the dog daily, particularly around the head, neck and ears.
Snakes are a genuine risk and dogs frequently investigate them. Keep dogs on lead in bush and long grass, and know where the nearest veterinary clinic with antivenom is on remote legs.
Cane toads across the north are toxic if mouthed and cause rapid poisoning. In toad country, supervise dogs closely at night when toads are most active.
tips: Tick preventatives on the east coast
Keep dogs leashed in long grass
Cane toads are toxic if mouthed

sections.heading: Snakes, ticks and emergency vets
body: Snake bite in dogs is a genuine risk in warm months and requires immediate veterinary treatment. Know where the nearest clinic with antivenom is before heading somewhere remote, because time is the deciding factor.
Paralysis ticks on the east coast require preventatives and daily checking. In remote areas, the nearest vet may be hours away, which changes the risk calculation for taking a dog at all.
Where a national park is unavoidable, kennels and day-boarding operate in most regional towns and are usually inexpensive for a single day.
1080 baiting notices are published in advance by state agencies, and checking them before entering any forest or reserve with a dog is essential.
tips: Know the nearest vet with antivenom
Daily tick checks on the east coast

faq: Can you take a dog camping in Australia?
In many places, but not national parks. Dogs are banned from almost all Australian national parks, and state forests, council reserves and caravan parks are where dog-friendly camping actually is.
Why are dogs banned in Australian national parks?

Because of the risk to native wildlife, and because 1080 baiting for foxes and wild dogs is used in and around many parks. A baited dog dies quickly, and the baits are not always signed as clearly as you would hope.

caravan-park-vs-holiday-park.title: Caravan Park vs Holiday Park vs Campground: Which to Choose
caravan-park-vs-holiday-park.description: Caravan park vs holiday park vs campground: who runs each, the facilities you get, booking rules and 2026 national park fees, in one comparison table.
caravan-park-vs-holiday-park.imageAlt: Caravan park beside an Australian beach
caravan-park-vs-holiday-park.intro: A caravan park and a holiday park are much the same thing: commercial parks with powered sites, amenities and usually cabins, with holiday parks leaning towards pools, playgrounds and family facilities. A campground in a national park or state forest trades those services for the setting and a lower fee or none. Match the stay to what the trip needs that night rather than using one type for the whole route.

sections.heading: Caravan park or holiday park: what the names mean
body: The two names overlap and operators use them loosely. Both describe a commercial park with powered and unpowered sites, amenities blocks and usually cabins; holiday park tends to signal more family facilities such as a pool, a playground or activities, and often more cabins.

The bigger difference is between commercial parks and public campgrounds. Parks sell services, power and convenience, while national park and forest campgrounds sell the location and leave most of the services to you.

sections.heading: Bush campgrounds
body: National park and forest campgrounds trade services for location. Toilets may be basic, water may be untreated or absent, power is rare and generators are often restricted.

They also cost less. In 2026 Queensland charges $7.75 per person a night, Western Australian parks $10 to $20 per adult, and Victoria's bookable sites start from $16 a night, while camping in most NSW state forests is free. Check road access and booking before driving in.

sections.heading: Use a mixed strategy
body: A simple bush camp followed by a powered holiday park makes laundry, charging and water refills easier. Roofed accommodation can rescue a route during severe weather.
Budget for a few service nights instead of expecting every camp to provide everything.

sections.heading: Judge by specification, not label
body: What matters is the specification rather than the name: whether sites are powered, how modern the amenities are, and whether there is a camp kitchen, laundry, pool or dump point, plus the site dimensions for your rig.

Some park chains sell paid memberships with discounts on nightly rates. Work out whether the saving covers the fee for the number of nights you will actually spend in that chain's parks before buying one.
tips: Check site size for your rig

sections.heading: Where each type earns its place
body: A commercial park is worth paying for after several nights of free camping, before an early start, in bad weather, or when laundry, hot showers, charging and water all need attention at once. Counted against the jobs it replaces it is usually good value.

National park and forest campgrounds cost less and give you the setting, at the price of self-sufficiency and usually no power. Rest areas cost nothing and provide little beyond a place to stop for a limited time.
A common pattern on long trips is two or three low-cost nights followed by one serviced night that resets everything. That balance keeps both the budget and the vehicle workable.
tips: Serviced night resets the whole vehicle
National parks give setting, not services
Two or three cheap nights, then one paid

sections.heading: Booking and peak season
body: Coastal parks in school holidays, at Easter and over Christmas book out months ahead, often impose minimum stays and charge peak rates. Book as soon as your dates are fixed.
Declare your vehicle length accurately, because sites are allocated by size and under-declaring produces an awkward conversation at check-in. Say if you need drive-through access or are towing.
Ask about late arrival when booking. Many parks close reception in the evening and leave an envelope with a gate code, but you need that information before standing at a locked boom gate.

sections.heading: Shared space and the amenities
body: Quiet hours are enforced and parks are dense environments where sound carries. Keep to your site boundary, supervise children around internal roads and pools, and check the pet policy before arriving with a dog.

Use the camp kitchen and laundry deliberately, because they are what you are paying for. A single evening can clear a week of washing, charge everything and refill water while emptying waste in the right order.
Never fill drinking water from a tap near the dump point, and ask which taps are potable. Not all of them are, and the signage is not always obvious.

sections.heading: Reading reviews usefully
body: Review scores tell you less than the specific complaints. Repeated mentions of amenity cleanliness, road noise, site size or management attitude are the signals worth acting on.
Photographs from guests are more reliable than the park's own. Look for the site type you are booking rather than the pool and the playground, which every park photographs well.
Ask about a powered site's amperage if you intend to run air conditioning, because some older parks supply less than a modern van draws.
tips: Look for your site type specifically

faq: What is the difference between a caravan park and a holiday park?

Very little in practice: both are commercial parks with powered and unpowered sites, amenities and usually cabins. Holiday park usually signals more family facilities such as a pool, playground or activities, and often more cabins.
When is a caravan park worth the money?

When you need power, hot showers, laundry and a resupply at once, or when the free and low-cost options nearby are full. Many long-trip travellers book one serviced night after two or three nights of bush camping.

sources.label: Where to camp in Queensland parks
Queensland Parks camping bookings and fees

dump-points-australia-guide.title: Dump Points in Australia: Locations by State and How to Use
dump-points-australia-guide.description: Where to find caravan and campervan dump points in each state, how many have a washout tap, how to use one correctly and what to do with grey water.
dump-points-australia-guide.intro: Empty a caravan or campervan toilet only at a dump point. They sit at caravan parks, showgrounds, rest areas and visitor centres, and the Australian Government's National Public Toilet Map records public ones with their facilities. AussieCamps maps 347 in New South Wales but only 23 in the Northern Territory, so on remote legs plan the next dump point as carefully as the next fuel stop.

sections.heading: Dump points by state
body: The counts below are public dump points from the National Public Toilet Map that AussieCamps carries, by state. Caravan parks often have their own dump point too, but those are private and not counted here.
A washout is a tap for rinsing the cassette or hose after emptying, and only about one dump point in six has one. Carry your own rinse water rather than counting on it.

table.caption: Public dump points in AussieCamps by state, data as of September 2026
head: State
Public dump points
With a washout tap

sections.heading: Finding one before you need it
body: The habit that prevents problems is knowing where the next dump point is before the tank is nearly full. Check access hours, vehicle clearance and whether a key, code or fee is needed, because some are locked overnight.

In the north and the outback the gaps are long, and a dump point can be closed for maintenance. Keep a second option on every remote leg, and ask at caravan park reception whether non-guests can use theirs.
tips: Find the next one in advance
Keep a backup on remote legs

sections.heading: Carry the right kit
body: Use a secure hose and fittings that match the vehicle, wear gloves, and keep drinking-water equipment completely separate. Never use a drinking-water tap to rinse a waste hose.
Carry disposable gloves and hand sanitiser with the waste gear, because handwashing facilities at dump points are not guaranteed.

sections.heading: Using one correctly
body: Park so other vehicles can pass, because many dump points sit on a single access lane. Empty black water first, rinse, then grey water, and rinse the area afterwards rather than leaving it for the next person.
Never fill fresh water from a tap at a dump point unless it is clearly marked as drinking water, and wash your hands before touching anything in the vehicle.
Use toilet chemicals the receiving system can handle. Some rural dump points feed septic systems, and harsh chemicals can damage the biological process that makes them work.

sections.heading: Cassette or fixed tank
body: A cassette toilet can be carried to the dump point, so you can empty it without moving the vehicle. Some dump points are built into public toilet blocks and shown on the Toilet Map, but only empty a cassette into a toilet or dump point signed for that use.
A fixed black tank means driving to a dump point and positioning over it, which matters at busy facilities and in towns with tight access.
If your setup allows it, a spare cassette roughly doubles how long you can stay away from a dump point on a remote leg.
tips: Fixed tanks need the vehicle there

sections.heading: Grey water
body: Grey water from showers and sinks goes into a dump point or wherever the campground directs, not onto the ground beside the van. Rules differ by land manager, so read the campground page.

Where you camp without facilities, Victoria's state forest rules show the standard: tip washing-up water at least 50 metres from rivers and creeks, and dig toilet holes at least 30 cm deep and 100 metres from any waterway.

sections.heading: What not to do and the penalties
body: Stormwater drains run straight to waterways with no treatment, and dumping onto the ground or into the bush is a pollution offence under state environment law.

New South Wales strengthened its illegal dumping penalties in April 2024, including a specific offence for dumping more than 50 litres of waste in a public place, with heavier penalties on sensitive land such as national parks and beaches.
Illegal dumping also gets free camping areas closed. Residents report it, councils act on it, and the site closes for everyone.
tips: Over 50 litres is a specific offence in NSW

sections.heading: Building it into the routine
body: Many travellers empty on a schedule, usually whenever they pass a dump point with tanks more than half full, rather than when the gauge forces them.

Know your capacity in days rather than litres: how long the fresh water lasts, when the grey tank needs attention and how many days the toilet supports for your group. Those numbers set how far off grid you can go.
tips: Empty on schedule, not on demand

faq: Where can you empty a caravan toilet in Australia?

At a dump point. Public ones sit at showgrounds, rest areas, visitor centres and roadhouses and are listed on the National Public Toilet Map, and many caravan parks have their own. Never use a drain or the ground, and use a toilet only where it is signed for cassette disposal.
Can you empty grey water on the ground in Australia?

Not as a rule. Grey water goes into a dump point or wherever the campground directs, and where there are no facilities the Victorian state forest standard is to tip washing-up water at least 50 metres from waterways.

camping-water-planning.title: Water planning for remote camping
camping-water-planning.description: Carry enough for drinking, cooking and delays, then verify every refill before relying on it.
camping-water-planning.imageAlt: Water containers packed for remote camping
camping-water-planning.intro: Water planning starts with the longest gap between confirmed potable supplies, then adds margin for heat, walking and a delayed day.

sections.heading: Calculate a real allowance
body: Count drinking, cooking and basic hygiene for every person. Hot weather, altitude and physical work increase demand quickly.
Do not reduce drinking water to protect a low tank. Reduce washing or leave the route earlier.

sections.heading: Confirm the source
body: A tap icon does not always mean potable water. Read signs, ask the manager and treat uncertain natural water before use.
Remote tanks can run dry or be reserved for emergencies. Carry enough to reach the next confirmed source.

sections.heading: Store it safely
body: Use several containers rather than one large tank so a leak does not remove the whole supply. Secure heavy water low in the vehicle.
Clean containers between trips and keep fuel, waste hoses and chemicals away from drinking-water equipment.

sections.heading: How much you actually need
body: Plan on a minimum of four to five litres per person per day for drinking and cooking in temperate conditions, and considerably more in the heat. In outback summer, seven to ten litres per person per day is realistic.
That is drinking and cooking only. Washing, dishes and any showering come on top, which is why a vehicle tank empties faster than the arithmetic suggests.

Always carry a reserve that is not part of the working supply, ideally in a separate container. A vehicle breakdown in remote country turns water from a convenience into the thing that keeps you alive.
tips: Four to five litres per person per day minimum
Seven to ten in outback heat

sections.heading: Where you can refill
