public-transport-costs-australia-2026.title: Public transport costs across Australian cities in 2026
public-transport-costs-australia-2026.description: Compare Brisbane, Perth, Melbourne and Sydney fares without confusing per-trip prices with daily caps.
public-transport-costs-australia-2026.imageAlt: Public transport in an Australian city
public-transport-costs-australia-2026.intro: Australian city fares use different rules, payment methods and caps. A flat Queensland journey, a Perth DayRider and Sydney’s daily cap answer different questions, so compare the full day you expect to travel.

sections.heading: Compare the same unit
body: A fare per journey is not a daily maximum. Count the expected trips, understand transfers and then apply the operator’s current cap rules.
Use the accepted payment method correctly. Contactless, stored-value and cash fares can differ, and tapping errors can remove a cap or create an incomplete trip.

sections.heading: Airport travel is often separate
body: Private or station-access charges may sit outside ordinary public-transport pricing. Brisbane’s Airtrain is excluded from Queensland’s 50-cent fare, while Sydney Airport charges an access fee in addition to the rail fare.
Price the airport leg separately before deciding whether rail, bus, shuttle, taxi or rideshare works best.

sections.heading: Use transport to avoid city driving
body: Parking, tolls and unfamiliar traffic can make public transport valuable even when several people share a car. Compare the full vehicle cost, not only the train fare.
Leave the campervan or caravan at a legal base where possible and use city transport for dense central areas.

sections.heading: Each city has its own card
body: Australia has no national transport card. Sydney uses Opal, Melbourne Myki, Brisbane and southeast Queensland go card, Perth SmartRider and Adelaide metroCARD, with contactless bank card payment available in some but not all.
Melbourne is the notable exception where contactless is not accepted on most services, so a Myki is required. Check before arriving rather than assuming your bank card will work.

Daily and weekly caps exist in most systems and change the arithmetic substantially once you make several trips. Work out the expected number of journeys before choosing between a pass and paying per trip.

sections.heading: Airport connections
body: Sydney charges a station access fee on top of the rail fare, making the airport train considerably more expensive than an ordinary trip. Brisbane's Airtrain is similarly priced as a separate service.
Melbourne, Perth, Adelaide and Darwin have bus or rail links at more ordinary fares. With three or more people and luggage, a rideshare is sometimes competitive with individual fares.
None of these are typically covered by a standard day pass. Price the airport leg separately when comparing options.
tips: Sydney adds a station access fee
Rideshare can beat fares for groups

sections.heading: When to leave the vehicle behind
body: Driving a campervan into central Sydney or Melbourne is unpleasant, parking is expensive and height restrictions catch large vehicles out constantly. Leaving it at a caravan park and taking transport in is faster and cheaper.
The same applies in most capitals. Base yourself outside the centre and use the local network for the days you want to be in the city.
Outside the capitals and a handful of regional centres, public transport is minimal to non-existent. A trip planned around buses works between cities and does not reach campsites or trailheads.
tips: Height limits catch vans in city car parks

sections.heading: Concessions and visitor passes
body: Concession fares generally require an Australian concession card, and overseas student or senior cards are usually not accepted. Budget for full adult fares unless you have confirmed otherwise for that specific network.

Some cities sell visitor passes bundling transport with attractions. Work out the number of trips and entries you will actually use before buying, because these usually assume a busier itinerary than most travellers keep.
Where you are staying more than a few days in a city, a weekly cap or pass usually beats daily fares and removes the need to think about it.
tips: Visitor passes assume a busy schedule

faq: Can you travel Australia without a car?
Between the capitals, yes. Beyond them the network thins fast, and the coastal and outback places most people come for are effectively unreachable without a vehicle or a tour.
How much does public transport cost in Australian cities?

The guide gives dated fares for Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Perth. All run tap-on cards with daily and weekly caps, and several now accept a contactless bank card directly, which saves buying a travel card at all.

sources.label: Transport for NSW adult Opal fares

priceTable.note: Adult benchmarks checked 12 August 2026. Airport services, eligibility, concessions and payment methods can change the result.

domestic-flight-costs-australia-2026.title: Domestic flight costs in Australia: realistic 2026 sale floors
domestic-flight-costs-australia-2026.description: Observed fares for short, northbound and transcontinental routes, plus the extras that turn a headline into a total.
domestic-flight-costs-australia-2026.imageAlt: Aircraft flying over the Australian landscape
domestic-flight-costs-australia-2026.intro: Australia’s scale makes flying attractive, but the cheapest advertised seat is a dated sale example rather than a standing fare. These observed 2026 floors show the shape of the market before baggage, seats and peak dates.

sections.heading: Sale floor versus trip total
body: Add checked baggage, seat selection, payment charges, airport transport and the cost of reaching or replacing the vehicle. A cheap flight can still be the expensive option for a gear-heavy trip.
Compare matching dates and luggage rather than two headline numbers.

sections.heading: Distance changes the value
body: Flying can save days across the continent, while a short east-coast sector may compete with rail, coach or a one-way vehicle plan. Time has a budget value too.
One-way vehicle fees and restricted rental roads can matter more than the ticket.

sections.heading: Use sale examples honestly
body: The table records published promotions from Virgin Australia and Jetstar. Both had limited inventory and travel conditions, so no reader should expect the same fare today.
Search the exact dates directly with carriers and compare the complete checkout amount before changing the route.

sections.heading: When flying beats driving
body: Australia's scale makes flying genuinely useful on the long legs: Perth to the east coast, anywhere to Darwin, or Tasmania. On those the time saved is days rather than hours.

It rarely makes sense for shorter hops that a good drive covers well, and it never makes sense if it means paying for a vehicle sitting idle at the other end. Price the whole arrangement, not the fare.

One-way vehicle relocation fees can exceed the airfare, so check them before assuming a fly-one-way plan is cheaper. Relocation deals occasionally make it dramatically cheaper if your dates and direction match.
tips: One-way fees can exceed the airfare

sections.heading: Baggage is where the cheap fare goes
body: The lowest advertised fares are seat-only, and adding checked baggage, seat selection and any flexibility can double the price. For campers with packs, a tent and cooking gear, checked baggage is not optional.
Regional aircraft on routes to smaller towns have tighter weight limits than the main trunk services, and they are enforced. Check the specific route rather than assuming a single airline standard.
Camping gas cylinders and some fuels cannot be carried at all, so plan to buy them at the destination rather than transporting them.

sections.heading: Booking windows and disruption
body: Domestic fares are cheapest booked several weeks out and rise sharply in the final fortnight. School holidays and the period around Christmas see both higher fares and full aircraft.
Wet season weather in the north and fog in the south both cause cancellations, and regional routes with a single daily service leave no recovery option that day.
Never connect a domestic flight tightly to an international departure. A night in the departure city is far cheaper than a missed long-haul flight.
tips: Single daily services have no backup

sections.heading: Airports and getting to them
body: Several low-cost carriers use secondary terminals or airports further from the city, and the transfer cost and time can erase the fare saving. Check which terminal and airport your fare uses before comparing prices.

Regional airports are frequently small, with limited hire desks that close outside flight times. If you are collecting a vehicle at a regional airport on an evening arrival, confirm the desk will be staffed.
Check baggage allowances against your actual gear before booking, because camping equipment routinely exceeds what a discount fare includes.
tips: Transfer cost can erase the saving

faq: How much are domestic flights in Australia?

The guide gives realistic sale floors and typical fares on the main routes rather than headline prices. On the long legs, such as the east coast to Perth or Darwin, flying is often cheaper than driving once fuel and time are counted.
Is it cheaper to fly or drive in Australia?
For crossing the continent, flying usually wins on both cost and time. For anything under a day's drive, the vehicle wins, especially once a one-way rental drop-off fee is in the comparison.

sources.label: Reserve Bank of Australia exchange rates

priceTable.note: Expired 2026 promotional one-way fare examples. They demonstrate observed sale floors, not current bookable quotes.

bus-train-costs-australia-2026.title: Long-distance bus and train costs in Australia
bus-train-costs-australia-2026.description: Compare an interstate coach, a Queensland transport train and a luxury rail journey without pretending they are the same product.
bus-train-costs-australia-2026.intro: Australia’s long-distance transport ranges from a functional overnight coach to an all-inclusive rail experience. Price, travel time, sleeping arrangement and inclusions must be compared together.

sections.heading: Transport and experience
body: A coach seat and an all-inclusive sleeper train do not solve the same need. One buys movement; the other may bundle accommodation, meals and excursions.
List what the fare includes before comparing it with flights, driving or several hotel nights.

sections.heading: Time, sleep and arrival
body: An overnight service may save a room but deliver a poor night for someone who cannot sleep seated. Daylight arrival and onward transport also matter.
Check luggage limits, bicycle or surfboard rules and the distance between the terminal and the actual destination.

sections.heading: Treat old fare sheets carefully
body: Queensland Rail directs travellers to current information, while the publicly indexed sheet provides only a dated benchmark. Do not reproduce it as a current guaranteed fare.
Industrial action, track work and seasonal timetables can change service. Confirm directly before building fixed bookings around the arrival.

sections.heading: The long-distance coach network
body: Greyhound and a handful of regional operators connect the major cities and many towns along the east coast and through the centre. Booked well ahead they are the cheapest way to move without a vehicle, and fares rise sharply close to departure.

Coaches are slower than driving and stop frequently. What they do not do is reach national parks, trailheads or campsites, so a bus-based trip is shaped by the network rather than by where you would ideally go.

Hop-on hop-off passes exist for backpacker routes along the east coast. Compare the pass against the individual fares you would actually book rather than the maximum possible use, because most people use fewer trips than expected.
tips: Book coaches early for low fares

sections.heading: The long-distance trains
body: Australia's long-distance rail is largely an experience product rather than transport. The Ghan, the Indian Pacific and the Spirit of Queensland each bundle accommodation, meals and in some cases excursions into the fare.
Prices reflect that, and comparing a Ghan fare with a flight is comparing two different purchases. One buys movement, the other buys several days of travel that is itself the holiday.
There are also ordinary regional services, particularly in New South Wales and Queensland, which are inexpensive and useful for reaching regional towns without a car.
tips: Regional services are cheap and useful

sections.heading: Ferries and island access
body: The Spirit of Tasmania is the only vehicle route to Tasmania and is a substantial fixed cost priced by vehicle size. Foot passenger fares are far cheaper, which occasionally makes hiring on the island worth pricing.

Kangaroo Island, Fraser Island and the Whitsundays all have vehicle or passenger ferries, and the vehicle fares are considerably higher than passenger ones. On some islands a vehicle is unnecessary anyway.
Book vehicle crossings well ahead in peak season. These services have limited capacity and sell out, and a missed crossing can cost days on an island itinerary.
tips: Vehicle ferries sell out in peak season
A vehicle is unnecessary on some islands

sections.heading: Luggage, comfort and the overnight question
body: Coach luggage allowances are generally generous but camping gear, surfboards and bicycles frequently need pre-booking and attract a fee. Confirm before turning up with an oversized item.

An overnight coach saves a night's accommodation and delivers a poor night's sleep for most people. Factor in that you will arrive tired and probably lose the following morning, which changes the real saving considerably.
Book the seat as well as the ticket where the operator allows it, since long-distance services fill and the remaining seats are rarely the good ones.
tips: Overnight coaches cost you the morning

faq: How much do long-distance buses cost in Australia?

Greyhound and the regional operators are the cheapest way to cover distance without a car, and the guide gives dated fares on the main corridors. Passes priced by distance or by time suit a slow east coast run.
Are Australia's long-distance trains worth it?

As an experience rather than transport. The Ghan and the Indian Pacific are priced as journeys in their own right and cost far more than flying the same route, so treat them as the holiday rather than the way to it.

sources.label: Queensland Rail 2025–26 Spirit of Queensland sheet

priceTable.note: Dated provider benchmarks. Queensland Rail’s figure is from the indexed 2025–26 sheet; request the current 2026–27 fare before booking.

driving-in-australia-road-rules-visitors.title: Driving in Australia for the first time: essential road rules
driving-in-australia-road-rules-visitors.description: Drive on the left, understand speed and restraint rules, and know why licence conditions matter across state borders.
driving-in-australia-road-rules-visitors.imageAlt: Australian road seen from the left-hand driving position
driving-in-australia-road-rules-visitors.intro: Australia drives on the left, but safe visitor driving involves more than remembering the side of the road. Speed, alcohol, mobile devices and licence conditions all need a cautious, jurisdiction-aware approach.

sections.heading: Left-side habits
body: Take extra care after stops, at turns and when entering roundabouts, when old right-side habits can return. Keep the driver near the centre line and the passenger side near the kerb.
Set navigation, mirrors and controls before moving. If orientation feels wrong, stop legally and reset rather than correcting while driving.

sections.heading: Speed, restraints and devices
body: A posted limit is the legal maximum in good conditions, not a target. Slow for weather, visibility, wildlife, gravel and the vehicle’s size.
Every occupant needs the correct seating position and restraint. Portable-device rules and exceptions vary, so the safest practice is not to touch a phone while driving.

sections.heading: Alcohol and jurisdiction differences
body: Never present 0.05 as a universal allowance. Learner and provisional drivers can require zero BAC, while some heavy or passenger-vehicle categories have lower limits.
The Australian Road Rules are a national model, but every state and territory enacts its own law and can add differences. Read the authority for the place you are driving.

sections.heading: Roundabouts, hook turns and school zones
body: Roundabouts run clockwise and you give way to your right, signalling left as you exit. Multi-lane roundabouts require the correct entry lane, marked on the road surface.

Melbourne's central grid uses hook turns, where a right turn is made from the left lane after waiting for the signal. They are signed and unique to that city, and they catch out Australian drivers as well as visitors.
School zones drop to forty kilometres per hour at set times on school days and are enforced heavily with cameras. The signs show the times and they apply whether or not children are visible.
tips: Give way to the right on roundabouts

sections.heading: Level crossings, trams and cyclists
body: Many rural level crossings are passive, marked only with signs rather than lights or booms. Slow, look both ways and be aware that trains on regional lines are infrequent enough that people stop expecting them.
In Melbourne and Adelaide, trams share the road. You must stop behind a stationary tram when passengers are boarding or alighting unless there is a safety zone, and this is strictly enforced.

A minimum passing distance for cyclists applies in most states, generally one metre under sixty kilometres per hour and one and a half metres above it. Crossing a centre line to achieve it is permitted where safe.

sections.heading: Mobile phones and enforcement
body: Mobile phone laws are strict and enforced with dedicated detection cameras in several states. Touching a phone while driving, including while stationary in traffic, is an offence with substantial fines and demerit points.
Hands-free use through a cradle or Bluetooth is generally permitted for full licence holders but prohibited entirely for learner and provisional drivers. Set navigation before moving.

Camera fines go to the registered owner, so a rental company will name you as the driver and usually add an administration fee. Overseas licence holders still collect demerit points, and too many in one state means losing the right to drive there.
tips: Rentals pass on fines with a fee

sections.heading: Parking rules and signage
body: Parking signage in Australian cities is dense and strictly enforced, with clearways, permit zones, loading zones and time limits often stacked on one pole. Read the whole sign from the top down, because the most restrictive condition applies.

Clearways prohibit stopping entirely during posted hours and vehicles are towed rather than ticketed. In Sydney and Melbourne this catches visitors regularly and recovering a towed campervan is expensive and time consuming.
When unsure at an intersection, giving way costs a few seconds and resolves almost every uncertainty safely.
tips: Read the whole sign, top down

faq: What are the most important road rules for visitors to Australia?

Drive on the left, keep to the posted limit, which is enforced by camera far more than by patrol, and observe the 0.05 blood alcohol limit. Give way rules at roundabouts and the rules for school zones catch visitors out most often.
What is the speed limit in Australia?

Typically 100 or 110 km/h on the open road and 50 km/h in built-up areas, but limits are set per state and differ. The Northern Territory has some 130 km/h sections, and school zones drop sharply at posted times.

sources.label: Queensland: driving on an overseas licence
VicRoads: driving with an overseas licence
NT visiting drivers and traffic offences
Revenue NSW: nominate someone else for a fine

overseas-driver-licence-australia-state-.title: Can you drive in Australia with an overseas licence?
overseas-driver-licence-australia-state-.description: A state-by-state visitor guide to validity, translations, IDPs, vehicle class and conversion deadlines.
overseas-driver-licence-australia-state-.imageAlt: Driver holding an overseas licence beside a rental vehicle
overseas-driver-licence-australia-state-.intro: There is no single nationwide deadline for driving on an overseas licence. Visitor status, residency, language, vehicle class and the state or territory all affect what documents and time limits apply.

sections.heading: Visitor rules are jurisdiction-specific
body: NSW temporary visitors can generally drive for up to six months when eligible, while Victoria also describes a six-month visitor period. Queensland and Western Australia use their own validity and residency rules.
Do not carry one state’s rule across a border. Open the authority page for every jurisdiction on the route.

sections.heading: Translations and document conditions
body: A non-English licence may require an approved English translation or International Driving Permit. Carry the physical documents required and obey every condition on the original licence.
An IDP supports the home licence; it does not replace an expired, suspended or otherwise invalid licence.

sections.heading: Vehicle class matters
body: A standard car class in NSW and Queensland generally covers no more than 4.5 tonnes GVM and 12 occupants including the driver. A larger motorhome may require a different authorised class.
Rental permission and insurance do not override licensing law. Confirm all three before accepting the vehicle.

sections.heading: Carrying the right documents
body: Carry the original overseas licence at all times, along with an English translation or International Driving Permit if it is not in English. The permit supports the licence rather than replacing it and both must be present.
Obtain the permit in your home country before travelling, because it generally cannot be issued after arrival. It is inexpensive and available from the relevant motoring authority.
Police can require both at a roadside stop, and being unable to produce them is an offence in its own right regardless of whether you are otherwise entitled to drive.
tips: Get the IDP before you travel
Failure to produce is an offence

sections.heading: Becoming a resident changes everything
body: The visitor periods apply to visitors. Once you become a resident of a state, the clock is different and conversion becomes mandatory within a defined period, frequently three months.

What counts as becoming a resident varies and can be triggered by a visa type, employment or simply length of stay. Working holiday visa holders in particular should check the position in the state they are living in.
Driving on an overseas licence after the residency deadline is driving unlicensed, with the insurance consequences that follow if anything happens.
tips: Past the deadline is unlicensed driving

sections.heading: Conditions and vehicle classes
body: Any condition on your original licence applies here: corrective lenses, automatic transmission only, or a graduated or probationary restriction. Driving outside those conditions is driving unlicensed.

A standard car class generally covers vehicles to 4.5 tonnes and twelve occupants, which covers most rental campervans but not all larger motorhomes. Check the vehicle specification against your class before booking.
Towing is assessed on the combination weight rather than the vehicle alone, so a car licence may not cover a heavy caravan behind a large four-wheel drive.
tips: 4.5 tonnes is the usual car limit
Towing is assessed on combined weight

sections.heading: What to do if you are stopped
body: Pull over promptly and safely, stay in the vehicle unless asked otherwise, and have your licence and any translation or permit ready. Random breath testing is routine and does not imply suspicion of anything.
Police in Australia are generally straightforward at roadside stops. Being unable to produce a licence is an offence in itself, so keeping the documents in the vehicle rather than in luggage matters.
Keep a photograph of every document stored separately from the originals, so a lost wallet is an inconvenience rather than the end of the driving.
tips: Failure to produce is an offence

faq: How long can you drive on a foreign licence in Australia?

As a genuine visitor, for the length of your stay in most states. The clock only starts when you become a permanent resident, and then the window to convert is short, often three months, and it differs by state.
Which state's rules apply if you are driving across Australia?

The state you are in at the time, not the one you landed in. Licence recognition, demerit points and the rules for probationary drivers are all state matters, which is why they change as you cross a border.

australian-road-signs-visitors-guide.title: Australian road signs visitors should know
australian-road-signs-visitors-guide.description: Regulatory, warning, advisory and roadwork signs explained for people starting an Australian road trip.
australian-road-signs-visitors-guide.imageAlt: Australian warning and regulatory road signs
australian-road-signs-visitors-guide.intro: Australian signs use familiar shapes and colours, but a visitor needs to distinguish a legal instruction from a hazard warning or advisory speed. Temporary traffic control matters just as much as a permanent sign.

sections.heading: Regulatory signs
body: Stop, Give Way, speed limit, Keep Left, No Entry, prohibited turns, roundabouts and shared zones create legal requirements. A Stop sign requires a complete stop.
Give Way requires slowing and stopping when necessary, then applying the priority rule for the intersection.

sections.heading: Warnings and advisory speeds
body: Warning signs identify bends, merging or narrowing lanes, animals, unsealed surfaces, floodways and railway crossings. The hazard changes how you drive even when the posted maximum stays the same.
A regulatory speed sign is not the same as an advisory speed displayed for a bend or crest. Slow to the conditions and vehicle.
tips: Do not treat advisory speed as a target

sections.heading: Roadworks and road trains
body: Temporary speed limits, traffic lights and traffic-controller directions at roadworks must be obeyed. Conditions can change between trips.
A yellow ROAD TRAIN or LONG VEHICLE panel attached to a truck identifies that vehicle. Give it space; do not mistake the panel for a roadside direction.

sections.heading: Signs you will not have seen elsewhere
body: Floodway markers with depth indicators appear on roads that cross watercourses, and the numbered posts show water depth. Never enter if the depth is unknown or the water is moving.
Grid signs warn of cattle grids, which can be rough at speed. Open range and stock warning signs indicate unfenced roads where animals may be on the carriageway at any time.
Road train and long vehicle signs on trucks identify combinations up to 53.5 metres. The sign is attached to the vehicle rather than being a roadside instruction, which confuses many visitors.
tips: Road train signs are on the truck

sections.heading: Speed signage and variable limits
body: Speed limits are in kilometres per hour. Where no speed sign applies, the default limit outside built-up areas is 100 km/h in most states and 110 km/h in Western Australia and the Northern Territory. Some highways are signposted at 110 km/h, and the Northern Territory allows 130 km/h only on sections of the Stuart, Barkly, Victoria and Arnhem highways where signs show it.
Variable message signs and electronic speed signs override posted limits and are common around roadworks, tunnels and school zones. Roadwork limits apply whether or not work is visibly happening.
Advisory speeds on yellow signs at corners are not legal limits but are set for a car in good conditions. In a loaded campervan or towing, the safe speed is lower again.
tips: Default open limits vary by state
Yellow advisory signs assume a car

sections.heading: Wildlife and fatigue signage
body: Animal warning signs indicating kangaroos, wombats, cassowaries or camels mark areas with genuine strike risk, concentrated around dawn and dusk. Treat them as a reason to reduce speed rather than decoration.
Driver reviver and rest area signs mark places to stop for fatigue, and on long routes the distance to the next one is often shown. Use them rather than pushing on.
Some remote routes carry signs stating the distance to the next fuel or water. Those are not suggestions; on the Nullarbor and through the outback they are the information your trip depends on.
tips: Animal signs mark real strike zones
Rest area signs show the next distance

sections.heading: Distance markers and location signs
body: Roadside distance markers and location reference signs are how you describe where you are to emergency services in remote areas. Noting the nearest one before making a call saves a great deal of time.

Many highways carry signs showing the distance to the next fuel, water or rest area. On outback routes these are planning information rather than trivia, and they are frequently the most useful signs on the road.
Spend ten minutes with a signs guide before the first driving day, because recognising an unfamiliar sign at speed is considerably harder than learning it in advance.
tips: Note markers before calling for help
Fuel distance signs are planning data

faq: What Australian road signs do visitors need to know?

The ones with no overseas equivalent: floodway and depth markers, road train warnings, kangaroo and livestock signs, and the yellow advisory speed on a curve. Grid and unfenced stock signs mean animals may be on the road.
What does a floodway sign mean?

That the road crosses a watercourse and can be under water without warning. The depth markers beside it show how deep, and the rule is the national one: if it is flooded, forget it. Most flood deaths in Australia happen in vehicles.

campervan-driving-australia-safety-guide.title: Campervan driving in Australia: size, safety and legal limits
campervan-driving-australia-safety-guide.description: Check licence class, vehicle dimensions, restraints and road exclusions before the first long driving day.
campervan-driving-australia-safety-guide.imageAlt: Campervan travelling on an Australian highway
campervan-driving-australia-safety-guide.intro: A campervan may feel like a large car until braking, crosswind or a low branch exposes its real size. The safe handover begins with dimensions, loaded weight, licence class and rental conditions.

sections.heading: Know the vehicle before moving
body: Record the height, length and GVM, locate the fuel type and learn the mirrors, blind spots and controls. A vehicle above 4.5 tonnes may fall outside an ordinary car licence.
Confirm tyre, awning, roof, gas and interior stowage procedures with the operator.

sections.heading: Everyone travels in a proper seat
body: Beds and living areas are not passenger positions while moving. Every occupant must use an approved seat and the required restraint.
Secure loose items before every drive. A cupboard or bottle becomes dangerous under sudden braking.

sections.heading: Drive for the loaded vehicle
body: Allow more stopping distance, turn smoothly and slow before bends, gravel, crosswinds and narrow shoulders. A legal maximum can still be unsafe.
Rental exclusions, insurance conditions and government road rules are separate requirements. Permission from one does not cancel the others.

sections.heading: Wind, road trains and overtaking
body: A high-sided campervan catches crosswind badly, and a passing road train produces a significant push followed by a pull. Hold the wheel firmly with both hands and do not correct sharply.
Overtaking in a campervan requires far more clear road than a car needs, and most Australian highways are two-lane with limited passing lanes. If an overtake feels marginal, do not attempt it.
When traffic builds behind you, use the next slow vehicle bay and let it past. Frustrated following drivers cause overtaking crashes, and removing that pressure is both courteous and safer for you.

sections.heading: Unsealed roads and what your agreement allows
body: Most standard rental agreements prohibit unsealed roads entirely or name specific exclusions, with damage on them uninsured. Vehicles are tracked, so driving them anyway is not a private decision.
On gravel, reduce speed well below sealed-road pace, brake and steer gently and separately, and leave a very large gap behind anything raising dust. Windscreen damage is the most common claim.
Lowering tyre pressures for corrugations improves comfort and reduces damage, but you must reinflate before returning to sealed roads. Carry a gauge and a compressor if you intend to do this.
tips: Huge gap behind anything raising dust

sections.heading: Heat, tyres and vehicle checks
body: Australian heat is hard on tyres, and underinflated or old tyres fail at speed on hot bitumen. Check pressures cold, set them for the loaded vehicle, and inspect the spare before a remote leg.
Check coolant, oil and washer levels regularly, particularly before long outback legs. A breakdown in remote heat is a safety problem rather than an inconvenience.
Carry more water than the trip requires. If the vehicle stops in remote country, water is what keeps the situation manageable while you wait, and you should always wait with the vehicle.
tips: Check the spare before remote legs

sections.heading: Parking and manoeuvring in towns
body: Height restrictions in urban car parks are the most common source of expensive campervan damage, and the barrier is usually the first warning. Write the vehicle height somewhere visible from the driver's seat and check every entrance.
Many towns provide oversized vehicle parking on the outskirts or at showgrounds. Using it and walking in is faster than circling a town centre looking for a space that fits.
Do a full walk around the vehicle each morning, checking tyres, lights and that nothing is left on the roof or open underneath.
tips: Write the height on the dashboard
Car park barriers are the first warning

faq: What do you need to know about driving a campervan in Australia?

Its height, its width and how it behaves in crosswind, because all three matter on narrow roads and when a road train passes. Most rental agreements also restrict unsealed roads, which rules out a lot of the good camping.
Do campervans have a different speed limit in Australia?
Under 4.5 tonnes, generally no. Heavier vehicles and anything towing face lower limits in some states, and the limit is a maximum rather than a target for a high-sided vehicle in wind.

towing-caravan-australia-road-rules.title: Caravan Towing Laws Australia 2026: Speed, Weight, Licence
towing-caravan-australia-road-rules.description: Caravan towing laws for 2026: what a car licence covers, WA and NSW towing speed limits, ball weight and the four load limits to check before you hitch up.
towing-caravan-australia-road-rules.imageAlt: Car and caravan travelling on an Australian road
towing-caravan-australia-road-rules.intro: Safe towing starts with the actual loaded combination, not the empty caravan brochure. Manufacturer limits, ball load, licence conditions and jurisdiction rules all need to agree.

sections.heading: Weights and connection
body: Keep the loaded caravan within the tow vehicle, towbar, coupling and manufacturer limits. Secure the load and inspect chains, hatches, tyres, brakes and lights.
Repeat the inspection during long trips. Heat, vibration and rough surfaces can expose a problem that was not visible at departure.

sections.heading: Nobody rides in the caravan
body: A towed caravan or trailer is not a passenger compartment. Everyone travels in an approved vehicle seating position with the correct restraint.
Extra length and mass require longer stopping distance, wider cornering lines and smooth steering and braking.

sections.heading: Speed rules vary
body: Western Australia limits a vehicle towing a trailer or caravan to 100 km/h and has a 60-metre following rule behind certain heavy or towing vehicles unless overtaking.
NSW’s cited 100 km/h cap applies when the towing vehicle or combination exceeds 4.5 tonnes. Never turn one jurisdiction’s rule into a nationwide towing speed.

sections.heading: Reversing, parking and campgrounds
body: Practise reversing in an empty car park before the trip. Caravan park sites frequently require a reverse into a defined space with neighbours close on both sides, and doing it for the first time with an audience is how vans get damaged.
Book sites suited to your combination length and say you are towing when booking. Many parks keep drive-through sites, which removes most of the difficulty from arrival.
Unhitching gives you an ordinary vehicle for day trips and is worth doing on any stay longer than one night. Use wheel chocks and levelling ramps and check the handbrake holds first.
tips: Unhitch for stays over one night

sections.heading: Roads and conditions to avoid
body: Many mountain and coastal roads are unsuitable for large combinations, and some are prohibited outright. Check before committing, because turning a caravan around on a narrow road is frequently impossible.
On descents, select a lower gear and use engine braking rather than riding the brakes, which fade and can fail entirely on a long grade with a heavy van behind.
Unsealed roads with corrugations are hard on caravans and cause structural damage over time. Many insurance policies exclude or limit cover for damage sustained on them.

sections.heading: Weights and the paperwork that matters
body: The limiting figure is whichever is lowest of the tow vehicle's capacity, the towbar rating, the caravan's aggregate trailer mass and the tow ball rating. Exceeding any of them affects handling, braking and insurance.
Weigh the loaded combination rather than estimating. Public weighbridges are widely available and inexpensive, and most caravans travel heavier than their owners believe.

Keep about 5 to 10 percent of the loaded caravan's weight on the tow ball, as NSW guidance advises, and check your vehicle and caravan manuals for their limits. Load heavy items low and over the axle. Rear-loading a caravan is the most common cause of sway.

sections.heading: Before every driving day
body: Walk around the combination: check the coupling is latched and pinned, safety chains are crossed and connected, the jockey wheel is up, lights and brakes work, and nothing is loose on the drawbar or roof.
Repeat a quick check at the first stop of the day. Heat, vibration and corrugations loosen fittings, and a problem found at a fuel stop is trivial compared with the same problem found at speed.
Consider a towing course before a first long trip, since a day of instruction covers reversing, weight distribution and sway recovery far better than reading about them.

faq: What is the speed limit for towing a caravan in Australia?

It depends on the state. Western Australia caps any vehicle towing a trailer or caravan at 100 km/h. In NSW the 100 km/h cap applies when the towing vehicle's GVM or GCM is over 4.5 tonnes; below that the posted limit applies. Check each state's towing rules before crossing a border, and drive to the rig's stability and the conditions.
Do you need a special licence to tow a caravan in Australia?

A standard car licence covers a tow vehicle of up to 4.5 tonnes gross vehicle mass (GVM); a heavier vehicle needs a light rigid licence or higher. The licence does not raise towing limits: the loaded caravan must stay within the lowest of the vehicle's towing capacity, the towbar and coupling rating, the caravan's own rating and the tyres' load rating. In NSW, learners cannot tow and P1 drivers may only tow trailers up to 250 kg unladen.

driving-with-road-trains-australia.title: How to share Australian roads with road trains
driving-with-road-trains-australia.description: Overtaking, dust, stopping distance and single-lane-road behaviour around vehicles up to 60 metres long.
driving-with-road-trains-australia.imageAlt: Road train on a remote Australian highway
driving-with-road-trains-australia.intro: A road train can be roughly 27.5 to 60 metres long. It needs space to stop, turn and pass, and the safest driver is predictable rather than helpful in an improvised way.

sections.heading: Following and overtaking
body: Stay well back, especially on unsealed roads where dust can erase visibility. Never pass without a long, fully visible clear stretch.
Do not overtake a turning road train or cut in after passing. Its stopping distance is much greater than a car’s.

sections.heading: When a road train passes you
body: Northern Territory guidance says to maintain speed and keep left, then slow only once the truck has moved out to pass. Sudden early slowing can disrupt the manoeuvre.
Do not rely on informal flashing lights or UHF directions as if they were legal traffic control.

sections.heading: Single-lane and unsealed roads
body: On an NT single-lane highway, slow and pull off, moving slowly on the shoulder for an approaching road train when safe. Expect dust and loose stones.
Choose a safe place and avoid a soft, steep or damaged shoulder. Conditions and jurisdiction guidance still control the decision.

sections.heading: Where you will meet them
body: Road trains operate across the Northern Territory, outback Queensland, northern South Australia and much of Western Australia, with the longest combinations on designated routes. Triples and quads are normal on those roads.

They are also present on approach roads to mines and cattle stations, frequently on unsealed surfaces where dust makes them nearly invisible until close. Assume they may be around any blind corner on a station road.
Their length means they cannot stop, swerve or move over meaningfully. Every safety decision on these roads is yours to make rather than theirs.
tips: They cannot swerve or stop quickly

sections.heading: Overtaking one safely
body: You need a very long, fully visible clear stretch, considerably more than for a truck at home. Judging the length of a road train from behind is difficult, and misjudging it is the classic fatal error on these roads.
Never begin an overtake on a crest, a curve or where dust limits visibility. If you cannot see the entire combination and a long clear road beyond it, wait.
Once past, do not cut back in early. Their stopping distance is far greater than a car's, and pulling in close in front removes the only margin they have.
tips: You need far more clear road
Never overtake into dust or a crest
Do not cut in close after passing

sections.heading: When one is passing you or approaching
body: When a road train overtakes, maintain your speed and hold your line to the left. Slowing suddenly disrupts the manoeuvre and lengthens the time it spends on the wrong side of the road.
On single-lane bitumen, common in the outback, slow down and move onto the shoulder for an approaching road train, keeping both left wheels off the seal. Expect flying stones and a large dust cloud.
On unsealed roads, pull well over and stop if visibility will disappear. Waiting thirty seconds for dust to clear is the correct response, not driving blind through it.
tips: Hold speed and line when passed
Move off single-lane seal for oncoming
Stop and wait for dust to clear

sections.heading: Road trains at roadhouses and rest areas
body: Roadhouses are working stops for road train drivers, and the parking areas are laid out for vehicles that cannot easily reverse or turn. Park clear of the truck bays and the entry and exit lines.

Drivers are on regulated rest breaks and the parking bays exist for that. Blocking them is both inconsiderate and creates a genuine safety issue when a driver has to move a fifty metre combination around a badly parked van.
A UHF radio on channel 40 lets you hear truck drivers discussing conditions ahead, which is genuinely useful information on remote highways.
tips: Drivers are on mandated rest breaks
Keep entry and exit lines clear

faq: How do you safely overtake a road train?

With a very long clear stretch and a firm decision. A road train can run to 53.5 metres, so overtaking takes far more road than a truck, and pulling back in early is what causes the crashes. If in doubt, do not.
What should you do when a road train comes the other way?

Slow down, move as far left as you safely can and expect a wall of air and stones as it passes. On a single-lane bitumen road you are expected to put your left wheels onto the gravel, and the driver will do the same.

australia-road-trip-fatigue-wildlife-saf.title: Fatigue, wildlife and night driving on Australian road trips
australia-road-trip-fatigue-wildlife-saf.description: Recognise fatigue early, plan real breaks and reduce the risk of dawn, dusk and remote-road driving.
australia-road-trip-fatigue-wildlife-saf.imageAlt: Kangaroo beside a quiet Australian road at dusk
australia-road-trip-fatigue-wildlife-saf.intro: Long distances do not make fatigue inevitable; tight itineraries do. Sleep is the only cure, wildlife is harder to see around dawn and dusk, and a daylight arrival gives every backup more room.

sections.heading: Recognise fatigue before it becomes a crisis
body: Yawning, heavy eyes, lane drift, forgotten kilometres and inconsistent speed are warnings to stop. Music, open windows and caffeine do not replace sleep.
Plan a break at least every two hours. Victorian guidance recommends no more than eight hours of driving in a 24-hour period.

sections.heading: Wildlife and night
body: Animals and livestock are particularly active around dawn and dusk. Reduce speed when animals are near the road and avoid swerving, which can cause a rollover or another collision.
Prefer daylight on unfamiliar roads and finish before fatigue begins choosing the speed, lane position or next stop.

sections.heading: Remote breakdown preparation
body: Carry extra water, food, fuel margin and an appropriate communication method where services are sparse. Tell someone the route and expected arrival.
Official WA remote-travel guidance says to remain with the vehicle if stranded. A vehicle provides shelter and is easier for rescuers to find.

sections.heading: Why distances here cause fatigue
body: Australian driving involves long, straight, monotonous roads with little to react to, which produces highway hypnosis far more readily than winding roads do. The absence of stimulus is itself the hazard.

Fatigue is a factor in a substantial share of regional crashes, and it accumulates across days rather than resetting overnight. A week of long driving days leaves you impaired even after a full night's sleep.
Plan the itinerary so no day requires more than about four hours of driving, and build in days where nobody drives at all. Most fatigue problems are planning problems.

sections.heading: Recognising it too late
body: Yawning, heavy eyes, drifting within the lane, missing a turn and having no memory of the last stretch are late signs. By the time you notice them, reaction time is already substantially impaired.
Stop every two hours as a rule rather than when you feel tired. A twenty minute nap is genuinely effective; coffee, music, open windows and conversation mask symptoms while the impairment continues.
Driver reviver stops and rest areas exist across the country for exactly this. Use them rather than treating a planned arrival time as fixed.
tips: Stop every two hours by rule
Coffee masks, it does not fix

sections.heading: Animals and the case against driving at night
body: Kangaroos, wombats, cattle, camels and emus are most active from dusk to dawn and are drawn to roadside vegetation. A strike at highway speed disables a vehicle and in remote areas that becomes a serious situation.
Do not drive between dusk and dawn in rural Australia if you can avoid it. This single decision removes most of the animal strike risk and much of the fatigue risk at once.
If an animal is on the road, brake in a straight line rather than swerving. Swerving is what turns a strike into a rollover, and in a high-sided vehicle the rollover risk is significant.
tips: Do not drive dusk to dawn
A strike in remote country is serious

sections.heading: If you do hit an animal
body: Stop when safe, and move the vehicle off the road. Do not approach a large injured animal such as a kangaroo or a wombat, because a distressed animal can cause serious injury with its hind legs or claws.

Call the relevant state wildlife rescue service, which can be reached from most areas with coverage. In marsupial country, checking a female's pouch is worth doing only if you are trained; otherwise report the location and let rescuers handle it.
Share the driving where you can, and treat the second driver as a real part of the plan rather than a backup who never actually drives.

faq: Why should you avoid driving at night in outback Australia?

Because that is when kangaroos, cattle and camels are on the road, and they move toward headlights rather than away. Almost every experienced outback driver keeps to the hours between sunrise and late afternoon for this reason.
What should you do if an animal runs onto the road?
Brake in a straight line and accept the hit rather than swerving. Swerving at highway speed is what rolls vehicles, and it turns an insurance claim into a serious crash.

australia-road-rules-state-differences.title: Australian road rules that change across states and territories
australia-road-rules-state-differences.description: Default speeds, towing, devices and licence conditions compared without turning local rules into national advice.
australia-road-rules-state-differences.imageAlt: Australian highway crossing a state border
australia-road-rules-state-differences.intro: Australian road rules are broadly consistent, but the legislation belongs to each state and territory. Default speeds, mobile-device exceptions, provisional restrictions, towing and overseas-licence periods can change at a border.

sections.heading: Model rules and local law
body: The Australian Road Rules provide a national model. Jurisdictions enact and amend their own versions, so a summary cannot replace the current local authority.
Posted signs, licence conditions and lower vehicle-specific limits always take priority over a general default.

sections.heading: Default unsigned speed examples
body: Queensland and Victoria describe 50 km/h in built-up areas and 100 km/h outside built-up areas. Western Australia states 50 km/h built-up and 110 km/h on open roads.
The Northern Territory generally uses 60 km/h in built-up areas unless gazetted lower and 110 km/h outside, with signed 130 km/h sections on specified highways.

sections.heading: The other differences that matter
body: Mobile-device exceptions, learner and provisional conditions, towing speeds and overseas-licence conversion periods all vary. A rental company can also impose tighter road exclusions.
Save direct state authority links before travel and review them whenever the vehicle, licence status or jurisdiction changes.

sections.heading: Why the rules differ at all
body: Road law in Australia is made by each state and territory rather than nationally. The Australian Road Rules provide a model that jurisdictions adopt with variations, so the base is consistent and the details are not.
The practical consequence is that speed defaults, mobile device exceptions, towing limits, licence conditions and even some signage change as you cross a border, frequently with no reminder.
On a trip crossing several states this matters. Check the position in each jurisdiction on your route rather than carrying one state's rules across the whole country.
tips: Each state makes its own road law
Borders change the rules without warning
Check each jurisdiction on the route

sections.heading: The differences most likely to catch you
body: Default open road limits vary from 100 to 110 kilometres per hour, with specified Northern Territory sections at 130. Built-up area defaults also differ, with the Territory using 60 rather than 50.
Towing speed limits differ, with Western Australia capping towing at 100 and other states applying limits based on vehicle mass. Following distance rules behind heavy vehicles also vary.
Mobile phone rules, learner and provisional restrictions and the treatment of overseas licences all differ between states, and the penalties for getting them wrong are real.

sections.heading: Crossing borders in practice
body: Quarantine checkpoints operate at several state borders, restricting fresh produce, honey, plants and soil. These are enforced with fines and, at some crossings, detector dogs.

Time zones change at some borders and not others, and several states observe daylight saving while others do not. Queensland, the Northern Territory and Western Australia do not, which creates larger gaps in summer.
Fuel prices, alcohol restrictions and even the availability of particular fuel grades change across borders. Check what applies where you are going rather than where you have been.

sections.heading: Practical border checklist
body: Before each border, run through the short list: quarantine produce, time zone change, fuel top-up, alcohol restrictions ahead, and any change to speed or towing limits. It takes two minutes and prevents most border problems.
Save the relevant state road authority page for each jurisdiction on your route while you have reception. Rules change and the authority page is the only source that reflects the current position.
When in doubt, follow the stricter rule you know of. It is never an offence to drive more cautiously than the local limit permits.
tips: Run a border checklist each time

faq: Do Australian road rules change between states?

Yes, more than visitors expect. Speed limits, towing limits, mobile phone penalties, keep-left rules and the treatment of overseas licences are all set by each state and territory, and they apply from the moment you cross the border.
Which rules differ most across Australian states?

Towing speed limits, the minimum passing distance for cyclists, the rules for driving on unsealed roads in a rental, and school zone times. Most states record demerit points from an interstate offence on your home licence, although Western Australia does not.

wikicamps-alternatives.title: 6 Best WikiCamps Alternatives in 2026 for Camping in Australia
wikicamps-alternatives.description: Six alternatives to WikiCamps Australia compared on price, data sources and what works without signal, from official-data apps to free and curated ones.
wikicamps-alternatives.imageAlt: Bush campsite beside a river in central Victoria
wikicamps-alternatives.intro: WikiCamps Australia is still one of the most useful camping apps in the country, so the right alternative depends on what you want it to do differently. We make AussieCamps. That is why it is listed first, and each entry explains when another app, or WikiCamps itself, is the better choice. Prices, ratings and features were checked on 20 October 2026.

sections.heading: Why travellers look beyond WikiCamps
body: WikiCamps earns its reputation with a community database its website puts at more than 65,000 sites, with 1.3 million reviews, for a one-off A$9.99 and no subscription. Most people who go looking for something else are not unhappy with that model; they want something it does not do.

Some reasons are documented by the developer itself. Version 6 rebuilt the app, older versions were retired from March 2026, and the help centre says key features will be reintroduced over time. A small number of ads now appear in the reviews, fees and photos sections. The purchase is tied to one store, so moving from Android to iPhone means paying again. Offline use starts with downloading the main Australia content, with a limit of three trips saved for offline use.
Others come down to preference: wanting listings drawn from park agencies rather than from users, wanting sites checked by an editorial team, or simply wanting a free app.
tips: Each platform is a separate purchase

sections.heading: The alternatives at a glance
body: Each row says when the app is the better choice than WikiCamps, not which app is better overall. WikiCamps is included for reference.

sections.heading: 1. AussieCamps: the official-data alternative for iPhone
body: AussieCamps takes the opposite approach to WikiCamps. Instead of user listings, its records come from published datasets such as NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, Parks Victoria, Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service, Main Roads WA and the National Public Toilet Map, which suits travellers who would rather start from what the land manager publishes. The current data covers 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas, 1,393 dump points and 3,004 drinking water points.

There is no region to download and no trip limit. The whole place directory installs with the app, so details for every place stay readable when the signal goes. Map tiles, directions, weather and photos still need a connection, as they do in most apps. Trips hold ordered stops with the distance and time for each leg, arrival dates with a forecast for each stop, a packing list, and an optional sync to your calendar.

The download is free, as are the hotels, motels, B&Bs, holiday parks and tours listed by BookEasy, the same booking partner WikiCamps uses. Campgrounds, rest areas, dump points, water, parks, guides, collections and trips need the AussieCamps Pass, sold as a weekly subscription or a one-off lifetime purchase, with in-app purchases from A$2.99 to A$9.99 on the Australian App Store.

Where it falls short of WikiCamps: it is on iPhone only, it carries far fewer places, and it has no traveller reviews, so you lose the recent comments that make WikiCamps useful at a free camp. Many travellers keep both.
tips: Every place detail works with no signal

sections.heading: 2. CAMPS Australia Wide: the curated alternative
body: If the worry with WikiCamps is that anyone can add or edit a listing, CAMPS is the closest answer. Camps Australia Wide says its team has checked sites in person since 1992, lists more than 16,000 campsites and takes no paid listings. Reviews from users sit alongside that editorial base.

Pricing is the main difference. After a 7-day free trial, the app needs an A$14.99 annual subscription, which includes offline maps with site information, live fuel prices, a trip planner and booking.
Choose it over WikiCamps if you value checked listings and do not mind a yearly fee. Stay with WikiCamps if you want its large pool of traveller reviews or a one-off price.
tips: Sites checked by its own team
A$14.99 a year after the trial

sections.heading: 3. CamperMate: the free alternative
body: CamperMate is free to download with no in-app purchases on the Australian App Store, and it covers New Zealand as well, which makes it a natural fit for a trans-Tasman trip. Like WikiCamps it is built on community reviews, photos and place suggestions, and the developer claims more than 70,000 points of interest.

Maps and key information can be downloaded for use without signal, and the app runs in 27 languages. It carries advertising, offers camping deals and bookings in the app, and is the official travel partner of campervan brands Apollo, Maui, Britz and Mighty Camper.

Choose it over WikiCamps if cost or a second country matters most. Some App Store reviews from May to August 2026 reported campsites not loading or not showing on the map; updates since then have reworked the map and offline data, so test it on your route before you depend on it.
tips: Test loading on your route first

sections.heading: 4. Full Range Camping: the membership alternative
body: Formerly FreeRange Camping, this directory lists more than 11,000 camping spots and businesses and is built around a paid membership. Premium is listed at A$49.99 a year or A$99.99 for life and adds offline listings, weather radar and member discounts that the company puts at up to 30 per cent at some campgrounds. New Premium sign-ups were paused when we checked on 20 October 2026, with the website citing an update to the app's mapping.
The membership also opens house sitting and work exchange listings, which interest long-term travellers trying to cut accommodation costs over months rather than weeks.
Choose it over WikiCamps if you will actually use the discounts or the house sitting. For finding sites alone, it is a smaller directory with far fewer App Store ratings.
tips: Premium A$49.99 a year or A$99.99 for life

sections.heading: 5. Hipcamp: the private-land alternative
body: Hipcamp answers a different question from WikiCamps. Instead of mapping every camp, it lets farmers, station owners and other landholders list sites you book and pay for in advance, from bush tent spots to glamping and caravan pitches. It has 4.8 stars from more than 22,000 Australian ratings.

The app keeps your booked trips and messages with hosts available offline. It is not built for free camps, rest areas or dump points, so it is a companion to a camping app on a long trip rather than a replacement.
Choose it over WikiCamps for a planned weekend somewhere you could not otherwise camp.

sections.heading: 6. ExplorOz Traveller: the outback alternative
body: For 4WD touring, ExplorOz Traveller can stand in for both a camping app and a paper map. Its EOTopo topographic map covers the whole country with named tracks and trails, and the developer lists more than 100,000 places including camps, fuel and water.

The app costs A$59.99 and offline use needs one in-app option: EOTopo at A$59.99 a year, the 2026 edition at A$79.99 for four years, or Pro Access at A$99.99 a year with live tracking and GPX export. Once the map is on the phone, it works without signal anywhere in Australia.
Choose it over WikiCamps if your route leaves the bitumen for days at a time. For coastal and highway trips it is more app, and more cost, than you need.
tips: Topo map of all of Australia

sections.heading: When WikiCamps is still the better choice
body: If you travel on Android, AussieCamps is not an option and WikiCamps remains a strong choice alongside CAMPS and CamperMate. If recent first-hand reviews matter most to you, for instance on whether a free camp floods or how busy it gets in school holidays, the 1.3 million reviews WikiCamps reports are a depth of comment that is hard to match.

A single A$9.99 for years of use is also hard to beat on cost. The developer's help centre acknowledges that many recent reviews relate to the move to the rebuilt app, and updates are still arriving, so read the latest App Store reviews before deciding.

sections.heading: How we compared them
body: Each app was checked on the Australian App Store on 20 October 2026 for price, in-app purchases, rating and latest version, and against the developer's own pages for data sources and offline behaviour. WikiCamps details come from its website and help centre. Where we quote a count or a discount, it is the developer's own figure.
We make AussieCamps and it is paid for by the Pass. No other app here paid to be included. If something has changed since we checked, tell us through the support page and we will correct it.

faq: What is a good alternative to WikiCamps?

It depends on what you want to change. AussieCamps uses official park and road authority data with every place detail available offline on iPhone, CAMPS lists sites its own team has checked, and CamperMate is free and also covers New Zealand.
Is there a free alternative to WikiCamps?

CamperMate is free with no in-app purchases on the Australian App Store. Hipcamp is free to download, but you pay each host for a booking. AussieCamps is a free download, though its campground, rest area and dump point data needs the Pass.
Is WikiCamps still worth it in 2026?

For many travellers, yes: A$9.99 once per platform buys a community database its website puts at more than 65,000 sites, with no subscription. Version 6 changed some features, so read recent App Store reviews before you buy.
Does WikiCamps have ads?
Yes. The App Store lists advertising, and the developer says a small number of ads appear in the reviews, fees and photos sections. It has said it is considering a paid option to remove them.

campermate-alternatives.title: 5 Best CamperMate Alternatives in 2026 for Australia
campermate-alternatives.description: Five alternatives to CamperMate for Australian road trips, compared on price, where the listings come from and what still works out of signal.
campermate-alternatives.imageAlt: Backpacker campervan parked on a coastal street in Australia
campermate-alternatives.intro: CamperMate is free, covers Australia and New Zealand and speaks 27 languages, which is why so many campervan travellers install it first. When it is not enough, the better replacement depends on what was missing. We make AussieCamps, which is why it heads this list. Each entry says when it beats CamperMate and when it does not. Everything below was checked on 20 October 2026.

sections.heading: What CamperMate does well, and where people want more
body: CamperMate costs nothing, has no in-app purchases on the Australian App Store and lists more than 70,000 points of interest by the developer's count, from free camps and holiday parks to dump stations, toilets and wifi. Maps and key information can be saved for use out of signal, and version 5.8 added a satellite view that works with downloaded offline maps.

Its listings grow from traveller reviews, photos and suggested places, and the app shows ads, takes bookings and lists campervan hire companies and holiday park groups among its partners. Travellers who move on usually want one of four things: listings that start from the land manager rather than other users, sites an editor has visited, more reviews from people who stayed last week, or a way to book private land. Some App Store reviews from May to August 2026 reported campsites failing to load; updates since then have reworked the map and offline data, so check the latest reviews.
tips: Listings built and updated by travellers

sections.heading: 2. WikiCamps Australia: more reviews for a one-off price
body: WikiCamps works on the same community principle as CamperMate but on a larger scale for Australia, with more than 65,000 sites and 1.3 million reviews by the developer's figures. Version 6, released in late 2024, changed several features, so read recent App Store reviews before buying. A separate app, bought separately, covers New Zealand.

body: CAMPS is built on a different idea from CamperMate: a team that has been visiting and checking sites since 1992, more than 16,000 campsites, and a promise of no paid listings. Users add reviews on top of that base.

Everything is open for a 7-day trial, after which the app costs A$14.99 a year. That includes downloadable offline maps with site details, live fuel prices, trip planning and booking. It runs on phones and tablets, with no laptop version.
tips: A$14.99 a year after the trial

sections.heading: 4. Hipcamp: for nights you book in advance
body: CamperMate shows you holiday parks and free camps; Hipcamp shows you private land you can book. Landholders list tent sites, glamping and caravan spots on farms, stations and vineyards, and you pay the host through the app. Its rating, 4.8 from more than 22,000 Australian ratings, is the highest of the apps compared here.

Booked trips and conversations with hosts stay available offline. It is not built for free camps, rest areas or dump points, so on a long campervan trip it complements a camping app rather than replacing one.

body: Full Range Camping, previously called FreeRange Camping, lists more than 11,000 camping spots and businesses. The app is free, and Premium membership, listed at A$49.99 a year or A$99.99 for life, unlocks offline listings, weather radar and member discounts the company says reach 30 per cent at some campgrounds. On 20 October 2026 its website said Premium memberships were currently unavailable while the app's mapping software is updated, so confirm it is open again first.

It also includes house sitting and work exchange listings, which can matter more than the directory on a trip measured in months. For a two-week campervan holiday, CamperMate or WikiCamps will usually cover more ground.

sections.heading: Travelling Australia and New Zealand on one trip
body: One reason to stay with CamperMate is that a single free app covers both countries. None of the alternatives here covers New Zealand in the same app: WikiCamps sells a separate New Zealand app, and our New Zealand app is KiwiCamping.
If your trip crosses the Tasman, keeping CamperMate for the second country while using a dedicated app for the longer leg is a sensible split.

body: We checked each app's Australian App Store listing on 20 October 2026 for price, in-app purchases, rating and version, then read the developer's own site for data sources and offline behaviour. CamperMate's ownership and partners come from its terms and about pages, and review themes come from its most recent Australian App Store reviews.
AussieCamps is ours and is paid for by the Pass. No app paid to appear here. If a detail has changed, tell us through the support page and we will fix it.

faq: What is better than CamperMate?

It depends on what you want that CamperMate does not give you. AussieCamps uses park agency and road authority data with every place detail available offline on iPhone, WikiCamps Australia has 1.3 million traveller reviews by its own count for A$9.99 once, and CAMPS lists sites its own team has checked.
Is CamperMate free?
Yes. As of October 2026 it is free to download with no in-app purchases on the Australian App Store. It shows ads and offers bookings and deals from partners.
Does CamperMate work offline?
Partly. You can download maps and key information for use without signal, and version 5.8 added a satellite view that works with those downloaded maps.
Is there one app for camping in Australia and New Zealand?
CamperMate covers both countries in one free app. WikiCamps sells separate apps for each country, and AussieCamps and KiwiCamping are separate iPhone apps for Australia and New Zealand.

best-fuel-price-apps-australia.title: Best Fuel Price Apps in Australia 2026: 7 Compared for Road Trips
best-fuel-price-apps-australia.description: Petrol Spy, FuelCheck, Servo Saver, FuelWatch and more compared state by state, with where each gets its prices and which to use on an interstate road trip.
best-fuel-price-apps-australia.imageAlt: Outback roadhouse fuel stop at Cadney Homestead on the Stuart Highway
best-fuel-price-apps-australia.intro: Every state and the Northern Territory now make stations report their prices, though the ACT does not, and each publishes them its own way, so the right fuel app depends on where you are driving. We make AussieCamps, which does not show fuel prices, so it is not ranked here. These are the apps we would use ourselves, checked on 20 October 2026.

sections.heading: The short answer
body: For an interstate road trip, Petrol Spy is the app here that pulls official prices from the most states into one map, and it is free. Inside one state, the government's own tool is the cleanest source: FuelCheck in New South Wales and the ACT, FuelCheck TAS in Tasmania, Servo Saver in Victoria, FuelWatch in Western Australia and MyFuel NT in the Northern Territory.

Queensland and South Australia have no official consumer app; their reporting schemes feed private apps instead, including Petrol Spy. If you are an NRMA member, the My NRMA app adds a per-litre discount at participating stations on top of whatever price you find.

sections.heading: 1. Petrol Spy: one map for most of the country
body: Petrol Spy shows real-time prices for Queensland, South Australia, New South Wales, Western Australia, Tasmania and the Northern Territory, drawing on official feeds such as FuelCheck and FuelWatch and on Queensland's reporting scheme. It has more App Store ratings than any other app here, about 185,000 averaging 4.8, and users report prices too.

Its listing still describes Victorian prices as user-submitted, even though Victoria now runs mandatory reporting through Servo Saver, so in Victoria compare it with the official app. Price cycle graphs for eight capital cities help you judge whether to fill up today or wait. The app is free with ads; Premium removes them for A$2.89 a year or A$14.99 once.
What we like: one app across state borders, cycle graphs and lots of users reporting prices. What to weigh: advertising in the free version, and a last update in July 2025.
tips: Best single app for interstate trips
Free, or A$2.89 a year without ads

sections.heading: 2. FuelCheck: the official source in New South Wales
body: The NSW Government's FuelCheck app lists over 2,300 service stations in New South Wales and about 60 in the ACT, with prices uploaded by the stations themselves. It is free, carries no ads and is rated 4.8 from about 123,000 Australian ratings.

Beyond the map, it sends price-drop alerts for favourite stations, finds the cheapest stations along a route with My Trip, and shows trends such as the cheapest day of the cycle. You can report a price that does not match the bowser.
What to weigh: it stops at the border, so an interstate trip needs a second app.

sections.heading: 3. Servo Saver: Victoria's official prices
body: Since mandatory reporting started in Victoria, stations must report price changes within 30 minutes and set the next day's maximum price in advance; it applies from 6am for 24 hours. Servo Saver, inside the free Service Victoria app, shows today's prices, and from 4pm it also shows tomorrow's cap, so you can decide where to fill.
It is ad-free and official. The catch for visitors is that it lives inside a broader government app, and it covers Victoria only.

sections.heading: 4. FuelWatch: plan around tomorrow's price in Western Australia
body: Western Australia has the longest-running scheme. Retailers submit tomorrow's price by 2pm, it is published from 2:30pm, and it is fixed for 24 hours from 6am the next day. Knowing tomorrow's price is useful on a long WA leg, where you may pass one roadhouse in a day.
FuelWatch runs on the WA Government website and in the ServiceWA app rather than as its own app.

sections.heading: 5. FuelCheck TAS: Tasmania's version
body: Tasmania uses the same FuelCheck system as New South Wales, in a separate free app covering more than 200 stations. Stations can also report when they have run out of a fuel, which matters on the island's quieter roads. It has a 4.7 rating from about 3,500 Australian ratings.

sections.heading: 6. Fuel Map Australia: a simple map from the WikiCamps team
body: Fuel Map Australia combines a crowd-sourced station database with official real-time prices for Western Australia, New South Wales and Queensland, including WA's next-day prices. It also keeps a fuel log. It is free with ads, or A$2.99 once to remove them.
What to weigh: its last update was in October 2022, and outside those three states the prices depend on users.
tips: Official prices in WA, NSW and QLD

sections.heading: 7. My NRMA: a discount rather than a price map
body: My NRMA is a membership app, not a price comparison tool. Members show a code at participating Ampol Foodary stations for 5 cents a litre off premium fuel and 4 cents off regular. The NRMA sells the discount through My NRMA Rewards, at A$5 a month after a free first month, so work out whether your fills over a trip cover the fee.
tips: 4 to 5 cents a litre at participating Ampol

sections.heading: Fuel is the biggest cost you can plan
body: On most road trips fuel costs more than campsites, and the cheapest litre comes from planning the stops rather than from any single app. Knowing the distance of each leg tells you which towns you must fill in and where you can afford to wait for a cheaper price.

AussieCamps does not show fuel prices, but trips in AussieCamps, part of the Pass, show the driving distance and time for every leg between the stops in your trip, which is the number a fuel plan starts from. Pair it with one of the apps above for the price, and fill up before long remote stretches whatever the price.
tips: Plan the legs, then the price

sections.heading: How we chose
body: We checked each app's Australian App Store listing on 20 October 2026, and each state's reporting rules on its official government page. Ratings are rounded to the nearest hundred or thousand. Prices you see in any app are reported by stations or users and can lag behind the bowser, so check the pump before you fill.
tips: The bowser price is what you pay

faq: What is the best app for cheap fuel in Australia?

For travel across state lines, Petrol Spy shows official prices from most states in one free app. Within one state, the government tool is the cleanest source: FuelCheck in NSW and the ACT, Servo Saver in Victoria, FuelWatch in WA, FuelCheck TAS and MyFuel NT.
Is there a fuel price app for Victoria?
Yes. Servo Saver in the free Service Victoria app shows prices that stations must report within 30 minutes, and from 4pm it shows the next day's maximum price.
Can you see tomorrow's petrol prices in Australia?
In Western Australia and Victoria, yes. FuelWatch publishes WA's next-day prices from 2:30pm, and Servo Saver shows Victoria's next-day caps from 4pm. Both apply from 6am for 24 hours.
Which fuel app should I use in Queensland?

Queensland has no government app. Its reporting scheme sends station prices to private apps, and Queensland Treasury lists those that receive the data, including Petrol Spy, FuelMap, MotorMouth, Pumped and RACQ Fuel and Deals.

best-road-trip-planner-apps-australia.title: Best Road Trip Planner Apps for Australia 2026: 6 Compared
best-road-trip-planner-apps-australia.description: AussieCamps, Google Maps, Apple Maps, Wanderlog, WikiCamps and ExplorOz compared on stops, distances, offline use and price for an Australian road trip.
best-road-trip-planner-apps-australia.imageAlt: Roadside tourist map of the Stuart Highway route through South Australia
best-road-trip-planner-apps-australia.intro: Planning an Australian road trip means two different jobs: deciding where you will stop and sleep, and getting from one stop to the next. No single app does both best. We make AussieCamps, and it is first here because it is built for the first job. Every app below was checked on 20 October 2026, with notes on when another one is the better pick.

sections.heading: Quick comparison
body: Navigation apps are excellent at the drive itself and not designed to show where you can stay overnight. Most trip planners are the reverse. Most travellers use one of each, and the table shows where each app sits.
