sections.heading: 1. AussieCamps: plan where you will stop and sleep
body: AussieCamps treats a trip as a list of places rather than a line on a map. You add campgrounds, caravan parks, rest areas or any saved place as stops, put them in order, and see the driving distance and time for each leg and for the whole journey. Each stop can carry an arrival date, and the app shows the forecast for arrival dates within the forecast range, which is the detail that changes plans most often in Australia.

Around the route it keeps a trip checklist and packing list, notes, a cover photo, and visited progress as you go. A trip can be shared or synced to your calendar with its stops and dates. Because the place directory lives on the phone, details for every stop stay readable out of signal, while the map, directions and forecasts need a connection. When it is time to drive, directions open in Apple Maps or Google Maps.

The download is free, as are bookable hotels, motels, B&Bs, holiday parks and tours from BookEasy. Trips, collections and the campground, rest area and dump point data need the AussieCamps Pass, sold as a weekly subscription or a one-off lifetime purchase, with in-app purchases listed at A$2.99 to A$9.99 on the Australian App Store.
Choose something else if you need turn-by-turn navigation inside the planner, if you are on Android, or if your trip is mostly cities, where a general itinerary app fits better.
tips: Stops, dates and forecasts in one plan
Navigation hands off to Apple or Google Maps

sections.heading: 2. Google Maps: the navigator most people already have
body: Google Maps is free, covers Australia well and gives live traffic and turn-by-turn directions. For planning, it allows up to 9 stops on a route, counting the final destination, which is enough for a day's drive but not for a two-week loop, so long trips end up split across several routes or saved lists.

Download the areas you will drive through before you leave. Google's help pages say offline driving directions work only when the whole route is inside a downloaded area, offline maps expire unless updated, and traffic is not available offline.

sections.heading: 3. Apple Maps: the iPhone default, with more stops
body: Apple Maps is built into every iPhone and its support guide allows a multi-stop driving route with up to 14 stops, which goes further than Google Maps for a single route. Offline maps can be downloaded, and Apple says they support turn-by-turn driving directions without a connection.

Apple notes that offline maps are not available in every country or region, so download a test area before you rely on it. Like Google Maps, it plans the drive rather than the nights: it will not tell you which rest areas allow an overnight stop.

sections.heading: 4. Wanderlog: an itinerary builder for mixed trips
body: Wanderlog is a general travel planner with a 4.9 rating from more than 5,000 Australian ratings. Its App Store listing says you can add unlimited stops for free and see times and distances between places, which suits a trip that mixes drives with days in Sydney or Melbourne and flights between.

Its help centre, though not its store listing, lists offline access to trip plans and route optimisation as Pro features. The Australian App Store lists several Pro prices, from A$50.99 to A$99.99 a year and A$25.99 a month, so check the price shown to you. It has no dedicated camping or rest area directory and no in-app navigation.

sections.heading: 5. WikiCamps Australia: trip planning inside a camping app
body: WikiCamps includes a Trip Planner: you create a trip, add sections such as regions or days, then places and notes, and drag a progress bar as you travel. Enter your vehicle's fuel use and a price per litre and it estimates fuel use and cost between the places in your trip.

It costs A$9.99 once per platform, and up to three planned trips can be downloaded for use without signal. Its help pages do not mention drive times per leg, so pair it with a navigation app for timings.

sections.heading: 6. ExplorOz Traveller: route planning off the bitumen
body: For outback and 4WD trips, ExplorOz Traveller plans and navigates on its own EOTopo topographic map, which shows named roads and 4WD tracks, with track access notes. With EOTopo access downloaded, it works across Australia with no signal.

The app is A$59.99, and offline use needs EOTopo at A$59.99 a year, the 2026 edition at A$79.99 for four years, or Pro Access at A$99.99 a year. That is far more than a sealed-road trip needs, and exactly what a Simpson Desert crossing does.
tips: Offline topo map with EOTopo access

sections.heading: Also worth knowing
body: TripIt organises bookings rather than routes: forward confirmation emails and it builds an itinerary with flights, hire cars and accommodation, available offline. Polarsteps plans and then tracks your route automatically, which suits travellers who want a record of the trip as much as a plan.
We left out Roadtrippers, a popular planner in North America, because its App Store listing says it is designed for road trips in the USA and Canada only.
tips: Roadtrippers is USA and Canada only

sections.heading: How we compared them
body: Each app's price, in-app purchases, rating and limits were checked on the Australian App Store and in the developer's own help pages on 20 October 2026. Stop limits are the ones the developers publish. We looked at what matters on an Australian road trip: how far apart the stops are, whether you can see where to sleep, and what still works out of signal.
Our own app earns its money from the Pass, and none of the others paid for a place here. Tell us through the support page if anything has changed.

faq: What is the best app to plan a road trip in Australia?

Use two kinds of app. A planner such as AussieCamps decides the stops, nights and dates, with distance and drive time for each leg, and a navigation app such as Google Maps or Apple Maps handles the drive itself. For remote 4WD tracks, ExplorOz Traveller does both on its own maps.
How many stops can you add in Google Maps?

Up to 9 stops on one route, counting the final destination, according to Google's help pages. Apple Maps allows up to 14 stops on a driving route. Longer trips need splitting into several routes or a dedicated trip planner.
Does Roadtrippers work in Australia?
Its App Store listing says it is designed for road trips in the USA and Canada only, so it is not a good fit for Australia.
Can I plan a road trip offline in Australia?

Partly. Google Maps and Apple Maps can navigate within downloaded areas, AussieCamps keeps place details on the phone with the Pass, and WikiCamps keeps up to three downloaded trips. Live traffic, forecasts and new routes still need signal in most apps.

best-free-camping-apps-australia.description: Which apps find free camps in Australia, which cost nothing to use, and which charge for the data, compared with prices checked in October 2026.
best-free-camping-apps-australia.imageAlt: Picnic table under the trees at Firth Park Campground in Wombat State Forest, Victoria
best-free-camping-apps-australia.intro: A free camping app can mean two things: an app that costs nothing, or an app that finds places where camping costs nothing. Few apps are both, and the difference decides what you will pay. We make AussieCamps, which is free to download but charges for its camping data, and we have still put it first for the reasons below. If you want to pay nothing at all, CamperMate is the app to start with. Prices were checked on 20 October 2026.

sections.heading: 1. AussieCamps: official camping data, with the Pass
body: AussieCamps draws its campgrounds, rest areas, dump points, drinking water and toilets from state park agencies, road authorities and public facility datasets, and lets you filter places by cost. That matters for free camping because the rules sit with the land manager: those places are different things, and the app keeps campgrounds, national parks and roadside rest areas as separate categories, with each place's fees listed. The current data has 1,838 campgrounds and 5,552 rest areas.

It is first here because free camps tend to be where the signal is weakest, and its place details are stored on the phone with no region to download. The map, directions and weather still need a connection.

It is not free to use for camping. The download, map and search are free, as are bookable hotels, motels, holiday parks and tours from BookEasy, but campgrounds, rest areas, dump points and water need the AussieCamps Pass, a weekly subscription or one-off lifetime purchase with in-app purchases from A$2.99 to A$9.99. It is iPhone only and has no traveller reviews, which free campers often rely on to hear whether a site is still open.

sections.heading: 2. CamperMate: free, with no in-app purchases
body: CamperMate is free with no in-app purchases on the Australian App Store and lists free camps alongside holiday parks, dump stations and toilets across Australia and New Zealand. Travellers add reviews and photos and suggest places, alongside partner listings, and maps and key information can be downloaded for use without signal.
It is supported by advertising, bookings and deals, so paid options appear next to free ones. For a traveller who wants to spend nothing on apps, it is a good first install.

sections.heading: 3. Full Range Camping: a free directory with a Free Camps category
body: Full Range Camping, formerly FreeRange Camping, keeps its directory of camping spots and businesses free to browse and has a Free Camps category. Its app uses online maps unless you have Premium, which adds offline caching, weather radar and member discounts.
Premium is listed on the App Store at A$49.99 a year or A$99.99 for life, but when we checked, the company's website said new Premium memberships were unavailable while its app mapping is updated.

sections.heading: 4. WikiCamps Australia: not free, but the free camps are well reviewed
body: WikiCamps costs A$9.99 once per platform, so it is not a free app. It earns a place because of its free camp filter and its reviews, 1.3 million by its own count, which tell you whether a free spot is quiet, crowded or closed.
Offline use needs the main Australia content downloaded first, with up to three planned trips saved for use without signal.

sections.heading: 5. CAMPS Australia Wide: low cost, checked sites
body: CAMPS lists more than 16,000 campsites that Camps Australia Wide says its team has checked in person, with no paid listings. It is free for 7 days and then A$14.99 a year; the company retired its free app access in December 2024, so there is no free tier after the trial.

sections.heading: 6. Free government tools from the land managers
body: The agencies that run campgrounds publish their own maps and booking pages, free to use. They are the place to confirm fees, bookings and closures, even if an app found the site.

Free does not always mean no booking. In Queensland, every camp in a national park, state forest or recreation area needs a paid permit booked before arrival. Almost all of Victoria's state forest campgrounds are free and cannot be booked, and Main Roads WA allows stays of up to 24 hours only at its rest areas signed for it. The guide to whether free camping is legal sets out each state.

faq: What is the best free camping app in Australia?

If the app itself must cost nothing, CamperMate is free with no in-app purchases and lists free camps among its places. AussieCamps is free to download but needs the Pass for its official campground and rest area data, and WikiCamps costs A$9.99 once per platform.
Is there a free app for free camps in Australia?

Yes. CamperMate is free, and Full Range Camping's directory, including its Free Camps category, is free to browse. Government park and forest agencies also publish their campgrounds for free, though many of those sites charge a camping fee.
Do free campsites still need booking?

Sometimes. Queensland needs a paid permit for every camp in its parks and forests, NSW National Parks charges a booking fee even where camping is free, and almost all Victorian state forest campgrounds are free and cannot be booked. Check the land manager for each site.
Can you sleep at rest areas in Australia?

Only where the road authority or sign allows it. Queensland lets vehicles stop at rest areas for up to 20 hours unless signed otherwise, and Main Roads WA allows up to 24 hours only at rest areas signed for it. Read the sign before you stay.
